Under normal circumstances, I would’ve scoffed at the difference between us.
Even so, I had a gut feeling I wouldn’t be able to dodge all their attacks.
And while my body refused to move, one ridiculous thought crossed my mind.
If I level up, would it heal me even if my limbs got cut off?
Fortunately, I didn’t have to worry about that unpleasant first experience—the sort only someone like Cheongpung might enjoy.
The next moment, an enormous rush of air sounded from somewhere and swept my worries away.
Whoooosh!
It happened in the blink of an eye.
A huge shadow rose over the shoulders of the enemies charging toward me.
With it came a two-section staff, big and beautiful just as its name suggested, cleaving through the air like lightning.
Craaaack!
If anyone ever asked whether I’d seen five heads knocked flying with a single swing of a bat, I could nod without hesitation.
I could even name the top prospect who’d tear through the modern Major Leagues, now a playground for Awakened Ones.
Of course, that lunatic hulk would introduce himself before anyone else got the chance.
Just like now.
“Taishan!
Came!
Saw!
Hit!”
“Well done!
Now, Body Slam!”
Starting with Namho, perched on the shoulder of Taishan—who had just delivered a line to make Julius Caesar weep—familiar faces burst onto the scene like streaks of light.
“Young Master!
No, Benefactor!
No, Pavilion Master!”
Shhk!
Ju Hwaran split an enemy’s skull while blurting out a three-step change of address that even Transformers would’ve had trouble keeping up with.
“Fools!
You dare try to harm the Captain?
Your courage is admirable, but first you’ll have to get past me—the Captain’s right arm and heart!
I, Hyuk Mu—whoa, shit!”
Clang!
Hyuk Mujin had charged in with a grand entrance, only to scramble backward when his opponent’s counterattack proved stronger than he’d expected.
“Uh, does that guy know how to fight with his mouth shut?”
“You should try shutting yours first.”
Thrust!
Song Ilseom saved Hyuk Mujin and cut down the remaining enemies in a flash.
And... wait, who was that black, shaggy old guy?
“The Seven Masters of the Black Horse?”
The name slipped out before I knew it.
The middle-aged man, a former mounted bandit, twisted his already fearsome face.
“Not Black Horse—White Horse!
I’m Ma Junggeol, eldest of the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang!
Who do you think I went through all this shit for?
And you forgot me...!”
“Lower your voice.
While I’m asking nicely.”
At Ju Hwaran’s chilling warning, Ma Junggeol clamped his mouth shut.
A laugh escaped me before I knew it.
It was just good to see them.
To know we hadn’t lost anyone.
And...
Because I could see the one last person I’d thought I’d never meet again.
“You made it?”
Sama Pyo, who I hadn’t even seen arrive, shrugged.
“Am I late?”
No.
Not at all.

chapters.title: Chapter 1057
paragraphs: No further surprises came in the great battle that day across the vast snowfield.

Just a few shichen earlier, the forces of Dark Heaven had flaunted their overwhelming might. Now they were no more than candles before the wind, while the allied forces—led by Supreme Peak masters and wave after wave of reinforcements—were like a tremendous storm.
A storm of steel and killing intent, tearing through everything in its path.
Crraack!
Thud! Shhk!
Fountains of blood erupted on every side.
With thick blood mist draped over them like cloaks, the allies charged, stabbing and cutting down every enemy in their path without the slightest hesitation.
An eye for an eye.
A tooth for a tooth.
And death repaid with death. That was the law of this world—of Murim—and the very essence of war.
“Heaven above and earth below, all demons—”
Thwack!
A guard’s spear pierced a cultist’s arm. An arrow and a sword from somewhere tore through his face and chest.
Before the cultists could finish their eight-character doctrine, they fell, spraying blood. The allied forces trampled over their bodies and tightened the cordon around the vast slaughterhouse.
Quickly. Ferociously.
Against Dark Heaven’s cultists, who had lost their reason, persuasion and taking prisoners were luxuries. The immense sacrifices the allies had suffered here today had made them forget mercy.
That was truest of the band who had joined last, yet were now sweeping through the enemy ranks at the very front.
Shh-shh-shhk!
Blood-soaked robes fluttered.

They plunged straight into the heart of the enemy lines as if they cared nothing for their lives. Their movements were elusive as the wind, and the sword light surging from the old man’s blade at their head was cruelly dazzling.
Boom!
A thunderous blast shook the earth.
Flesh mangled beyond recognition and blood flew in every direction.
Where the Force had passed, nothing remained.
Nothing but blood and death.
And the tremendous roar of the allied forces as they crashed into the broken enemy formation and crushed it completely.
“Waaah!”
“Charge! Charge!”
“Don’t leave a single one alive!”
In that moment, the allied forces were a single wave, though each part had a different color.
The Embroidered Uniform Guard charged in orderly ranks, keeping their composure amid the chaos.
The soldiers and martial artists of Gansu followed behind them, squeezing out their last strength.
Then there were the Zhongnan Sect Disciples, far fewer than at the start—and the mysterious mounted fighters who had appeared out of nowhere to join the allies.
Thud-thud-thud-thud!
The ground shook as if an earthquake had struck.
Deafening shouts echoed without end. A forest of steel filled the land, engulfing the invaders and blooming with countless flowers and branches.
Red flowers made of blood, white branches made of bone.
That was how the long, brutal battle ended.
Another half day passed. Of the fully thirty thousand Dark Heaven cultists, not one still stood on the battlefield of his own will.
Not one.
In modern military terminology, annihilation means the loss of combat effectiveness.
Troops, equipment, supplies, morale, and so on.
Generally, if at least thirty percent of a fighting force has been killed or wounded and the survivors’ will falters, the force is judged incapable of continuing to fight—and considered annihilated.
But here in Murim, what lay before Jin Taekyung at this moment was different.
Annihilation.
The word meant exactly what it said.
No, perhaps even that word wasn’t enough.
Killing. Massacre.
Or...
...Slaughter.
The word he couldn’t bring himself to say lingered on the tip of his tongue. Taekyung looked around, his gaze heavy.
Red. Everything in sight was stained red.
The once-white snowfield. The faces of corpses submerged in pools of blood, their eyes wide open.
And the bloodshot eyes searching for enemies who might have survived, picking through rivers of blood and mountains of corpses.
Shhk!
A sword came down hard, piercing the chest of an enemy who had been writhing among the countless dead.
A miracle wouldn’t happen twice. Having survived once was a misfortune.
If he’d died sooner, his end would have been much quicker and more peaceful.
Craack.
The blade buried deep inside him slowly twisted.
At the dreadful sound of bone and flesh being crushed—and the killing intent, even more palpable than the sound—the faces of the Fire Dragon Pavilion members beside Taekyung stiffened.
“Captain.”
“Even so, this is...”
Taekyung raised a hand to stop them before they could finish.
He knew what they wanted to say.
This wasn’t murder. It was slaughter, like butchering livestock.
Yet he also understood the feelings of those giving such a cruel end to enemies who no longer had the strength to resist.
“Wait here.”
He tossed the words to the Fire Dragon Pavilion members and slowly started walking.
One step. Then another. Unbearable fatigue washed over him with each step, but a hand reached out from somewhere and steadied him when he staggered.
“I’m pretty sure I told you to wait.”
At Taekyung’s mutter, almost spoken to himself, Sama Pyo shrugged.
“Well, I didn’t hear you.”
“You’ve heard me now. Step back.”
“I can’t do that.”
“That’s an order.”
“An order? So that’s how you’re going to play it?”
“Yeah.”
Taekyung’s voice was firmer than ever. Sama Pyo’s answer was just as firm.
“Fine. Then as of this moment, I’m leaving the Fire Dragon Pavilion.”
Taekyung’s eyes widened. Sama Pyo gave him a faint smile.
“What? Didn’t see that coming?”
“I’ve enjoyed our time together, Pavilion Master. But this is where we part ways.”
He met Taekyung’s gaze calmly and added, “I can’t keep bringing trouble to you or anyone else. Whatever happens, I’ll have to bear it alone.”
He knew why Taekyung, who had been at his limit for a long time, was still clinging to consciousness.
And he knew how great a danger might be waiting at the end of the road he now had to walk alone.
He could remain calm because he had already made up his mind.
“Whatever happens, don’t get involved. And if something should happen to me...”
His voice trailed off. His gaze shifted toward Taishan—and Taekyung, who had been watching him, cut in.
“Nope.”
“What?”
“I said no, asshole. Look after your own man. Don’t dump him on someone who’s already got enough on his plate.”
Sama Pyo fell silent for a moment. Then he understood what Taekyung meant and let out a short laugh.
“You’re right. I have to look after him to the very end. I will.”
If I can. If I can survive, like you said.
Swallowing the words he couldn’t bring himself to say, Sama Pyo set off alone.
Taekyung watched him go, then suddenly spoke.
“Something just occurred to me... Do you remember the day we left the Jin Family of Taiyuan?”
Of course Sama Pyo did.
It had been recent—not years or months ago, but barely more than a month.
And he could guess why Taekyung had brought it up.
“Of course. Right before we left for the west, Elder Namho and Taishan came looking for me.”
That night, Sama Pyo had been reading a secret letter from Gansu.
He had already read it, then read it again. Over and over, even as the two approached his door.
“You’re usually punctual to the second, but that day you dragged your feet. Like you were waiting for someone to come looking for you.”
Sama Pyo stopped walking at Taekyung’s quiet remark.
“I had a lot on my mind that day.”
“Elder Namho’s old, but he’s a fine agent. His nose is pretty sharp for his age, too.”
“True. Though his hearing’s bad, so he talks loudly.”
A giant nearly nine feet tall who made the ground shake just by walking, and an old man who talked a lot and had a booming voice.
They stood out wherever they went, and there was no missing the sound of them.
Sama Pyo had heard them that night too, alone in his quarters with the secret letter.
“You planned it, didn’t you? From the start.”
“No. Not at all.”
A blatant lie.
Sama Pyo had been waiting there.
Waiting for his oldest friend, who would come looking for him before anyone else.
No—for the old Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent who was always at Taishan’s side.
Deep down, he had hoped Namho would notice at least something of the secret Sama Pyo couldn’t say aloud.
That he would take it as a warning.
“Why? Why go that far?”
At Taekyung’s quiet question from behind him, Sama Pyo resumed walking.
“Even so... he’s my father.”
He had wanted to believe in him until the very end, whatever it took.
But when that trust was betrayed, he didn’t want the people beside him put in danger.
So he had deliberately left a clue as a warning. Before he could bring himself to report his father’s suspicious actions, he wanted them to become suspicious on their own.
Even if they suspected Sama Pyo too, he didn’t care, as long as it kept everyone safe.
He was used to being suspected and hated.
That was what it meant to live as the blood relative of Sima Gong, the Black Night King, and the Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate.
And yet it was strange.
Even after Namho’s gaze toward him had grown sharper and more searching, Taekyung hadn’t said a word.
Not once, even now.
“Then why didn’t you ask me anything? Not once, all this time?”
The question had been circling in Sama Pyo’s mind for so long. The moment he finally voiced it, a short answer came from behind him without a hint of hesitation.
“Even so, we’re friends.”
The answer sent a sharp tingle through Sama Pyo’s chest.
“Shit, I don’t know. You look dark and gloomy on the outside, but... I kept wanting to trust you. Even as everything went more and more to shit, I still wanted to.”
Sama Pyo couldn’t say anything.
He clenched his teeth against the heat rising in his eyes and kept walking, his steps unsteady.
Taekyung’s voice reached him from somewhere far behind.
“Don’t die. That’s an order.”
Sama Pyo didn’t answer that gentler-than-ever command.
He kept walking toward the band still moving through the ruined battlefield, slaughtering the enemies who had survived.
Or, to be exact, toward the old man at their center.
Splash.
At last, he stopped, sending ripples through a pool of blood.
Sama Pyo took a deep breath. The stench and reek of blood were foul enough to make him gag, but his heart was strangely calm and still.
As calm and still as the expression of the old man before him, who gazed at his enemy’s son with eyes too deep to read.
“This junior, Sama Pyo, pays his respects to the Sect Leader of the great Kongtong Sect.”
At that moment—
Shwaaah.
Killing intent, immense enough to be terrifying, surged up from every direction and pressed down on Sama Pyo’s entire body.

chapters.title: Chapter 1058
paragraphs: It happened in an instant.
The Blood-Clad Men, drenched head to toe in blood as they slaughtered their enemies, surrounded Sama Pyo and unleashed a terrifying wave of killing intent.
Shhhhhh.
There were about a hundred of them.
Their qi was so fierce that the lingering heat of the battlefield seemed to freeze. The air shifted all at once, and I could feel it clearly.
Even from thirty-odd yards away, where I’d stopped to watch.
And so could the Fire Dragon Pavilion members farther off, waiting as ordered with no idea what was happening.
“My Lord! It’s dangerous!”
The killing intent was so thick it seemed to erase the distance between them.
Taishan sensed Sama Pyo’s danger at once. With an urgent shout, he launched himself forward—only to be stopped in his tracks.
By me.
“What do you think you’re doing, Pavilion Master!”
He practically growled the words, his fighting spirit blazing.
I’d never seen him like this before.
But I couldn’t back down either.
This wasn’t some damn twist of fate or stroke of bad luck. Sama Pyo had made his own choice.
“Don’t go. Not yet.”
“Taishan will not obey such an unreasonable order!”
“I’m not ordering you. I’m asking. Just like Sama Pyo asked me not to interfere.”
Taishan’s huge eyes wavered.
The Fire Dragon Pavilion members caught up, but before any of them could speak, Namho cut in with an unusually subdued voice.
Though perched on Taishan’s shoulders, he didn’t look especially authoritative.
“I know how you feel, but now isn’t the time.”
“Namho, but—”
“Oh, look at this angry bull!”
Smack!
Namho landed a sharp slap on Taishan’s forehead and gave him a stern scolding.
“Was it not enough to let sentiment blind you? Have you gone deaf too? Did you even hear what the Pavilion Master said?”
He was right.
I’d told Taishan clearly.
Not yet... Don’t go yet.
That’s right. Not yet.
I murmured it to myself and patted Taishan’s shoulder as, after a moment’s struggle, he lowered his two-section staff.
Then I turned toward the hundred figures radiating killing intent.
The Blood-Clad Men—or rather, the Kongtong Sect Disciples.
At their center stood an old man, watching Sama Pyo with deep, unreadable eyes.
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon.
The Sect Leader of the Kongtong Sect, one of the Nine Sects and One Gang. The greatest martial artist in Gansu.
And...
Another man bent on revenge, betrayed by those he’d trusted as allies and forced to lose countless Disciples.
Whoooosh.
His sleeves swelled with the force of his formidable internal energy.
At that moment, the emotionless, ink-black eyes—so deep their depths were impossible to discern—didn’t reflect Sama Pyo.
They reflected the bloodline of his enemy: a man Hyeoncheon would gladly tear to pieces.
Rumble.
The air trembled for yards around them. It was hard to breathe.
In the moment the overwhelming qi began slowly tightening around him from every direction, like the hand of an invisible giant, Sama Pyo froze. Then Perfected Being Hyeoncheon suddenly spoke.
“Lately, I keep remembering the first time I met your esteemed father, my friend. It was in the middle of the Great Faction War.”
The old Daoist had devoted his entire life to the Dao, from infancy to old age. His gentle nature had earned him the respect of many.
He had never joined the ranks of the Ten Kings, but even as Sect Leader of the renowned Kongtong Sect, he had always been humble.
Yet even the largest vessel has its limits.
“At the same time, I regretted it. I wondered if I should have killed him then and there.”
Sama Pyo said nothing to the deep sigh in Hyeoncheon’s voice.
No—he couldn’t answer.
He hadn’t told the old Daoist the truth, but Hyeoncheon had already glimpsed part of it.
He had first heard of it from a woman.

“At first, I didn’t want to believe it. I tried to convince myself it was a ploy to stir up internal strife among the survivors from Dunhuang—that we were being used as stepping-stones for an even greater scheme.”
Hyeoncheon had tried to forget what he’d heard while hiding silently in the undergrowth. But his suspicions had only deepened with each passing day.
His distrust of one man: Sima Gong, the Black Night King.
Everything, including the ominous signs he’d sensed before setting out for Dunhuang, fitted together like the teeth of a gear.
“The more I thought about it, the stranger it seemed. Every piece of information we received from the Black Dragon Demon Gate was wrong. And we were the only ones who bled.”

Kongtong Mountain, the Kongtong Sect’s home since ancient times, lay at the southeastern edge of Gansu. The Black Dragon Demon Gate’s territory, by contrast, covered the Dunhuang region in the northwest.
So the Kongtong Sect and the many sects that followed it had acted on information provided by the Black Dragon Demon Gate—and suffered a crushing defeat.
“Thousands died. In that single day.”
At the slight tremor in Hyeoncheon’s voice, the hundred Disciples surrounding Sama Pyo clenched their teeth.
How could they forget that horrific battle, which had begun like a bolt of lightning?
No. It had been a one-sided slaughter.
“Defending the city meant nothing. When that enormous army appeared out of nowhere, we couldn’t do a thing.”
The Three Elders of Tianshan.
The three old fiends from Tianshan, returned after decades away, had led the charge. Behind them came tens of thousands of cultists who knew no fear.
Neither the defenders’ unceasing volleys of arrows nor the city walls—built of solid stone coated with yellow earth—could stop them.
That immense human tide, black as night, had brought down the high walls in an instant and swept away everything in its path.
It swallowed the lives of fellow Disciples, friends, and family who had stood beside them for years.
“I would rather have fought there with them and died. Heroically, with my last breath.”
Hyeoncheon wasn’t alone in that wish. A hundred pairs of eyes, reddened and now glistening with tears, showed it.
But they had survived.
They’d had to.
If only to avenge those who had died screaming.
“So we ran away like cowards. We received unexpected help along the way and shook off our pursuers easily. The others weren’t so lucky.”
Luck wasn’t shared equally.
Thousands had died in Dunhuang alone. Those who fled in tears were still prey.
They scattered to survive, and thousands more were killed or wounded as they were hunted down.
Yet even after escaping Dark Heaven’s encirclement, Hyeoncheon and the Kongtong Sect Disciples hadn’t returned to the rear.
More precisely, they couldn’t return right away. Every one of them had been injured, some more seriously than others.

The suspicion the Grand Sorceress had planted deep in their hearts had already taken root. And as Hyeoncheon lay groaning from the severe injuries he’d suffered in battle against Dark Heaven, he suddenly realized whose familiar faces had passed through his mind.
It had happened as he hovered between life and death, vowing revenge.

They weren’t the faces of the mysterious woman behind the silver-white veil, or of the Three Elders of Tianshan and the Blood-Sword Demon Lord, who had captured and killed two Elders and hundreds of Disciples.
They belonged to the allies he’d trusted to guard their backs.
“Strange, isn’t it, my friend?”
His voice was low.
After three days at death’s door, Hyeoncheon had barely recovered from his injuries. He’d thought then:
Why?
Why, at the very moment he’d vowed revenge with the bitterness of chewing bear gall, had they come to mind?
The Black Night King, Sima Gong. The Roaring Fury Swordsman, Song Il. The Taeeul Merciless Sword, Hwangbo Eom.
And the many leaders of Gansu who were little more than the Black Dragon Demon Gate’s servants.
Why did fire rise deep in his chest whenever he recalled each face and name the woman had revealed from behind her silver-white veil?
In the end, Hyeoncheon had found an answer.
He had come here with the surviving Disciples to confirm it with his own eyes.
And now, before he could begin his revenge, a young man had come to him of his own accord.
“Boy of the Sama family.”
His way of speaking had changed.
His voice was steady, edged with iron, but cold flames burned in the old Daoist’s eyes.
“Bring me your father. There’s something I must confirm before I draw my sword.”
Rumble.
The ground trembled faintly.
Sama Pyo looked down in silence at the ripples spreading across a pool of blood. Then he raised his head, which had remained bowed all this time, and spoke.
“He’s already gone. To a distant place from which he can never return.”
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon’s eyes flew open.
So did the eyes of the Kongtong Sect Disciples surrounding Sama Pyo, their suffocating killing intent still bearing down on him.
They understood at once what he meant.
He was dead.
The Black Night King, Sima Gong.
The enemy they should have put to death with their own hands. The traitor whose crimes cried out to heaven.
And Sima Gong wasn’t the only traitor to meet that fate.
“Sect Leader!”
A grief-stricken cry rang out from somewhere.
A Kongtong Sect Disciple closed a distance of well over a hundred yards in an instant, moving like an arrow. His face was streaked with grief and fury as he threw himself down before Hyeoncheon.
“They... those men...!”
Before his cry could give way to sobs, Hyeoncheon turned.
In the distance, he saw the Zhongnan Sect’s flag rising at an angle.
Or rather, the two pieces of white cloth tied to its pole, fluttering weakly.
“A mourning flag...!”
At the anguished whisper that slipped through someone’s clenched teeth, the qi surrounding them surged violently.
The white cloth signaled someone’s death. Then there was the reaction of the Disciple who had just returned.
The meaning was clear.
The Roaring Fury Swordsman, Song Il, and the Taeeul Merciless Sword, Hwangbo Eom.
The two Zhongnan Sect traitors they’d meant to punish after Sima Gong were gone too.
Gone somewhere no movement technique could reach: the afterlife.
“Dead? You’re telling me they’re dead? Just like that?”
Grrk.
Hyeoncheon bit his lip.
The flesh split and blood flew, but that pain was nothing beside the agony in his chest, which felt ready to burst.
“How... how dare they...!”
Hyeoncheon flew into a rage.
Despite his still-healing body, his immense qi pressed down all around him. Even the Kongtong Sect Disciples nearby had to hold their breath.
Only Sama Pyo stood his ground.
“I’ll take his place.”
He barely forced the words out as he endured the Supreme Peak master’s qi with his whole body. Hyeoncheon’s gaze darkened.
“What did you say?”
“I said I’ll take his place. I’ll accept the punishment my sinful father owes for what he’s done.”
Silence fell. Sama Pyo bowed his head to everyone, Hyeoncheon included, and went on.
“I know how presumptuous that is. I know my insignificant life can’t make up for the grievances of those who are gone.”
He was right.
A person’s heart couldn’t simply be filled whenever it was emptied.
Nothing could fill a hole once it had been torn open.
You could keep putting things into it, trying to forget. Or you could look at the hole that remained no matter how much you put in and remember.
What had vanished because of a single mistake. The regret of losing it.
That was why Sama Pyo stood here. Why he wanted to walk a different path from his father.
“An eye for an eye. A tooth for a tooth. Death for death.”
In Murim, a blood debt between martial artists could only be repaid with blood.
“Strike me down. I won’t hold it against you.”
And at that moment—
Shing.
A dazzling flash burst from the sword at Perfected Being Hyeoncheon’s waist.

Smack!

His sleeves swelled with the force of his formidable internal energy.

His gentle nature had earned him the respect of many.
He had never joined the ranks of the Ten Kings, but even as Sect Leader of the renowned Kongtong Sect, he had always been humble.
Yet even the largest vessel has its limits.

I wondered if I should have killed him then and there.”
Sama Pyo said nothing to the deep sigh in Hyeoncheon’s voice.
No—he couldn’t answer.

He had first heard of it from a woman.

His distrust of one man: Sima Gong, the Black Night King.

chapters.title: Chapter 1059
paragraphs: For me and everyone else, it lasted only an instant.
For someone, though, it might have felt unbearably slow and suffocating—a moment in a life flashing before their eyes.
Shing.
The sound of sharp steel slipping from its scabbard was so faint it raised goose bumps. The sword had been drawn with near-perfect skill.
Not a hair’s breadth off. Just the right force, at just the right speed.
And...
A clear path, following its master’s will as the blade cut diagonally across its target.
Shhk!
The distance was too short to dodge. The gap in their martial prowess was too great.
And Sama Pyo had quietly closed his eyes without even trying to evade, as if accepting his fate.
Nothing unexpected happened. The sword light flashed through that split second, scattering red flowers into the air.
Shwaaa!
Time started moving again.
Beyond Sama Pyo’s staggering back, a fountain of blood shot high into the air, searing itself into everyone’s vision.
The Kongtong Disciples nearby. The Fire Dragon Pavilion members and me.
And someone else, too, who had been doing everything in their power to hold back the urge to rush over.
“No!”
Taishan had watched everything unfold around Sama Pyo with mounting anxiety. That was as long as his patience could last.

With a thunderous shout that rang out on every side, the nine-foot-tall giant set down the poor old man riding on his shoulders as if tossing him aside. Then he shot forward faster than I’d ever seen him move.
Whoosh!
The wind roared around him, but his path was perfectly straight.
Before anyone could stop him, Taishan hurtled like a cannonball toward Sama Pyo’s back as Sama Pyo staggered backward.
He didn’t seem to care one bit about the Kongtong Disciples who had surrounded Sama Pyo, as if to box him in.
“You bastard!”
“Stop right there!”
Papat!
Shouts erupted from every direction, and figures blurred into motion.
Dozens of Kongtong Disciples moved with elusive speed to block Taishan’s path. Each raised a weapon and aimed it at him.

Their blades were slick with blood. And as if to show how they had survived the brutal, desperate battle at Dunhuang, every one of those blades gleamed with Sword Energy—proof that its wielder had reached the level of injuring others with Sword Energy.
But the two-section staff in Taishan’s hands bore the same light. Even with dozens of Peak Masters blocking his way, he only charged faster.
“Raaaargh!”
Tiger Giant Child.
True to his epithet, Taishan was usually as innocent as a child. But his inborn strength and martial prowess were those of a beast.
Roaring like an enraged tiger, he swung his two-section staff with all his might. A tremendous gale swept along with it.
Whoooosh!
Even a hardened Murim veteran would have felt a chill run down their spine at that terrifying whistle through the air.
But the Kongtong Disciples didn’t take a single step back.
Instead, they met Taishan’s menacing charge with dazzling sword light.
Shwiiing!
Killing intent filled the space in an instant.
The two-section staff crushing through the wind. The blades cutting through it.
Into that life-or-death moment, I took one forceful step.
Shhk.
One step.
That was enough.
Several yards vanished, and the scene around me changed.
I had already slipped between Taishan and the Kongtong Disciples. Without hesitation, I thrust out both palms.
Bang!
Compressed air exploded. A hot blast from the Flame Divine Palm, held back as much as I could manage, burst from my palms and drove everything apart.
The weapons being swung at one another—and the people holding them.
Clatter!
Weapons flew into the air without reaching their targets. Their wielders stumbled backward, swaying like reeds in the wind.
Dust rose from the blood-soaked ground. Through it, I looked at the bewildered faces of the men forced back and spoke in a tired, flat voice.
“Do you all have energy to burn? Take it down a notch.”
Before anyone could answer, I turned to Perfected Being Hyeoncheon, who had watched the sudden clash in silence.
“Apologies for the late greeting. We met once before in Henan.”
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon had briefly met me at the Mount Song Resolution, where the new Murim Alliance was first formed. He gave a slight nod.
“It’s been a while, my friend Jin.”
A corner of my heart ached.
Our acquaintance had lasted less than fifteen minutes, but it still hurt.
The old Daoist who had once praised my martial arts with a kind voice and laugh, like my own grandfather, was nowhere to be found.
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon’s voice was as dry and brittle as grains of desert sand. Traces of grief and anger remained around his mouth.
His sword trembled in his wrinkled hand.
Blood dripped slowly from the tip of the treasured blade he had likely carried all his life. Perhaps he still hadn’t managed to put those feelings aside.
“Pavilion Master! What are you doing? Move aside, now!”
Right. That guy was here too.
Taishan’s shout pulled me out of the feelings I’d sunk into. He had adjusted his grip on his two-section staff and was stepping forward again, so I stopped him.
In my own rough way.
Thump!
My fist drove straight into his abdomen. The nearly nine-foot giant doubled over like a shrimp and went rigid.
Taishan drew in a startled breath. Staring at me wide-eyed, he forced out a few words.
“P-Pavilion Master...”
“Cool your head.”
I brought the edge of my hand down on the back of his neck without hesitation.
Thud.
His skin and bones were so thick that even a Pressure-Point Strike looked unlikely to work. But overwhelming force was another matter.
The sound of him falling was like a bear hitting the ground. Silence followed.
The Fire Dragon Pavilion members who arrived a moment later, and the Kongtong Disciples who had been about to charge Taishan again, stared at me in bewilderment.
Everyone except Perfected Being Hyeoncheon, who watched with a somber gaze.
“I’d heard there was a giant tiger beside the young Black Dragon... He’s as strong as they say. Loyal, too.”
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon looked at Sama Pyo, who still lay motionless.
“You have a better subordinate than he looks. Wouldn’t you agree?”
“He’s as dumb as he is big, but he’s a good guy. And...”
I added bitterly, “The friend you showed mercy to is a much better man than you think, Sect Leader.”
The air around us gave a sharp, electric shiver.
Those who understood what I meant widened their eyes at once, as if on cue. Perfected Being Hyeoncheon closed his eyes without a word.
As though trying to wipe away the urge to kill still lingering in his heart.
“Do you... regret it?”
I broke the silence and looked at him.
From the moment he had drawn his sword and swung it, I’d known instinctively.
There had been conflict in that perfect draw, but not the slightest trace of killing intent.
That the old Daoist’s sword would never take someone’s life.
That was why I hadn’t stepped in.
His wavering sword tip had cut shallowly into Sama Pyo’s flesh, but I could tell it was because of that last bit of conflict.
“Regret it? Of course I do.”
“Then why?”
“His eyes. I saw those eyes.”
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon suddenly opened his eyes. He looked up at the Kongtong Sect flag fluttering above his head and continued.
“They were like my Disciples’ eyes when I last saw them in Dunhuang. Deep and upright. Unbowed even before death. Those were their eyes.”
Some say a person’s eyes are the windows and mirrors of the heart.
Perhaps that was why the old Daoist, who had come here seeking revenge, could not bring himself to kill his enemy’s son, even when the young man had come to him seeking death.
“I’m nothing but an old Daoist. I spent my life absorbed in the sword rather than the Daoist scriptures, and I couldn’t save my Disciples as they bled and died. But...”
A hot breath passed between his trembling lips.
“Someone I met recently said this to me. If you take a person’s life for no reason except that they share your enemy’s blood, what is that if not the Demonic Path?”
I understood.
Though Perfected Being Hyeoncheon was speaking to me, his words were meant for every Kongtong Disciple.
Splat.
A sword slipped from someone’s hand and fell into a pool of blood.
Only moments ago, the Disciples had radiated suffocating killing intent. Now they stared at one another with vacant eyes.

As if the sight of their fellow Disciples, drenched in blood from head to toe, showed them what they themselves had been doing: hunting down the enemies who had survived and slaughtering them like livestock.
They swallowed their tears.
In silence, they struggled to hold back the emotions stirred by the beloved faces passing before their eyes.
“We will have our revenge. But guilt by association will have no place in it. The Kongtong Sect we build anew from this day forward must be that way.”
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon made his declaration to every surviving Disciple.
The tower they had painstakingly built had fallen. They would build it again on bedrock.
And no innocent blood would stain the bedrock beneath that stronger tower.
Then he looked at his Disciples with tear-filled eyes and said, “Cry your hearts out. These may be your last tears today.”
I quietly closed my eyes and shut out the sound.
Every member of the Fire Dragon Pavilion did the same, as did the others who had belatedly noticed the commotion and come over.
The anguished wails and sobs filled the air. There was no way not to hear them, however hard we tried.
But it didn’t matter.
No one on this battlefield, covered in countless corpses and pools of blood, would hear or remember their crying.
Or perhaps...
Maybe everyone was already crying together.
Tap.
At the familiar touch of a hand on my shoulder, I wiped my damp eyes with my sleeve.
“Old Master.”
“I was worried I might be late, but it seems I worried for nothing.”
I turned. Jeok Cheongang and the Bow Saint stood there. They had disappeared somewhere around the time the shouts of victory began to ring out.
No—strictly speaking, they weren’t the only ones there.
“Ugh... sob... sob!”
A man was weeping as though his heart would break.
He also smelled worse than anything I’d encountered in my life. I’d spent years being worked like a dog in Gates where just standing still made me gag, but even I had never smelled anything like him.
The strange man suddenly held out a hand to me.
What the hell?
I blinked, my tears already gone, when the oddball grabbed my hand, yanked me close, and wrapped me in a tight embrace. Then he began to sob miserably.
“Waaah! Ooohhh!”
No, seriously. What was going on?
After my brain stalled for a moment, and whatever tears had been about to come out disappeared completely, I asked, “...Um, who exactly are you?”
Jeok Cheongang answered without hesitation.
“Madman.”
“What?”
“Some vicious-looking mounted bandits call him Great Sir, too.”

With a thunderous shout that rang out on every side, the nine-foot-tall giant set down the poor old man riding on his shoulders as if tossing him aside.
Then he shot forward faster than I’d ever seen him move.
Whoosh!
The wind roared around him, but his path was perfectly straight.
Before anyone could stop him, Taishan hurtled like a cannonball toward Sama Pyo’s back as Sama Pyo staggered backward.
He didn’t seem to care one bit about the Kongtong Disciples who had surrounded Sama Pyo, as if to box him in.
“You bastard!”
“Stop right there!”
Papat!
Shouts erupted from every direction, and figures blurred into motion.
Dozens of Kongtong Disciples moved with elusive speed to block Taishan’s path.
Each raised a weapon and aimed it at him.
Their blades were slick with blood.

And as if to show how they had survived the brutal, desperate battle at Dunhuang, every one of those blades gleamed with Sword Energy—proof that its wielder had reached the level of injuring others with Sword Energy.
But the two-section staff in Taishan’s hands bore the same light.
Even with dozens of Peak Masters blocking his way, he only charged faster.
“Raaaargh!”
Tiger Giant Child.
True to his epithet, Taishan was usually as innocent as a child.
But his inborn strength and martial prowess were those of a beast.
Roaring like an enraged tiger, he swung his two-section staff with all his might.
A tremendous gale swept along with it.
Whoooosh!
Even a hardened Murim veteran would have felt a chill run down their spine at that terrifying whistle through the air.
But the Kongtong Disciples didn’t take a single step back.
Instead, they met Taishan’s menacing charge with dazzling sword light.
Shwiiing!
Killing intent filled the space in an instant.
The two-section staff crushing through the wind.
The blades cutting through it.
Into that life-or-death moment, I took one forceful step.
Shhk.
One step.
That was enough.
Several yards vanished, and the scene around me changed.
I had already slipped between Taishan and the Kongtong Disciples.
Without hesitation, I thrust out both palms.
Bang!
Compressed air exploded.
A hot blast from the Flame Divine Palm, held back as much as I could manage, burst from my palms and drove everything apart.
The weapons being swung at one another—and the people holding them.
Clatter!
Weapons flew into the air without reaching their targets.
Their wielders stumbled backward, swaying like reeds in the wind.
Dust rose from the blood-soaked ground.
Through it, I looked at the bewildered faces of the men forced back and spoke in a tired, flat voice.
“Do you all have energy to burn?
Take it down a notch.”
Before anyone could answer, I turned to Perfected Being Hyeoncheon, who had watched the sudden clash in silence.
“Apologies for the late greeting.
We met once before in Henan.”
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon had briefly met me at the Mount Song Resolution, where the new Murim Alliance was first formed.
He gave a slight nod.
“It’s been a while, my friend Jin.”
A corner of my heart ached.
Our acquaintance had lasted less than fifteen minutes, but it still hurt.
The old Daoist who had once praised my martial arts with a kind voice and laugh, like my own grandfather, was nowhere to be found.
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon’s voice was as dry and brittle as grains of desert sand.
Traces of grief and anger remained around his mouth.
His sword trembled in his wrinkled hand.
Blood dripped slowly from the tip of the treasured blade he had likely carried all his life.
Perhaps he still hadn’t managed to put those feelings aside.
“Pavilion Master!
What are you doing?
Move aside, now!”
Right.
That guy was here too.
Taishan’s shout pulled me out of the feelings I’d sunk into.
He had adjusted his grip on his two-section staff and was stepping forward again, so I stopped him.
In my own rough way.
Thump!
My fist drove straight into his abdomen.
The nearly nine-foot giant doubled over like a shrimp and went rigid.
Taishan drew in a startled breath.
Staring at me wide-eyed, he forced out a few words.
“P-Pavilion Master...”
“Cool your head.”
I brought the edge of my hand down on the back of his neck without hesitation.
Thud.
His skin and bones were so thick that even a Pressure-Point Strike looked unlikely to work.
But overwhelming force was another matter.
The sound of him falling was like a bear hitting the ground.
Silence followed.
The Fire Dragon Pavilion members who arrived a moment later, and the Kongtong Disciples who had been about to charge Taishan again, stared at me in bewilderment.
Everyone except Perfected Being Hyeoncheon, who watched with a somber gaze.
“I’d heard there was a giant tiger beside the young Black Dragon...
He’s as strong as they say.
Loyal, too.”
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon looked at Sama Pyo, who still lay motionless.
“You have a better subordinate than he looks.
Wouldn’t you agree?”
“He’s as dumb as he is big, but he’s a good guy.
And...”
I added bitterly, “The friend you showed mercy to is a much better man than you think, Sect Leader.”
The air around us gave a sharp, electric shiver.
Those who understood what I meant widened their eyes at once, as if on cue.
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon closed his eyes without a word.
As though trying to wipe away the urge to kill still lingering in his heart.
“Do you... regret it?”
I broke the silence and looked at him.
From the moment he had drawn his sword and swung it, I’d known instinctively.
There had been conflict in that perfect draw, but not the slightest trace of killing intent.
That the old Daoist’s sword would never take someone’s life.
That was why I hadn’t stepped in.
His wavering sword tip had cut shallowly into Sama Pyo’s flesh, but I could tell it was because of that last bit of conflict.
“Regret it?
Of course I do.”
“Then why?”
“His eyes.
I saw those eyes.”
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon suddenly opened his eyes.
He looked up at the Kongtong Sect flag fluttering above his head and continued.
“They were like my Disciples’ eyes when I last saw them in Dunhuang.
Deep and upright.
Unbowed even before death.
Those were their eyes.”
Some say a person’s eyes are the windows and mirrors of the heart.
Perhaps that was why the old Daoist, who had come here seeking revenge, could not bring himself to kill his enemy’s son, even when the young man had come to him seeking death.
“I’m nothing but an old Daoist.
I spent my life absorbed in the sword rather than the Daoist scriptures, and I couldn’t save my Disciples as they bled and died.
But...”
A hot breath passed between his trembling lips.
“Someone I met recently said this to me.
If you take a person’s life for no reason except that they share your enemy’s blood, what is that if not the Demonic Path?”
I understood.
Though Perfected Being Hyeoncheon was speaking to me, his words were meant for every Kongtong Disciple.
Splat.
A sword slipped from someone’s hand and fell into a pool of blood.
Only moments ago, the Disciples had radiated suffocating killing intent.
Now they stared at one another with vacant eyes.

As if the sight of their fellow Disciples, drenched in blood from head to toe, showed them what they themselves had been doing: hunting down the enemies who had survived and slaughtering them like livestock.
They swallowed their tears.
In silence, they struggled to hold back the emotions stirred by the beloved faces passing before their eyes.
“We will have our revenge.
But guilt by association will have no place in it.
The Kongtong Sect we build anew from this day forward must be that way.”
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon made his declaration to every surviving Disciple.
The tower they had painstakingly built had fallen.
They would build it again on bedrock.
And no innocent blood would stain the bedrock beneath that stronger tower.
Then he looked at his Disciples with tear-filled eyes and said, “Cry your hearts out.
These may be your last tears today.”
I quietly closed my eyes and shut out the sound.
Every member of the Fire Dragon Pavilion did the same, as did the others who had belatedly noticed the commotion and come over.
The anguished wails and sobs filled the air.
There was no way not to hear them, however hard we tried.
But it didn’t matter.
No one on this battlefield, covered in countless corpses and pools of blood, would hear or remember their crying.
Or perhaps...
Maybe everyone was already crying together.
Tap.
At the familiar touch of a hand on my shoulder, I wiped my damp eyes with my sleeve.
“Old Master.”
“I was worried I might be late, but it seems I worried for nothing.”
I turned.
Jeok Cheongang and the Bow Saint stood there.
They had disappeared somewhere around the time the shouts of victory began to ring out.
No—strictly speaking, they weren’t the only ones there.
“Ugh... sob... sob!”
A man was weeping as though his heart would break.
He also smelled worse than anything I’d encountered in my life.
I’d spent years being worked like a dog in Gates where just standing still made me gag, but even I had never smelled anything like him.
The strange man suddenly held out a hand to me.
What the hell?
I blinked, my tears already gone, when the oddball grabbed my hand, yanked me close, and wrapped me in a tight embrace.
Then he began to sob miserably.
“Waaah!
Ooohhh!”
No, seriously.
What was going on?
After my brain stalled for a moment, and whatever tears had been about to come out disappeared completely, I asked, “...Um, who exactly are you?”
Jeok Cheongang answered without hesitation.
“Madman.”
“What?”
“Some vicious-looking mounted bandits call him Great Sir, too.”

chapters.title: Chapter 1060
paragraphs: Great Sir.
An unidentified Supreme Peak master. No one knew his name or anything about him.

About a dozen years ago, he had subdued the lawless Ningxia Province in a single stroke, then defied everyone’s expectations by settling into a life of idleness. My first impression of this extraordinary man was:
He looks like a beggar.
That wasn’t just a figure of speech. He really did.
His hair and beard were so long they covered his face and reached his waist. Worse, they were matted together.
His clothes were torn and stained in so many places that “rags” would have been more accurate. And the stench coming off his grime-caked body was innovative—no, revolutionary.
A beggar among beggars.
An utter pauper. The king of beggars.

Even Gung Gibang, the Beggars’ Sect’s Successor Beggar and a bona fide minor chief among its hundred thousand beggars, would take one look at this man and cry, “You beg like shit!” I could guarantee he’d cut the rope tied around his waist.
And yet...
“So this really is the beggar everyone’s heard about—or, I mean, the Great Sir?”
“Hard as it is to believe, it’s all true.”
The Bow Saint answered in a nasal voice. She was already standing well away, pinching her nose shut.
That was when—
“Greeeaat Siiiir! Why did you take so long to come?!”
With a plaintive wail, Ma Junggeol, eldest of the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang, came sprinting from far off and threw his arms around the strange man.
Or, more accurately, he tried to hug him, then recoiled as if burned and doubled over like a shrimp.
“Ugh. Blegh.”
Yeah, I understood.
I’d spent enough time rolling around in Gates to be able to stand there and take it. Even now, the stench was bad enough to make me wonder if it could really be coming from a human body.
Of course, even I was reaching my limit.
“Wait, just—give me a little space. Why are you doing this when we’ve only just met?”
My initial shock didn’t last long.

I desperately breathed through my mouth to block out as much of the smell as possible, then tried to push the man away. But his legs were planted deep in the ground like a thousand-geun boulder. He didn’t budge.
Looking at that, he really does seem to be the Great Sir...
Even though I’d held back, my strength was so far beyond ordinary limits that even a decent Peak master would have struggled to withstand it.
My head understood. My heart didn’t.
It was like finding out that Kim, the homeless guy who ruled the second exit at Seoul Station, was actually the chairman of a major corporation.
But seriously, why are you crying so hard?
As I stood there, unsure what to do and darting my eyes around, the strange man—no, the Great Sir—who’d been wailing in my arms finally spoke in a congested voice.
“Ahem. Ahem. Forgive me. It was such a moving moment that I couldn’t help crying.”
I looked down at the front of my chest, soaked and sticky, and corrected him.
“I don’t think tears were the only thing coming out.”
“My nose was running, too.”
I could understand tears and a runny nose, but why he had to let them both out while clinging to me was beyond me. Still, I nodded, summoning the bare minimum of patience and respect for my elder.
“Uh, sure. So you’re feeling better now?”
“Thanks to you, I’ve calmed down a little. Do you mind if I blow my nose?”
“You really do everything, don’t you?”
“Hmm? What was that?”
“Nothing. Go ahead.”
“Thank you.”
The Great Sir thanked me in a guileless voice, then blew his nose with a sound that seemed to clear out his entire head.
Phaaaang!
Into the hem of my clothes.
“Whew, that feels much better... Why are you making that face?”
Ah.
I was really about to snap.
To sum it up, even with half my sanity gone, I somehow managed not to punch the Great Sir in the head.

Starting a fight in the middle of a battlefield that hadn’t been fully secured yet would have been unwise. More than that, Perfected Being Hyeoncheon had quickly grasped what was happening and stepped in.
“Here you are, Great Sir.”
Anyone would have found the sight surprising. No, astonishing.
Who was Perfected Being Hyeoncheon?
The Sect Leader of the Kongtong Sect, one of the Nine Sects and One Gang; a hero of the Great Faction War; and a Supreme Peak master representing Gansu.

If we were talking about the Marine Corps, he’d be a legendary first-class veteran who’d taken part in the Incheon Landing Operation. He had the seniority to stand in the middle of the world and shout, “Everyone below me and above you, fall in!”
And yet this man, whose standing in Murim and martial prowess both ranked among the highest in the world, was the first to offer a fist-and-palm salute with the utmost respect.
To a strange man who looked worse than even the Beggars’ Sect leader.
It was enough to make Jeok Cheongang, watching from nearby, mutter:
“What the hell does he have on him...?”
For that moment, I had more or less the same thought.
Maybe the filthy-looking fellow had a video file titled something like Kongtong’s Perfected One H and His Secret Hand Games.
But there was a reason anyone could understand why Perfected Being Hyeoncheon would show such respect to a strange man followed by a bunch of former mounted bandits.
“This Great Sir was of tremendous help to us.”
The story went like this.
After their defeat at Dunhuang, Perfected Being Hyeoncheon and the Kongtong Sect survivors had no idea where to go.

They had to flee east to avoid Dark Heaven’s forces gathering like clouds in the west. But now that they felt betrayed by their allies, heading east would have been like walking straight into a tiger’s jaws.
So they chose to go north, toward the grasslands.
“We considered turning south for Qinghai, but we had no idea what Dark Heaven might already have done there. We had no choice but to head for the grasslands, where far fewer people lived.”
Though Qinghai lay at the far edge of the Central Plains, there were still plenty of eyes watching from every direction.
The grasslands, by contrast, were vast and sparsely populated, making them better for evading pursuit. If Dark Heaven had reached both places, anyone would have chosen the latter.

“We kept heading north without rest. Even after passing Anxi and entering the grasslands, we couldn’t let our guard down. We thought we might pause long enough to recover, then see what was happening in Gansu. Or perhaps cross the grasslands and go all the way to Shaanxi.”
But for the Kongtong Disciples, already suffering injuries both serious and minor from the fierce battle at Dunhuang, it was a grueling march.
Even Perfected Being Hyeoncheon, who had to lead them all, had reached his limit from a severe Internal Injury.
“Still, we couldn’t stop. Miserable and unsure what lay ahead, we had no choice but to keep moving. Then, after several days on the road, we saw a light flickering in the distance one night.”
The nights on the grasslands were deep and silent.
For the fugitives crossing that endless expanse, any light in the dark was something to be wary of.
“We crept closer, keeping as quiet as we could. A strange man was roasting camel meat. It was the first food we’d seen in four days, and we were all half out of our minds.”
Hyuk Mujin had drifted closer at some point and was listening intently. He let out a low, “Ah.”
“Was that the beggar—sorry, the Great Sir?”
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon nodded.
“Indeed. He saw us shivering in the cold and invited us to sit with him without hesitation.”
“Now that’s generous. He even offered you food. No wonder you’re grateful, Sect Leader.”
The heartwarming story made the air around us feel a little warmer. Then Perfected Being Hyeoncheon spoke again.
“No, we didn’t get any.”
“What?”
“As soon as he saw us, he wolfed down all the meat and told us we could warm ourselves by the fire for a while before we went our separate ways.”
What the hell?
Everyone’s eyes turned toward the Great Sir, mine included. He bashfully smoothed his wild, tangled hair.
“I only had enough for myself at the time...”
The air turned cold again. Perfected Being Hyeoncheon continued.
“Regardless, the Great Sir helped us greatly. He gave every Disciple of our sect, myself included, a place to hide for a while and treated the wounded.”
A master could recognize another master.
At first, Perfected Being Hyeoncheon had been wary of the unidentified Supreme Peak master, but he hadn’t had any other real options. Before long, he’d come to feel the man’s sincere goodwill.
“While we were there, we also had an unexpected visitor.”
“An unexpected visitor?”
“At first, we thought the enemy had found our hideout and come to attack. But that wasn’t it. It turned out some men called the Seven Masters of White Bones had come to escort the Great Sir.”
“The Seven Masters of Baekma Bang,” Ma Junggeol interjected through gritted teeth.
“Oh, I must have mixed that up. The Black-Horse Seven?”
“I said the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang! Honestly, this is driving me insa—”
Bap!
I smacked Ma Junggeol on the back of the head without question or explanation and shut him up. Then I looked around.
Quite a few riders were moving across the battlefield on snorting horses.
They wore relatively light leather armor and carried weapons such as lances and crescent-bladed polearms. Now I could finally be sure who they were.
“Then could those people be...?”
“You’re thinking of the right people. They’re the horse caravans of Ningxia Province.”
Ma Junggeol, grimacing as he rubbed the back of his head, spoke in a tiny voice.
“More precisely, the horse caravans centered around Baekma Bang... Gah!”
He clamped his mouth shut when our eyes met. But this time, instead of hitting him, I patted him on the shoulder.

The Seven Masters of Baekma Bang had promised a few days ago that they would bring the Great Sir back. They’d returned with the horse caravans under their command, and thanks to them, we’d been able to deal a decisive, fatal blow to the enemies who were on the verge of collapse.
So that’s how this worked out.
I’d more or less forgotten they existed.
Or perhaps it would be more accurate to say I hadn’t expected much from them.
You always had to prepare for the worst in a battle, and the horse caravans, made up of former mounted bandits, weren’t exactly people you could trust.

But they had kept the promise they made to me, even if they were a little later than planned. And with the Great Sir’s help, Perfected Being Hyeoncheon and the Kongtong Disciples had recovered from their injuries and returned to Gansu alongside thousands of horse-caravan riders.
Still, one question remained.
So who the hell is that guy, really?
I looked at the man they called the Great Sir, my eyes full of questions.

A moment ago, he’d clung to me and sobbed as if we were reuniting with a long-lost family. Now he was yawning widely just because the story had gotten a little long. As expected, he seemed far from sane.
Just as Ma Junggeol and his sworn brothers had told me.
Quietly, secretly, I reached out toward the Great Sir.
With a hand of detection, invisible and granted to me alone.
Skill: Activate Qi Sense.
Whooooosh.
The blue circle spread outward from me and finally reached the Great Sir.

Ma Junggeol, grimacing as he rubbed the back of his head, spoke in a tiny voice.
“More precisely, the horse caravans centered around Baekma Bang...
Gah!”
He clamped his mouth shut when our eyes met.
But this time, instead of hitting him, I patted him on the shoulder.
The Seven Masters of Baekma Bang had promised a few days ago that they would bring the Great Sir back.
They’d returned with the horse caravans under their command, and thanks to them, we’d been able to deal a decisive, fatal blow to the enemies who were on the verge of collapse.
So that’s how this worked out.
I’d more or less forgotten they existed.
Or perhaps it would be more accurate to say I hadn’t expected much from them.
You always had to prepare for the worst in a battle, and the horse caravans, made up of former mounted bandits, weren’t exactly people you could trust.
But they had kept the promise they made to me, even if they were a little later than planned.
And with the Great Sir’s help, Perfected Being Hyeoncheon and the Kongtong Disciples had recovered from their injuries and returned to Gansu alongside thousands of horse-caravan riders.
Still, one question remained.
So who the hell is that guy, really?
I looked at the man they called the Great Sir, my eyes full of questions.
A moment ago, he’d clung to me and sobbed as if we were reuniting with a long-lost family.
Now he was yawning widely just because the story had gotten a little long.
As expected, he seemed far from sane.
Just as Ma Junggeol and his sworn brothers had told me.
Quietly, secretly, I reached out toward the Great Sir.
With a hand of detection, invisible and granted to me alone.
Skill: Activate Qi Sense.
Whooooosh.
The blue circle spread outward from me and finally reached the Great Sir.

chapters.title: Chapter 1061
paragraphs: Jin Taekyung had two kinds of Qi Sense.
One was the Qi Sense he had honed as a martial artist, a means of survival.
The other was Qi Sense granted by the System as a separate Skill.
The first worked as naturally as breathing, even in everyday life. The second required him to activate the System with a clear intention and goal.
Back when I was weak, I had no choice but to rely on the Qi Sense Skill.
Though he’d used it far less often since his martial arts had reached a certain level, the Qi Sense Skill remained incredibly useful.
Especially when he wanted a closer look at someone whose identity he didn’t know.
Skill: Activate Qi Sense.
The moment Jin Taekyung gave the command in his mind, the blue circle of [Qi Sense], now at nine stars, shot outward.
Shwaaash.
The ability made no sound and had no visible form. Only a faint ripple betrayed it, one that a tiny handful of masters at the highest realms could sense.
And it offered another way to determine the identity of the strange man called Great Sir.
If the Skill succeeds, I’ll find out exactly who he is. If it fails, I won’t lose anything.
Of course, the Qi Sense Skill wasn’t all-powerful.
Masters beyond its limits might have their Levels displayed as question marks. Some could sense the ripple when the Skill activated and immediately deflect it.
During their first meeting, Jeok Cheongang had even controlled his qi to make his Level appear absurdly low.
What mattered to Jin Taekyung now was how this beggar-looking Supreme Peak master would react—and what the Skill he’d already activated would tell him.
Who the hell are you?
Jin Taekyung watched him closely.
The wild-haired oddball scratched vigorously at his greasy head, looking so unconcerned that Jin Taekyung couldn’t tell whether he had no idea what was happening or was pretending not to.
Then the blue circle that might lift the veil around the man finally reached him.
At the same time, a familiar alert sounded in Jin Taekyung’s ear.
Beep-beep!
The sharp noise announced failure. Jin Taekyung knew what that meant.
He’s a master. His Level is higher than mine.
But he wasn’t shaken.
He’d learned firsthand, more times than he cared to count, that Level was no absolute measure of strength.
Level could reliably distinguish the strong from the weak up to First Rate, or perhaps Peak. Masters beyond those realms were different.
Even back when he was at the Peak realm, Jin Taekyung had won fight after fight against enemies dozens of Levels higher than himself. A Level difference meant especially little to him.
Yet even he was left speechless by the line that appeared before his eyes.
System Skill Qi Sense was half successful!
The question slipped out before he knew it.
That wasn’t quite what the failure alert had told him. He blinked at the message.
Success was success, and failure was failure. What the hell was half successful?
Wait. Now that I think about it, that failure alert did sound a little strange...
Before he could finish the thought, the oddball whipped his head around as though he’d only just noticed something unusual.
“Huh? I thought a strange wind blew over from your direction just now. Did you feel it too?”
Jin Taekyung didn’t answer.
No—he couldn’t answer. He was too busy staring at something unlike anything he’d seen since gaining the ability to use the System.
System Lv. 119 ???
Three question marks.
That was all.
He rubbed his eyes with his sleeve and blinked hard several times. The question marks remained where the man’s name should have been.
...Has this ever happened before?
He already knew the answer.
No.
Not once. Ever.
He’d seen plenty of Levels displayed as question marks, but never a name.
Everyone had a name, whether it was an alias used to hide their identity or the real one someone had given them at birth.
But Great Sir—the oddball before him—didn’t.
The sheer strangeness of it left Jin Taekyung with no choice but to ask.
“What the hell are you?”
Bewilderment and a hint of suspicion came through in his abrupt question. Everyone around them looked at Great Sir at once, as if on cue.
His tone had been rude enough to draw a rebuke. Yet even Perfected Being Hyeoncheon and the Kongtong Disciples, who owed Great Sir so much, forgot to give him one.
They’d spent days and nights with their strange benefactor without learning who he was. They wanted to know at least a little about him.
The Fire King, the Bow Saint, and the members of the Fire Dragon Pavilion were no different.
A Supreme Peak master who’d spent more than a decade holed up in some remote corner of Ningxia Province was bound to make people curious.
With all those eyes on him, Great Sir calmly asked, “Hm? Were you asking me?”
“Yeah. You.”
“Oh, that’s a very good question.”
Great Sir scratched at his grime-streaked neck. Yellowed teeth showed between his long locks as he beamed.
“Come to think of it, we haven’t even introduced ourselves. Let me do it properly. I’m...”
The surroundings had gone deathly quiet.
Hundreds of pairs of eyes fixed on his lips as they slowly parted.
“Cough. All this dust has made my throat scratchy. Let me start again. I’m...”
His voice trailed off again after he cleared his throat. Everyone was about to go mad with curiosity.
Who could he be?
A reclusive master whose name of three syllables had yet to become known?
A master of the previous generation, long forgotten by the world?
Or perhaps... a former great fiend of the Demonic Cult who had turned over a new leaf?
As their guesses multiplied, Great Sir continued in a grave voice.
“Uh. So, I’m...”
“You bastard, you’re the biggest piece of shit under heaven!”

Jeok Cheongang, halfway out of his mind after hearing “I’m” for the third time, rolled his eyes and started forward. At that very moment, Great Sir let out a cry as though he’d attained some great enlightenment.
“That’s it! I think that’s it!”
“No matter how far the ways of the martial world have fallen, how can you pull this kind of dogshit—what?”
Jeok Cheongang stopped mid-step. Great Sir clapped his hands and shouted again.
“What you said just now! I think you’ve got it! Madman—that must be my name!”
A suffocating silence fell.
Every last person stared at Great Sir, then at one another. Their eyes exchanged the words no one said aloud.
What the hell?
Did I hear that wrong?
Madman? That’s someone’s name?
Does any of this make sense?

But no amount of exchanged looks changed the reality before them. Seized by a bewilderment he’d felt only a handful of times in his long life, Jeok Cheongang turned toward the person who’d already made him feel it several times.
His one and only Disciple.
“So... what sort of nonsense did that damned fool just spout?”
But, like his Master, his Disciple was just as incapable of fully understanding or accepting what was happening.
If anything, he was even more bewildered.
System Lv. 119 Madman
Jin Taekyung stared blankly at the holographic window above Great Sir’s head.
What the hell?
It had changed. It definitely had.
But...
So what the hell does that mean?
Could he even call that a proper change? Or had the System developed an error?
Countless thoughts and regrets streaked through his mind like a meteor shower. Then someone he’d momentarily forgotten spoke up beside him.
“Good grief. I thought he’d gotten a little better, but here he goes again.”
Everyone turned toward the voice. The fearsome-looking, middle-aged former mounted bandit flinched.
“Uh, don’t mind him. He’s always like this.”
“Always?”
At Jin Taekyung’s question, Ma Junggeol—once a mounted bandit in Ningxia Province, now the Chief of Baekma Bang and eldest of the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang—gave an uneasy nod.
“Well, yes. Didn’t I tell you before?”
Jin Taekyung vaguely remembered Ma Junggeol saying Great Sir wasn’t exactly normal.
“No, but still. What is this...?”
“A few months ago, when I went to see Great Sir where he was staying, do you know what his name was?”
“What?”
“Jeomsuni.”
“His name changes every time I visit. He’s been Gaettong—Dog Poop—and Sottong—Cow Poop, too.”
Jin Taekyung froze, unable to find a word to say. Great Sir suddenly drew a sharp breath and shouted.
“Gasp! Gaettong! Yes! I think it was Gaettong! I’m sure this time! Probably!”
Ding.
System Lv. 119 Gaettong
At that moment, Jin Taekyung gave up on thinking.

chapters.title: Chapter 1062
paragraphs: No matter how easy a life someone leads, they’re bound to meet a certain kind of madman at least once.
As for me, my life had been objectively rough—extremely rough—so that went without saying.
But I could say this with certainty:
Even I had never met anyone as purely insane as the oddball they called Great Sir.
...At this rate, should I start an encyclopedia of madmen?
I muttered to myself as I watched Great Sir’s back slowly recede into the distance.

Unable to find his true identity as Gaettong, he’d moved on to Sottong (Cow Poop) and Malttong (Horse Poop), completing a trilogy of poop names. Then he’d tried switching genders and becoming Jeomsuni. Jeok Cheongang had threatened to kill him, and now the horse-caravan riders were dragging him away to keep him apart from everyone else.
“I swear on everything I have...”
Standing shoulder to shoulder with me, Jeok Cheongang watched Great Sir go. His voice was grave.
“That man is one of two things: a highly trained Dark Heaven spy, or completely and utterly insane.”
Anyone who knew the circumstances would have nodded without thinking. I answered without hesitation.
“I doubt he’s a spy.”
“It’s true that he led the horse caravans of Ningxia Province to help our side. But we mustn’t trust him completely. You know that as well as I do, don’t you?”
Of course I did. I’d been stabbed in the back often enough to be sick of it.

First the Head Elder of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, then even the Murong Family, one of the Five Great Families, had joined forces with Dark Heaven. Blindly trusting some unidentified Supreme Peak master who’d crawled out of who-knows-where would be stupid.
But...
“There’s no reason we can’t trust him if we have enough evidence.”
“Evidence?”
At Jeok Cheongang’s question, I barely moved my lips.
“System.”
The brief Sound Transmission reached his ear, and his eyes widened.
I’d already told Jeok Cheongang what the System was, though the word meant nothing in this world. He lowered his voice.
“So what has that marvelous ability of yours told you?”
“He’s mad. Thoroughly mad.”
“Meaning he isn’t a spy?”
“Yes. I can’t say it with absolute certainty, though.”
“If you had to put a number on it?”
“Ninety-nine point nine percent. That’s the chance the madman—no, Great Sir—isn’t a spy.”
“Great Sir, my ass. He’s a lunatic.”
Jeok Cheongang frowned slightly and smacked his lips.
“You’re suspicious of everything, though it doesn’t suit you. If you’re saying this, you must be all but certain... So you think he truly suffers from madness?”
I hesitated, then nodded.

Even I, who thought I had a pretty good grasp of most of the System, had never encountered anything like this. I couldn’t be a hundred percent sure, but otherwise, there was no explaining why Great Sir’s name kept changing from one moment to the next.
At least he isn’t lying. Fooling the System is practically impossible, no matter what you try.
That left only one answer.
Gaettong, Sottong, Malttong, Jeomsuni—whatever the name, Great Sir firmly believed it was his, and the System reflected that belief.
In the purest sense of the word, he was mad.

“He’s dressed so badly that Myriad-Mile Pursuit, that head beggar, would weep. But he doesn’t look old enough to be suffering from the infirmities of old age... I haven’t the faintest idea where that stray cur came from.”
Jeok Cheongang had casually reduced the Beggars’ Sect Leader to “that head beggar.” He frowned, but even he had little chance of working out Great Sir’s identity on the spot.
Too many people remained hidden across the vast Nine Provinces and Eight Wastes, the Four Seas and Five Lakes.
Eccentrics in remote mountain valleys, far from the rest of the world. Heirs of secret sects who had chosen to be forgotten.
Fugitives and killers living quietly out of sight somewhere.
Jeok Cheongang himself had stayed shut away on Mount Jiuhua until he was nearly sixty, devoting himself entirely to martial arts. Great Sir might well be someone like him.
In fact, quite a few reclusive masters had joined the Murim Alliance since it was newly founded at the Mount Song Resolution.
Unlike Great Sir, of course, they must have been thoroughly vetted. The Murim Alliance wasn’t a college club. This was wartime, with betrayal and intrigue everywhere.
But how should I put it?
A sudden conviction came over me, and before I knew it, I’d spoken aloud.
“Let’s take him in as an ally.”
“What?”
“Like I said, I don’t think Great Sir is a Dark Heaven spy. No—I’m sure he isn’t.”
Jeok Cheongang looked at me in surprise. I sounded more certain than usual.
“Well, that’s strange. What makes you trust that suspicious madman so much?”
“That’s...”
I let the words trail off.
Honestly, I didn’t know.
The System didn’t tell me who was friend or foe. But alongside my curiosity about Great Sir, I felt a strangely strong conviction that this unidentified Supreme Peak master was not our enemy.
I couldn’t give a reason for it, even to myself.
...Maybe I’m just exhausted.
As soon as I remembered how tired I was, my vision wavered. I looked around.
After half a day of fighting, the snowfield was covered in blood and bodies.
People were clearing the battlefield, the brief joy of victory already forgotten. Birds had gathered in a black mass overhead, circling in the air.
Dark clouds hid the sky. The ground beneath them was red.
Through my wavering vision, it looked like a future that would repeat forever.
“Did we... really win?”
My voice came out faint. Jeok Cheongang answered.
“Yes. At least for today.”
But why?
Why, after defeating more enemies than I could count, saving so many lives, and finally winning a great victory that had kept Gansu Province safe—
Why, when I was still alive and breathing—
It didn’t feel like we’d won.
I wasn’t happy at all.
Not even when a clear chime rang in my ears.
Ding, ding, ding.

System Quest conditions have been met. Mission: Eliminate all enemies in the Gansu Province area (Complete). Quest Path of Blood successfully completed. You have acquired a massive amount of EXP and Fame. A new chain Quest has been created. Would you like to check the updated information? Y / N
I suddenly lifted my head.
Beyond the translucent holographic window, pitch-black clouds still hid the sky. I took a deep breath, and the air that sank deep into my body reeked of blood.
When would I finally be free of this sight?
How much more would I have to suffer, how many more deaths would I have to watch, before I could escape this horrible cycle?
But as always, I had no choice but to answer.
Accept.
It had been a cruel fucking day.
Crack. Crunch.
Beyond the faintly flickering candlelight, a pair of eyes watched a writhing shadow in silence as the gruesome sounds of tearing flesh filled the room.

At first glance, the eyes seemed so deeply sunk that it was impossible to guess what lay behind them. Even so, they held a trace of contempt and disgust—and that look remained even after the tearing sounds stopped.
The shadow’s convulsions gradually subsided. At last, it rose and immediately voiced its displeasure.
“You bitch. What’s with that look?”
It was a rough greeting after so long apart, but the woman paid it little mind.
She had always prided herself on being rational. She knew better than to expect a mere beast to show human courtesy.
That didn’t mean she had anything kind to say to it.
“Wipe yourself off. And stop stinking up the place.”
“What? I stink?”
At the woman’s sharp words, the shadow started to reply, then gave a quiet laugh.
“Fine. I’ll do as I’m told. You’re already in a bad mood, aren’t you?”
“...What nonsense are you talking about now?”
“Don’t pretend you don’t know when it doesn’t suit you. Don’t. It makes you look pathetic.”
Swish.
Cloth slid over smooth muscle and skin.
In the darkness beyond the candlelight, the shadow wiped the blood from its body and spoke.
“Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung.”
“I heard you nearly failed... So, how was it, you miserable bitch? You mocked me last time, but it wasn’t so easy when you had to face him yourself, was it?”
The Grand Sorceress silently bit her lip.
She had little room to argue. It was the truth.
When her silence dragged on, the shadow laughed aloud and continued.
“You should’ve been much more careful. I don’t care if you die, but you nearly caused a serious setback to the grand plan.”
The Grand Sorceress frowned at the continuing taunts and shot back.
“The same goes for you.”

“Isn’t it embarrassing to compare this with what happened then? I caused a bloodbath in the heart of the Central Plains with just a handful of idiots. Even squinting, you can see these are different matters.”
Step.
The shadow—no, the Blood Lord—chuckled as if to mock her, then stepped into the faint light.
“And I had an important item to secure on top of that.”
He had not shown himself since the Shaolin Bloodshed that shook the whole world. Now he crossed the spacious room with a jaunty stride.
He sat in a grand chair that bore the marks of centuries and gave off an inexplicable air of authority. Propping his chin on one hand, he gazed at the Grand Sorceress.
As if he were the ruler of a kingdom.
“Well, enough about the past. What matters is the present and the future. Don’t you agree?”
This time, the Grand Sorceress gave a quiet laugh.
She shook her head and stared at the Blood Lord sitting in the grand chair.
“Stop talking as if you’re someone important. You’re a stupid beast. No—a monster.”
“A monster, huh? To the people of the Central Plains, aren’t we as bad as each other?”
“No. Serving that person is the only thing we have in common. None of us is like you.”
Despite the contempt in her voice, the Blood Lord merely shrugged.
“True. That’s the first thing you’ve got right.”
“...What?”
The Grand Sorceress was taken aback by the response, which was nothing like what she’d expected. A smile, deep as blood, spread across the Blood Lord’s lips.
“Of course none of you is like me. No one—not even you—has ever achieved as much as I have.”
He laughed gleefully and stroked the grand chair.
More precisely, he stroked the two characters carved into part of it in a bold, vigorous hand.
Kunlun.
A whirling snowstorm swept past the jagged mountain peaks and crept into the Taiqing Hall, where the two of them faced each other.
