chapters.title: Chapter 1068
paragraphs: If anyone asked me how to shake off enemy pursuers, I’d answer without a moment’s hesitation.
There were only two things that mattered:
Speed and stamina.
But knowing what to do and doing it were two different things.
Every one of us knew that, yet reality stood before us like a high, solid wall.
Our force of some three thousand hadn’t had a proper rest. The pursuers closing in by the moment were monsters that didn’t even feel fatigue.
“Northwest! About two thousand feet out!”
We’d been coming down the mountains without a break for barely two hours when—
“There! The bastards are here!”
The people who spotted the distant cloud of dust cried out. I immediately turned and sized up the hazy yellow cloud.
Three hundred at least. Maybe five hundred.
The F-rank Hunter who used to scrape by in narrow, pitch-dark Gates was gone.
No—even if some part of that old me still remained, I’d changed in many ways.
I’d learned how to fight multiple enemies and make snap decisions in all kinds of situations.
“Old Master.”
We’d reached the point where we understood each other from a glance.
Jeok Cheongang read the meaning in my brief call and immediately poured internal energy into his voice.
“You slowpokes! What are you waiting for? Run like your feet are on fire!”
That wasn’t just a scolding from a cranky old man.
Jeok Cheongang’s mighty azure dragon’s roar shattered the fear lodged in our allies’ hearts and hurried their hesitant steps, if only for a moment.
And the great martial artist who’d come to be known as the Bow Saint after countless battles knew her abilities and her role precisely.
“Go. I’ll send it at the right time.”
I nodded, kicked off the ground, and charged toward the dust cloud.
Whoosh!
The wind split.
Dust billowed up from the ground beneath my feet, forming another cloud—one larger and denser than the cloud surrounding the several hundred enemies.
I see them.
Beyond the swirling sand and dust, the monsters who were neither dead nor alive came sharply into view.
I angled up the spear clenched in my hands just as a dazzling streak of light reached the enemy a step ahead of me.
Boom!
An arrow of Force exploded.
Shot from the Bow Saint’s fingertips, it swallowed dozens of monsters charging at the front and vaporized them in an instant.
I plunged into the gap it left behind, not about to waste that perfect opening.
Whoosh!
The hair on my arms stood on end at the faint, spine-chilling whistle.
Breath, speed, strength.
As if to prove my skill advanced with every passing day, everything came together without a hair’s breadth of error. The strike only grazed the enemies—but that was enough.
Slice! Splatter!
One cutting sound, but dozens of deaths within it.
A single downward-slanting sweep split rotting bodies and sent blood spraying.
Along with a clear chime, wholly at odds with the horrific sight.
Ding. Ding. Ding-ding-ding!

System You have slain a Lv. 56 Corrupted Lower-Rank Fanatic! You have slain a Lv. 75 Corrupted Mid-Rank Fanatic! You have slain a Lv. 52 Corrupted Martial Artist! ... ... ... EXP and Fame are calculated based on the level difference between you and your opponents! You have gained a small amount of EXP! You have gained a small amount of Fame!
I swung my spear as if entranced, listening to the System notifications ringing one over another.
Everywhere I looked, there were monsters. Enemies.
Each time my spear traced an arc, a dozen or even dozens of them crumpled like rotten logs, never to move again.
Freed from the chains that had bound them to this world, they returned to the order of things as it was meant to be.
Ding.
At the last chime, I confirmed that nothing else was moving and lifted my head.
Beneath a cloud that half-obscured the sun, a black-winged crow drifted through the air.
Its eyes glowed bloodred.
“Come down. Let’s talk.”
Naturally, I got no answer. I picked up someone’s sword from a pool of foul-smelling blood and added,
“If you don’t like that, come yourself.”
Whoosh!
The sword shot upward, tearing through the air. In an instant, its blade covered the crow’s red eyes.
Stab.
“Hmm.”
The man opened his eyes with a low groan and rubbed the space between them.
The pain that had come with the flash of light at the last moment still lingered, as though an awl were digging into his head.
What a monster. He’s gotten even stronger.
Ma Sanbao couldn’t help but be surprised.
Jin Taekyung’s martial skill, which he’d watched through another being’s senses, had advanced even further than when Ma had seen him at the imperial palace.
Was that even possible? In less than three months?
Ma Sanbao asked himself the question, then shook his head.
It was a stupid question.
The time to wonder whether it was possible had passed long ago.
What mattered was that Jin Taekyung had made it real—and that was precisely what made that young man, not even thirty yet, so exceptional.
Ma Sanbao already knew something else, too.
Unlike Jin Taekyung, his own role was set. He would never be the star of this stage.
For now, his most important task was to watch them closely and report back.
“My Lord.”
Ma Sanbao went to the superior he’d only recently begun serving and reported everything in detail. The Blood Lord listened, then furrowed his brow.
“Wait. They even found out you were watching them?”
“Yes. I’m ashamed to say that’s what happened—”
Boom!
A blast of palm force struck before he could finish.
Even an ordinary Peak master would have died on the spot if struck by that blow. Ma Sanbao was swept away by the force, yet despite the tremendous impact, he immediately prostrated himself.
“Huh. Look at how sturdy this body of yours is.”
“Please kill me.”
“Don’t rush me. I was just considering whether to beat you to death right here.”
“...My Lord.”
“What, are you finally scared? I suppose you have reason to be. Your master ended up dead like that too.”
Ma Sanbao bowed even lower.
Unlike his master, the Eastern Heaven Demon Lord, Ma hadn’t achieved Great Completion in the White Illusion Jiangshi Art. His fear of death was all the greater for it.
“Please show mercy...”
“Shut your mouth. If you want to live even fifteen minutes longer.”
The Blood Lord glared down at Ma Sanbao with irritation, but that was the extent of the punishment he could give.
Ma Sanbao was a useful expendable in many ways, and the Blood Lord had never intended to kill one of the few subordinates worth keeping.
He’d threatened Ma so harshly because he wanted to show off his authority and control in front of someone he disliked.
Of course, that someone paid no attention to his display and remained focused on another matter.
“They found out? This soon?”
The Blood Lord answered the Grand Sorceress’s question, which sounded almost like she’d asked herself.
“No need to make a fuss. It’s sooner than expected, but not all that surprising.”
“Looking at the result, sure. That’s about as far as your thinking goes.”
“What?”
“The Bow Saint, the Fire King, Jin Taekyung. And while he’s not on their level, even that old Daoist from the Kongtong Sect. They could’ve noticed. But that’s not what I want to know.”
The Grand Sorceress fixed the Blood Lord with a mocking look, then turned to Ma Sanbao.
“Come now. Don’t worry about your foolish superior. Tell me honestly: who was the first to notice your covert surveillance?”
“That was...”
“Once you’ve said something, you can’t take it back. I find it hard to believe the Eastern Heaven Demon Lord would take in a Disciple foolish enough to lie under these circumstances.”
Ma Sanbao hesitated. But when he met the Grand Sorceress’s fathomless gaze, he realized she already knew.
She had guessed what he’d been too afraid to say for fear of an even harsher rebuke from his violent superior.
“It was someone I’d heard of only vaguely, through brief rumors and scraps of information, more than a decade ago.”
At last Ma Sanbao answered cautiously. The Blood Lord let killing intent seep from him, while the Grand Sorceress wore a faint smile, as if she’d expected as much.
“I thought so. The East Depot wouldn’t be what it is otherwise.”
All under heaven lay within the borders of the Great Nation. To watch what lay both inside and beyond those borders, the imperial family had built a watchtower.
That watchtower was the East Depot.
From its commanding view of all under heaven, it had shared what it saw with Dark Heaven through the Eastern Heaven Demon Lord.
“Though the East Depot’s influence has waned in its conflict with the current Emperor, all manner of information still flowed in through the eyes and ears it had planted across the realm.”
“And among them was the man who noticed the surveillance today?”
“Yes. In Ningxia Province, he is called Great Sir.”
“Great Sir. An odd nickname for a martial artist.”
“It isn’t particularly well known, either. He’s a madman, and his past is shrouded in mystery.”
“Even the East Depot couldn’t find out who he was?”
“I can’t say for certain, but at the time, the Emperor was using the Embroidered Uniform Guard to keep the East Depot in check. That clearly limited what we could find out.”
Caught in those overlapping currents of the times, Great Sir had gradually been forgotten.
Until today, when Ma Sanbao dug through his old memories.
As she listened to the story of this mysterious man, the Grand Sorceress suddenly found an answer to a question she’d forgotten.
The Kongtong Sect. I wondered where Perfected Being Hyeoncheon and the Kongtong Disciples who survived Dunhuang had disappeared to along the way...
It was a suspicion close to certainty. At the same time, another question arose, and her gaze darkened.
Who in the world is he?

chapters.title: Chapter 1069
paragraphs: When someone changes in an instant, the people around them can’t help feeling uneasy.
Especially when it happens in the middle of a chase.
At Great Sir’s sudden groan, the silence shattered—and the air around us froze.
It hadn’t even been fifteen minutes since we’d shaken off the third group of pursuers.
We’d been moving quickly and quietly, keeping low among the shallow hills and reeds. Now everyone reflexively gripped their weapons. Jeok Cheongang was no exception.
“What is it?”
At his low question, everyone—including me—turned toward Great Sir.
His face had gone rigid without anyone noticing. His pupils, usually a little unfocused, had suddenly dilated, as if reflecting his state of mind. A bead of cold sweat rolled down his forehead.
“I have a bad feeling. A really bad one.”
If we’d been in Gansu, I might’ve wondered what crazy thing he was going to say this time and let it pass.

But however unhinged he was, Great Sir was an undisputed Supreme Peak master. We were in enemy territory, with threats lurking everywhere. And though it might have been a coincidence, he’d been the first to notice the enemy using birds to spy on us. We couldn’t simply brush off what he said.
A person’s innate sixth sense had nothing to do with how advanced their martial arts were.
“A bad feeling?”
Great Sir nodded at Jeok Cheongang’s grave question.
“That’s right.”
“Explain in more detail. And be polite if you don’t want to get beaten to death.”
“Understood.”
Jeok Cheongang chuckled at Great Sir’s answer, then turned to me.
“Would it be all right if this old man taught that lunatic a lesson?”
“Would it?”
“Probably not.”
“Then why ask?”
“I thought I’d check. So it really isn’t all right?”
“You can read his palm, but you can’t lay a hand on him.”
“Damn it. What’s become of the code of the martial world?”
Jeok Cheongang sighed up at the sky, then looked at Great Sir with a half-resigned expression.
“Fine. Keep talking. What exactly does it feel like?”
“How should I put it? Like an invisible hand is squeezing my insides.”
“And?”
“My stomach keeps churning, and I’m breaking out in a cold sweat.”
“Any idea what’s causing it?”
“I don’t know. It feels familiar somehow, but... Urgh!”
Before he could finish, another groan burst from him.
Great Sir’s face went pale, and he moved before anyone could stop him.
Whoosh!
He shot away so fast he left a blurred afterimage. As he vanished among the dense reeds, Jeok Cheongang, the other Supreme Peak masters, and I hurried after him.
Or rather, we were about to.
Then a sound rang out clearly from the reeds.
Prrt, splat-splat-splat!
What the fuck?
Just as we all began to dread the answer, Great Sir’s voice confirmed it.
“Ahhh, that’s a relief...”
A deathly silence fell. Jeok Cheongang stared at me in disbelief, then finally parted his tightly shut lips.
“Are you sure it’s not all right?”
“I won’t kill him. I’ll just break one thing. His arm or something, not his leg.”
At Jeok Cheongang’s earnest plea, Bow Saint muttered through her pinched nose.
“An arm might be all right...”
I’ll admit, I was tempted.
But with superhuman self-control, I resisted the urge and shook my head.
Sixth sense, my ass.
If he could just refrain from acting like a complete idiot for once, that’d be a miracle. What had I expected from someone who didn’t even know his own name?
Still, he more than pulls his weight.
I swallowed a sigh. Great Shit—no, Great Sir—emerged from the reeds after finishing his remarkably noisy business, looking completely at ease.
“Whew. I feel great.”
“...A minute ago, you said you felt terrible.”
“Me? I don’t believe I did. You must’ve misunderstood.”
“You’re really pissing me off.”
“Hm? What was that?”
“Nothing. Just talking to myself.”
“Hm. That’s a bad habit. I don’t mind, but you should break it soon. If you talk to yourself too often, people might think you’ve lost your mind.”
I must’ve lost my grip on reason for a moment.
My vision blurred, and when it cleared, a fierce-looking face was blocking my view.
“Whoa! Calm down, calm down!”
“Let go! Let go! That ugly face of yours is already bad enough. Want me to make it even worse?”
Ma Junggeol—the chief of the mounted bandits who’d somehow ended up following us this far, though he was in the horse-caravan business now—looked at me sadly.
“...That was a bit harsh.”
“Ah, sorry. I got carried away.”
Some of the sadness left his face at my apology.
“Calm down. You know Great Sir didn’t mean any harm.”
Of course I knew.
Maybe his innocence was what made it even more infuriating. He’d drawn everyone’s attention at a critical moment, and all that fuss had been over a satisfying bowel movement.
Even Shakyamuni himself would have shouted, “Amitabha, fuck this! Guanyin, drop dead!” and cracked Great Sir’s skull with a wooden fish.
But I can’t exactly leave him behind.
If pure evil existed, maybe Great Sir was it.
I heaved a sigh and raised a hand where everyone could see it, signaling them to move out.
Every moment mattered, and we’d already wasted nearly fifteen minutes for nothing. We needed to move faster.
At this rate, it could take us several extra days to reach our destination.
The first attack had come before we’d even made it all the way down from the mountain range. By now, the enemy had caught up with us three times.
Each time, the Supreme Peak masters, including me, had led the charge and wiped out the pursuers. But the important thing was how quickly and relentlessly the enemy caught up to us.
They have eyes to watch us—and monsters that can chase us without resting for a moment.
Monsters that had forgotten death, pain, and fatigue.
That was what made the undead truly terrifying.
Reborn from death, they’d lost their emotions. Though they weren’t dead, they were already as good as dead. They’d forgotten sensation, and for the same reason, they couldn’t feel fatigue.
We haven’t been down from the mountains for long. If they keep slowing us down like this...
The words surrounded and wiped out rose in my mind. I quietly swallowed them.
Anyone who thought about defeat from the start was bound to lose in the end.
Thousands, or tens of thousands.
Even if a hundred thousand undead came to close their hands around our throats, I had to lead everyone through this dense net and keep moving.
Toward our destination far to the east, where our allies in Qinghai—including the Kunlun Sect—should be waiting.
As if she’d sensed what I was thinking, Ju Hwaran broke away from the others as we moved out and came over.
“If we can make it to Qinghai Lake in the east, they won’t be able to pursue us so easily.”
Song Ilseom, who—as always—stayed close beside Ju Hwaran like a shadow, spoke up unexpectedly.
“You’re not wrong. But only if all of Qinghai’s forces have gathered there, and those monsters aren’t pursuing us with everything they have.”
“...Captain Song.”
“No, Young Lady Ju. He’s right.”
It was a discouraging thing to say, but Song Ilseom’s judgment was clear-eyed and accurate.
You could hold on to hope in a corner of your heart, but your head had to question everything.
Plan for the worst and strive for the best.
That was the surest way to survive and win.
“How far is it to Qinghai Lake?”
“Two days if we push ourselves to the limit. I’ve gone over the map thoroughly, and there’s no route that would get us there any faster.”
The old map in Ju Hwaran’s hands was anything but ordinary.
She’d inherited it from her grandfather, the man known as the Escort King. It marked secret roads hidden throughout the land and described the features of each region in detail.
But this was Qinghai Province.
The northwest in particular was an expanse of open plains and basins, with little but scattered vegetation and reed beds. For us, it was about the worst terrain imaginable.
And for them, it’s perfect.
Ju Hwaran had said that even if we pushed ourselves to the limit, it would take two days to reach Qinghai Lake.
If the pursuers kept catching up, it might take three days, four days, or even more than a fortnight.
They’re pursuing us harder than I expected. Stealth or speed—we’ll have to give up one of them.
That left me with only one choice.
And the first thing I needed to do was obvious.
“Take it off.”
I abruptly picked up the pace as I gave the order.
Jeong Hogun, moving hunched over at the rear of the Embroidered Uniform Guard, reflexively asked, “What?”
“Say that again.”
“...What did you say?”
“I said take it off. Now.”
At the sight of Jeong Hogun’s eyes practically shaking, I added an explanation to head off any misunderstanding.
“Don’t get any dirty ideas. I’m talking about that damn armor.”
I pointed at the armor, smeared with mud to hide its distinctive shine. Jeong Hogun frowned.
“I can’t. His Majesty personally bestowed this armor on every member of the Embroidered Uniform Guard.”
“So you refuse?”
“That’s right. Even an order from the Marquis of Shangshan cannot change the fact that this armor bears the authority and honor of the imperial family.”
“And you’re willing to die protecting that authority and honor?”
“That’s...”
“Fine. Keep wearing it. When you fall behind, we’ll just leave you there.”
After a brief silence, Jeong Hogun answered.
“On second thought, I believe His Majesty told us to give the Marquis of Shangshan’s orders the highest priority.”
“That’s a pretty ugly excuse.”
“Damn it.”
“I’ll take that as agreement. Don’t waste time—give the order to your men right now...”
I trailed off and stared into the hazy darkness that had settled around us.
Then I sighed and spoke to Jeong Hogun, who had just removed his helmet.
“Don’t take it off yet.”
At that moment—
Rrrrrumble.
A tremor unlike anything the previous pursuers had caused began to churn in the distance.

“Fine.
Keep talking.
What exactly does it feel like?”
“How should I put it?
Like an invisible hand is squeezing my insides.”
“And?”
“My stomach keeps churning, and I’m breaking out in a cold sweat.”
“Any idea what’s causing it?”
“I don’t know.
It feels familiar somehow, but...
Urgh!”
Before he could finish, another groan burst from him.
Great Sir’s face went pale, and he moved before anyone could stop him.
Whoosh!
He shot away so fast he left a blurred afterimage.
As he vanished among the dense reeds, Jeok Cheongang, the other Supreme Peak masters, and I hurried after him.
Or rather, we were about to.
Then a sound rang out clearly from the reeds.
Prrt, splat-splat-splat!
What the fuck?
Just as we all began to dread the answer, Great Sir’s voice confirmed it.
“Ahhh, that’s a relief...”
A deathly silence fell.
Jeok Cheongang stared at me in disbelief, then finally parted his tightly shut lips.
“Are you sure it’s not all right?”
“I won’t kill him.
I’ll just break one thing.
His arm or something, not his leg.”
At Jeok Cheongang’s earnest plea, Bow Saint muttered through her pinched nose.
“An arm might be all right...”
I’ll admit, I was tempted.
But with superhuman self-control, I resisted the urge and shook my head.
Sixth sense, my ass.
If he could just refrain from acting like a complete idiot for once, that’d be a miracle.
What had I expected from someone who didn’t even know his own name?
Still, he more than pulls his weight.
I swallowed a sigh.
Great Shit—no, Great Sir—emerged from the reeds after finishing his remarkably noisy business, looking completely at ease.
“Whew.
I feel great.”
“...A minute ago, you said you felt terrible.”
“Me?
I don’t believe I did.
You must’ve misunderstood.”
“You’re really pissing me off.”
“Hm?
What was that?”
“Nothing.
Just talking to myself.”
“Hm.
That’s a bad habit.
I don’t mind, but you should break it soon.
If you talk to yourself too often, people might think you’ve lost your mind.”
I must’ve lost my grip on reason for a moment.
My vision blurred, and when it cleared, a fierce-looking face was blocking my view.
“Whoa!
Calm down, calm down!”
“Let go!
Let go!
That ugly face of yours is already bad enough.
Want me to make it even worse?”
Ma Junggeol—the chief of the mounted bandits who’d somehow ended up following us this far, though he was in the horse-caravan business now—looked at me sadly.
“...That was a bit harsh.”
“Ah, sorry.
I got carried away.”
Some of the sadness left his face at my apology.
“Calm down.
You know Great Sir didn’t mean any harm.”
Of course I knew.
Maybe his innocence was what made it even more infuriating.
He’d drawn everyone’s attention at a critical moment, and all that fuss had been over a satisfying bowel movement.
Even Shakyamuni himself would have shouted, “Amitabha, fuck this!
Guanyin, drop dead!” and cracked Great Sir’s skull with a wooden fish.
But I can’t exactly leave him behind.
If pure evil existed, maybe Great Sir was it.
I heaved a sigh and raised a hand where everyone could see it, signaling them to move out.
Every moment mattered, and we’d already wasted nearly fifteen minutes for nothing.
We needed to move faster.
At this rate, it could take us several extra days to reach our destination.
The first attack had come before we’d even made it all the way down from the mountain range.
By now, the enemy had caught up with us three times.
Each time, the Supreme Peak masters, including me, had led the charge and wiped out the pursuers.
But the important thing was how quickly and relentlessly the enemy caught up to us.
They have eyes to watch us—and monsters that can chase us without resting for a moment.
Monsters that had forgotten death, pain, and fatigue.
That was what made the undead truly terrifying.
Reborn from death, they’d lost their emotions.
Though they weren’t dead, they were already as good as dead.
They’d forgotten sensation, and for the same reason, they couldn’t feel fatigue.
We haven’t been down from the mountains for long.
If they keep slowing us down like this...
The words surrounded and wiped out rose in my mind.
I quietly swallowed them.
Anyone who thought about defeat from the start was bound to lose in the end.
Thousands, or tens of thousands.
Even if a hundred thousand undead came to close their hands around our throats, I had to lead everyone through this dense net and keep moving.
Toward our destination far to the east, where our allies in Qinghai—including the Kunlun Sect—should be waiting.
As if she’d sensed what I was thinking, Ju Hwaran broke away from the others as we moved out and came over.
“If we can make it to Qinghai Lake in the east, they won’t be able to pursue us so easily.”
Song Ilseom, who—as always—stayed close beside Ju Hwaran like a shadow, spoke up unexpectedly.
“You’re not wrong.
But only if all of Qinghai’s forces have gathered there, and those monsters aren’t pursuing us with everything they have.”
“...Captain Song.”
“No, Young Lady Ju.
He’s right.”
It was a discouraging thing to say, but Song Ilseom’s judgment was clear-eyed and accurate.
You could hold on to hope in a corner of your heart, but your head had to question everything.
Plan for the worst and strive for the best.
That was the surest way to survive and win.
“How far is it to Qinghai Lake?”
“Two days if we push ourselves to the limit.
I’ve gone over the map thoroughly, and there’s no route that would get us there any faster.”
The old map in Ju Hwaran’s hands was anything but ordinary.
She’d inherited it from her grandfather, the man known as the Escort King.
It marked secret roads hidden throughout the land and described the features of each region in detail.
But this was Qinghai Province.
The northwest in particular was an expanse of open plains and basins, with little but scattered vegetation and reed beds.
For us, it was about the worst terrain imaginable.
And for them, it’s perfect.
Ju Hwaran had said that even if we pushed ourselves to the limit, it would take two days to reach Qinghai Lake.
If the pursuers kept catching up, it might take three days, four days, or even more than a fortnight.
They’re pursuing us harder than I expected.
Stealth or speed—we’ll have to give up one of them.
That left me with only one choice.
And the first thing I needed to do was obvious.
“Take it off.”
I abruptly picked up the pace as I gave the order.
Jeong Hogun, moving hunched over at the rear of the Embroidered Uniform Guard, reflexively asked, “What?”
“Say that again.”
“...What did you say?”
“I said take it off.
Now.”
At the sight of Jeong Hogun’s eyes practically shaking, I added an explanation to head off any misunderstanding.
“Don’t get any dirty ideas.
I’m talking about that damn armor.”
I pointed at the armor, smeared with mud to hide its distinctive shine.
Jeong Hogun frowned.
“I can’t.
His Majesty personally bestowed this armor on every member of the Embroidered Uniform Guard.”
“So you refuse?”
“That’s right.
Even an order from the Marquis of Shangshan cannot change the fact that this armor bears the authority and honor of the imperial family.”
“And you’re willing to die protecting that authority and honor?”
“That’s...”
“Fine.
Keep wearing it.
When you fall behind, we’ll just leave you there.”
After a brief silence, Jeong Hogun answered.
“On second thought, I believe His Majesty told us to give the Marquis of Shangshan’s orders the highest priority.”
“That’s a pretty ugly excuse.”
“Damn it.”
“I’ll take that as agreement.
Don’t waste time—give the order to your men right now...”
I trailed off and stared into the hazy darkness that had settled around us.
Then I sighed and spoke to Jeong Hogun, who had just removed his helmet.
“Don’t take it off yet.”
At that moment—
Rrrrrumble.
A tremor unlike anything the previous pursuers had caused began to churn in the distance.

chapters.title: Chapter 1070
paragraphs: Senses were a source of information.
Through sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch, people learned what was happening around them.
Just like now.
This is...
The sensation arrived without warning, like an uninvited guest. I held my breath and stared into the darkness, where I could barely make out objects a hundred feet away.
But as martial arts improved, so did the senses. The several jiazi of internal energy stored within me were more than enough to push mine beyond their limits.
“Don’t take it off yet.”
One short sentence was all it took.
Jeong Hogun’s eyes widened, answering for him.
Nearly at the same time—or, no, a hair before me—Bow Saint and Jeok Cheongang noticed the change. They spoke in turn.
“Dust cloud. About a thousand yards out.”
“They’re not like the ones we’ve faced so far. Everyone, prepare yourselves.”
Bow Saint told us what she’d seen and heard. Jeok Cheongang voiced his suspicion.
The same ominous suspicion I’d been having.
Rumble. Rumble.
A vibration traveled through the ground, drawing closer.
But something was different this time.
The rumble was incomparably louder and deeper than anything caused by the pursuers we’d fought on three separate occasions.
What is it?
I strained my senses further and finally caught a new clue.
Boom. Boom.
Amid the constant, faint tremors came the occasional, heavier impact.
No.
A thunderous boom.
The moment I realized, a chill ran down my spine.
That sound wasn’t something a mere human could make. It belonged to the cursed monsters that should never have existed in this world, yet had become real all the same.
Rooooom!
The boom drew closer and shook the earth. Another layer of darkness and stench spread over the low hill.
And then—
“Grrrraaaah.”
Something that could hardly be called human slowly raised its head above the hill, letting out a low, ominous roar.
No. A monster.
The moment the three thousand people saw the cursed monster with their own eyes, they froze.
Even the Embroidered Uniform Guard, whose loyalty was harder than steel.
Even the martial artists of the Black Dragon Demon Gate, who’d weathered every hardship the unorthodox martial world could throw at them.
Even the Disciples of the Zhongnan and Kongtong Sects, who’d spent long years refining their minds and bodies in the Daoist tradition.
In that moment, neither the level of their martial arts nor their experience in the martial world meant anything. Skill, age, experience—none of it could shield them from the shock.
It couldn’t have been otherwise. It was only natural.
What the hell... is that?
Everyone had the same thought as the monster appeared atop the hill.
It was huge. Just huge.
Faced with that overwhelming sight, they forgot measurements altogether. Anyone would have, seeing a monster nearly twenty feet tall with a torso as thick as an old tree.
“Grrrraaaah.”
A vast hole opened—the monster’s mouth—and wind blew from it.
Its cry was too slow to call a roar, which made it all the more chilling. The wind that poured out with it carried more than a horrible stench.
Fear.
It was fear.
The darkest emotion a human could feel—and, for some monsters, a power bestowed at birth.
There was no other word for it. People from another world called that power exactly what it was: Fear.
Hummmmmm.
The people felt the air tremble. Their vision grew hazy, and their legs would no longer lift from the ground.
“P-Primordial Heavenly Venerable...”
The groan that escaped one Daoist’s lips spoke for them all.
Supernatural powers?
The inexplicable?
No. Wrong. Not enough.
What words could possibly describe this moment, this monster, in full? Why had the god they followed allowed such a cursed being upon the earth?
Only days ago, countless followers of Dark Heaven had blackened the vast snowy fields of Great Snow Mountain. Even they hadn’t inspired this much terror.

Nor had the jiangshi who, following the Eastern Heaven Demon Lord’s bell, had stained the imperial palace’s great banquet hall with blood—the ones the Embroidered Uniform Guard remembered all too well.
At least they’d had human shapes. However far they’d fallen from being human, they’d retained something of their original form.
But—
This can’t be real.
It can’t be. This is impossible.
It’s a dream. Yes. It has to be.
Frozen where they stood, the people stared through distant, clouded eyes at the monster towering over the hill.
If Pangu, the primordial giant said to have opened the world with a single swing of his axe, had existed in some unimaginably distant past, perhaps he’d looked like that.
Of course, unlike Pangu’s majestic myth, passed down through rumor alone, this monster looked as though it had been dragged straight out of someone’s nightmare.
Boom. Rumble!
One step.
But no one who saw the low hill crumble in a single step could call it “just” a step. The monster’s heavy footfall trapped them in endless terror.

It was fear of something they’d never seen or heard of before. Just looking at it felt enough to stop their breath, as if that fear had become an invisible hand squeezing their hearts until they burst.
That was what would have happened—if a dazzling flash hadn’t erupted from somewhere at that very moment.
Whoosh!
In an instant, the pitch-black darkness split apart.
Space warped along a deep blue flame, dark yet bright, bright yet dark.
Something that was neither light nor darkness.
Fire.
Hellfire that held both darkness and light, powerful enough to burn and purify everything.
At the very tip of that fire, warping space as it surged forward, stood the enormous monster that had just stepped over the hill.
“Grrrraah!”
Its roar shook the air in every direction. At the same time, an arm as thick as a log swung toward the fire, bursting through the compressed air.
No.
It swung toward the small, unimpressive human flying at it as though he and his flame-wreathed spear were one.
Whoooosh!
A horrifyingly violent rush of air.
But even as the monster’s fist, packed with tremendous force, bore down on him, Jin Taekyung’s gaze didn’t waver. He rushed toward the monster, stepping on invisible stairs in midair.
Neither did his stride, his body hurtling forward—or the silver-white spearhead wreathed in deep-blue flame.
Shhk.
The spearhead suddenly moved with fluid grace, flames rippling along it. Their tremendous heat warped the space around them, making it look as though a fire dragon were moving through the air.
Just like the name of a spear form an old ancestor of the Fire Gate Clan had devised long ago after painstaking thought.
Fire Dragon’s Single Tail.
The fire dragon’s tail glided through the air and met the monster’s fist.
Slice!
Everyone on the ground heard the chillingly sharp cut and saw an enormous mass of flesh separate from its owner’s body.
The monster saw it too.
Puzzled, it looked at its huge fist—or rather, where its fist had been.
Only now did blood begin to bead along the cleanly severed edge.
Splaaash!
Blood erupted in a fountain. The pain arrived a moment late, while the question remained unanswered. Overwhelmed by a feeling it couldn’t comprehend, the monster writhed.
It never noticed the spearhead still streaking toward a single point.
Thud.
The monster felt something so hot its vision turned white, yet so cold it shuddered.
The spearhead had driven straight into its throat. It cut off the roar the monster had been about to unleash and poured out a fire it couldn’t possibly resist.
Just like the eyes of the man filling its vision.
“This isn’t a Troll or an ogre... What the hell are you?”
Jin Taekyung’s voice was low.
The monster lacked the intelligence to understand him. He saw as much in its large, bewildered eyes.
“Yeah. I figured. That’s all you were allowed, isn’t it?”
A monster’s Intelligence was proportional to its strength.

Jin Taekyung murmured the words as he studied it with a somber gaze. Unable to make a sound past the spearhead in its throat, the monster stared back at him, its eyes slowly dimming. He clenched his teeth.
“Who brought you into being? How?”
He wasn’t asking the monster for an answer.
It was a question for himself—and for the other enemies appearing beyond the giant’s shoulder.
Boom! Rumble!
Large and small shadows, cloaked in darkness, surged forward like a wave.
The ground, which had trembled faintly, now shook violently, as though an earthquake had begun. And it wasn’t happening in just one direction.
Rumble.
Beneath the tremendous noise of the enemies now a few hundred feet away, he felt fainter vibrations. They came from farther off, layer upon layer, in every direction.
Jin Taekyung muttered without realizing it.
“...A net over heaven and earth.”
There was no doubt. They’d been surrounded—and with meticulous care.
He knew better than anyone that low-Intelligence monsters could never have formed a net like this on their own.
Jingle. Jingle.
Faint bells sounded from all around, carried on the wind. Jin Taekyung twisted the spearhead embedded deep in the monster.
Crack. Splaaash!
The monster died without a final cry. Its body crumpled, and foul-smelling blood burst out, soaking his collar.
He didn’t care.
He’d have to be drenched in their blood countless times before the night was over. Perhaps for days to come.
It was the only way to tear through this horrifyingly tight net and make it east.
“You all saw that, right? These fuckers ain’t shit.”
Jin Taekyung spoke to everyone.
East, west, south, north.
There was nowhere to run. All they could do was fight.
“Let’s go.”
At his low command, three thousand weapons leveled toward the enemy.

chapters.title: Chapter 1071
paragraphs: I quickly took stock of our surroundings.
First, I gauged the enemy’s numbers from the dust clouds rolling in on every side and the force of the tremors coming through the ground.
At least ten thousand. No fewer than that.
Things weren’t looking good.
Even a rough count put them at more than three times our numbers. And the enemies closing in by the second were monsters that neither tired nor died easily.
There might even be another mutant like that one among them.
I turned toward the giant’s corpse. Its head was split in half, and it was dead for good.

Whatever that enormous thing had been, it wasn’t a Troll or an ogre. The monster encyclopedia recorded every kind of monster to appear since the Great Cataclysm had plunged the modern twenty-first century into chaos, and there was nothing like it in there.
As I’d thought earlier, mutant was the only word that fit. The same went for the other monsters that had begun appearing in Murim some time ago.
Right. It’s the same pattern as before.
This wasn’t the first time mutants had appeared.
Similar things had happened in Hubei and at the Nanman Beast Palace.
And I remembered clearly what had been at the center of those incidents every time: followers of the Lord of Heaven and the rifts they had brought about.
If that’s the case, could it be...?
An ominous thought flashed through my mind. I shook my head and pushed it aside.
Even if it was true, dealing with the enemies in front of us came first.
“Sama Pyo. Jeong Hogun.”
I spoke abruptly, looking the two of them straight in the eye.
“You’ll take the left and right flanks.”
They bowed without a word and moved at once.

Each commanded a thousand men. They would form our two wings, with help from a certain Supreme Peak master who’d held us up at the worst possible time—and, by a ridiculous coincidence, bought us time to prepare for the enemy.
“Great Sir.”
“Hm? Me? Can’t I sit this one out? I don’t have any particular grudge against them.”
“Fuck, Great Sir.”
“...Where should I go?”
“Both flanks. Move between them and help whichever one’s in trouble.”
“Ugh. All right.”
That would make our wings sharper and sturdier. Great Sir’s mind might wander, but a flank with a Supreme Peak master to support it wouldn’t break easily.
“And what would you have me do?”
I answered Perfected Being Hyeoncheon, the Sect Leader of the Kongtong Sect, at once.
“Please take the rear with the Kongtong Disciples, Sect Leader.”
“It’s unfortunate that the Zhongnan Sect has taken the vanguard from us, but in this situation, our sect must play the most important role. I understand your intentions, Daoist Friend.”
With the enemy’s encirclement nearly complete, the rear mattered more than the vanguard.
Hyeoncheon understood tactics better than most martial artists. He was a veteran who’d fought his way through the Great Faction War, and he’d grasped my intention immediately.
But even he hadn’t seen the whole picture.
“The Zhongnan Sect won’t take the vanguard.”
“What do you mean?”
Leaving Hyeoncheon looking puzzled, I called to a man who stood gripping his sword, his face tense.
“Hyuk Sopyung. You and the Zhongnan Sect will help the Kongtong Sect take the rear.”
Hyuk Sopyung—the Zhongnan One Dragon—stared at me, wide-eyed.
He was leading Zhongnan’s surviving Disciples in place of the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord, who’d been severely injured at Great Snow Mountain and had been forced to remain in Gansu.
And he wasn’t the only one surprised. Everyone nearby had been hanging on my every word, and they all reacted the same way.
“Then who’s taking the vanguard...?”
As Hyuk Sopyung trailed off, a rough voice cut through the crowd.
“What are you standing around for? Get your asses to the rear.”
The Fire King. Jeok Cheongang.
Beside the giant who’d stamped his mark so violently on the vast martial world stood a woman known not as a king, but as a star.
Click.
Bow Saint silently joined her two curved swords into a massive bow. Everyone fell quiet.
Who were they?
The Fire King and the Bow Saint.
The King of Kings, who held the fiercest flames. The star of the martial world, who’d ruled countless battlefields with a single bow.
Living legends of Murim.
And—
Step.
I, too, had earned the right to stand with them. I had become a symbol in my own right, someone who could walk toward the Fire King and Bow Saint.
I might be a little smaller than they were, and weaker still.
I, Jin Taekyung—the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon—was another giant who’d risen in this goddamn war.
Rrrrrumble!
The ground trembled. No, it writhed.
Apart from the low hill behind us, this reed bed had been open on every side. Now thick dust clouds surrounded it.
No—not dust clouds. Monsters we knew nothing about, from places we couldn’t name.
But—
“Anyone still scared of those worthless bastards?”
I wasn’t afraid of them.
The only thing I feared was someone dying because I’d made a mistake.
“If you’re afraid—if you want to get away—leave the formation now. I won’t blame you.”
I meant it.
Everyone had family, something they had to protect. There was no cowardice in trying to survive.
If anyone wanted to fall back so they could make it home alive, I’d gladly protect them.
Just as someone had protected me years ago in that dark, reeking cave.
And now, beside me, were people worth risking my life to protect.
“Fuck it, what’s life anyway? I’ve spent all this time following your ass around, Captain. Now I wouldn’t even flinch if the Heavenly Demon’s granddad showed up.”
Hyuk Mujin’s sudden remark drew quiet laughter from around us. Then he added, softly:
“I’ll follow you. Even to the edge of hell.”
For an instant, the air around us rang like a struck string.
The tremendous rumbling around us and the monsters’ roars beyond it might as well have vanished. In their place rose a wave of steel.
Clang, clang, clang, clang!
Weapons lifted, and a shout went up.
The fighters forgot their exhaustion and their fear of monsters they’d never seen. They roared like beasts, glaring into the shifting darkness.
They remembered why they had to be here. They remembered the faces of those they missed, the people the monsters had killed.
And at their head stood me.
“Remember only two things.”
I walked toward the vanguard as I spoke.
“First. Keep the formation, no matter what happens.”
Clack, clack, clack!
A tide of people parted before me, revealing the empty space beyond.
Unlike the other sections, where a thousand men had gathered in each, this vacant spot looked like a massive hole that could collapse at any moment. But it wasn’t one anymore.
“Second.”
Step.
I stopped among the reeds.
Bow Saint stood to my left, Jeok Cheongang to my right. Behind the three of us stood the members of the Fire Dragon Pavilion, who’d followed me as though it were the most natural thing in the world.
There were only a handful of us, but we filled the gap at the front. The formation was complete.
“Survive. Whatever it takes.”
The instant I spoke those final words—
Rrrrrumble!
A deafening roar sounded as if the sky had split open, and countless shadows poured in from every direction.
Toward the circular formation of some three thousand elite fighters.
No. Toward an enormous wheel armed in steel.
Whoooosh—BOOM!
A streak of light flew from Bow Saint’s fingertips, tore through the darkness, and exploded.
Craaaack!
The steel wheel—the wheel of death—met the monsters that did not belong in this world.
Jingle.
Beyond the swirling spray of blood, the eerie, sinister ringing of a bell carried through the air.
They were there in the deep darkness.
No. At least for now, perhaps they were the darkness.

They weren’t merely hiding in it. They wore it like a curtain, concealing their bodies behind it. Even if they hadn’t been covered head to toe in black, precious few people could have seen through that curtain.
The people capable of seeing through their concealment were hundreds of yards away, fighting countless monsters.
Monsters that, to be precise, were moving under the black-clad figures’ control.
Jingle.
One of the figures shook the sinister bell in his hand.

The sound from the old, blackened bell was dull, yet it carried clearly into the distance, conveying another set of orders and information. His comrades, hidden at regular intervals on every side, were doing the same.
“So it’s finally begun.”
BOOM!
A flash lit up the distance with a tremendous boom, and the man muttered to himself.
The monsters’ ceaseless roars made it impossible to tell much from sound alone. But that streak of light was unmistakably Bow Saint’s. The battle had begun.
“It’s not where we wanted them... Still, at least we managed to surround them.”
He couldn’t help feeling disappointed.
Fifteen minutes. If the enemy had moved just fifteen minutes faster and cleared the reed bed, he and his comrades could have begun the battle from a far more advantageous position.
“But it’s started now. Nothing to be done.”
The battle was underway, and the task assigned to the thirty sorcerers, himself included, was clear.
“Reduce their numbers as much as possible. If you can, capture Jin Taekyung alive.”
He quietly repeated the order the Blood Lord had sent half a day earlier and frowned.
“Capture him alive? Not kill him?”
He’d received information on the enemy before the order arrived. It was absurd.
Their force included no fewer than six Supreme Peak masters. Two of them were the Fire King and Bow Saint.
If the sorcerers threw everything they had at Jin Taekyung alone, they might well kill him. Capturing him alive was another matter entirely.
“Damn it.”
The curse at the Blood Lord slipped out before he could stop it. He sucked in a breath and glanced around.
But, as always, there were only monsters standing vacantly nearby, reeking horribly.
“...This is bullshit.”

He glared at his subordinates. He hated the sight of himself trembling at the thought of the Blood Lord, who was far away. Today, the mindless monsters that did nothing but stink seemed especially loathsome too.
“Stupid things.”
Jingle.
The black-robed man shook the evil bell with a shooing motion. The hundred monsters surrounding their master to guard him immediately took a step back without hesitation.
At least, that was what the black-robed man knew was supposed to happen.
Step.
He blinked.
Ninety-nine monsters had backed away. The remaining one had taken a step forward.
“What the hell is this?”
Before the black-robed man could find the words, the monster finally seemed to realize its situation. Its backside twitched as it fidgeted, then it said:
“W-Wow. Amazing. Never seen a monster like this before, have you?”
“I-I haven’t either. Damn it.”
The monster—or, clearly, someone who was a person—continued in a trembling voice, then wore a miserable expression and sighed.

chapters.title: Chapter 1072
paragraphs: At that moment, only one thought ran through the black-robed man’s mind.
Am I seeing things?
It was a reasonable question.
He was a sorcerer. An experienced one, and highly skilled.
He had neither internal energy measured in jiazi nor martial arts exceptional enough to be called divine. What he did have was the ability to control hundreds of monsters perfectly.
And yet...
What the hell is this guy?
He stared blankly at the monster before him—or rather, at the intruder who had clearly pulled a monster’s hide over himself.
Only after pinching his arm hard enough to confirm he wasn’t dreaming could he force out the question he’d been holding back.
“Who are you?”
The intruder flinched and answered haltingly.
“I-I’m a monster.”
“...You’re talking like a person.”
“A-aren’t there monsters that talk like people?”
“...There can’t be.”
Faced with the expert’s thoroughly logical rebuttal, the intruder fell silent for a moment. Then he opened his mouth.
“Grrroooar.”
“Ahem. Grrroooar.”
“G-grraaaah.”
Now he was even raising both arms like a jiangshi as he continued his uncertain attempts at a monster’s roar. The black-robed man, more confused than ever, shouted, “Stop!”
The intruder gasped. “Why?”
“What the hell are you doing?”
“I was trying my best to imitate them... Wasn’t that last one pretty close?”
“Well, the last one was a little close.”
“Wow, I knew it! Thank you!”
An exchange that strayed this far from common sense could paralyze the mind.

As the black-robed man stood speechless, the intruder, unable to hide his delight, added proudly, “All that practice for two days straight paid off. I guess it’s true what they say: hard work doesn’t betray you.”
The black-robed man blinked, still floundering in confusion.
“W-what did you just say?”
“Hm?”
The intruder tilted his head. His eyes, visible beyond the rotten hide, were clear and bright.
“Oh, about hard work not betraying you? My grandfather’s been telling me that since I was little...”
“Not that!”
“Oh, I know what you mean. The big people. Well, it’s not quite right to call them people, but anyway, I hid in there and kept trying to imitate them.”
“S-so you mean...”
“That’s right. Like I said, I’ve been doing it for two days.”
The answer was innocent enough, but the black-robed man felt a shock run down his spine.
For two days? And I never noticed?
It made no sense.
After grueling training, he’d gained the ability to control some five hundred monsters perfectly. He could detect the life energy of a living human with his eyes closed.
But...
He’s not lying.
He could feel it instinctively. Everything the intruder had said was true, without a single lie.
As far as he could tell, the man didn’t have the Intelligence to lie convincingly. And now that he’d been caught so plainly, he had no reason to hide anything.
That realization finally brought the black-robed man to his senses. Until now, he might as well have been bewitched.
“You... You’re an orthodox faction lackey.”
The intruder gasped and hurriedly waved his hands.
“N-no, I’m not!”
“Shut up, you madman.”
“Madman? That’s a very vulgar and bad word. My grandfather told me never to say it.”
“You little piece of—!”
The black-robed man felt his blood rush to his head. However unexpected the situation, he’d let this lunatic play him, if only for a moment.
He shook the evil bell in his hand, putting all his anger into the motion.
Jingle!
He hadn’t imagined the extra force in its sound.
The death energy possessed by sorcerers who commanded monsters made the ringing clearer and more sinister. That chilling note carried two messages.
First, it alerted the other sorcerers stationed nearby to what was happening.
And second—
Whoosh! Thud!
It ordered the hundred or so monsters he’d brought as guards to deal with the madman.
“You have one chance left to receive my mercy.”

The monsters swept around them with speed that belied their enormous frames, surrounding the intruder and forming an iron wall in front of the black-robed man. From behind it, he ground out his offer.
“Surrender quietly and tell me everything you know. I’ll give you a relatively quick and painless death.”
He wasn’t relying on numbers alone.
Each monster guarding him had skill comparable to a master ranging from at least Supreme First Rate up to Peak.
Their strength and speed surpassed human limits, and, more than anything, their tenacious vitality was a nightmare.
And there were a hundred of them.
Even if the intruder before him was a lunatic with tremendous skill, the outcome wouldn’t change in the slightest.
The monsters here weren’t the only ones he’d have to face.
“Struggle all you like. In a few moments, you won’t even be able to do that.”
Thinking of his fellow sorcerers, who should have received the signal and be rushing here already, the black-robed man curled one corner of his mouth.
“But why haven’t they answered?”
The intruder’s sudden question made the black-robed man reflexively ask:
“What?”
“Answered. Uh, should I call it an answering ring? Anyway, I watched you for two days. You always send a bell signal back, even for the smallest thing.”
The black-robed man suddenly realized something. He hurriedly looked around.
No. Looking would do him no good. He focused every bit of his attention on listening for his fellow sorcerers’ reply—for the sinister ringing of bells like his own.
But all he heard was the wind blowing in from far away and the breathing of the monsters around him. No answer came.
Nothing at all.
His heart lurched.
Something had gone wrong.
Terribly wrong.
As dread swept through him, his eyes turned toward the intruder. Despite being surrounded by monsters, the fellow had his ears pricked and his hands cupped around them like a trumpet, listening too.
“Oh. I definitely can’t hear anything. Nothing at all.”
“You... You...”
What could he say? How was he supposed to make sense of this?
The black-robed man could barely get the words out. Beyond the discolored monster hide, the intruder’s eyes curved clearly into crescents.
“What a relief. I knew I could count on Little Grandpa.”
“Little... Grandpa?”
“Yes. He teaches me all sorts of things. He gets really angry whenever I call him Little Grandpa, but sometimes I think he secretly likes it, too.”
The intruder caught himself rambling and snapped his mouth shut with a gasp.
“Oh, don’t tell Little Grandpa I said that. He’ll get angry again.”
The black-robed man didn’t answer. He no longer had the presence of mind to.
He stared at the intruder, who had finally stopped talking, and barely managed to force out the question that had just come to him.
“Who... No, who are you people?”
His vision swam. What he’d just heard had made him realize a truth he desperately didn’t want to believe.
The other thirty or so sorcerers who had come here with him were already dead.
They’d been killed the same way the intruder had slipped in beside him—or in a manner even more secretive and deadly.
If any were still alive, they wouldn’t be for long.
Not if the man whose sobriquet had just flashed through the black-robed man’s mind was here.
“Th-that Little Grandpa of yours... Don’t tell me he’s...”
“What did you just say?”
The flat voice suddenly pierced his ears, and a shock like lightning striking the crown of his head swept over him.
He was here.
Little Grandpa—no, that man.
Right behind him.
Yet the black-robed man hadn’t sensed his breathing. No breath had brushed the back of his neck when the man spoke. He’d detected neither the slightest presence nor a trace of life energy.
The breathless voice sounded again in the black-robed man’s ear. His body had gone rigid as a statue.
“I asked you. What were you babbling about?”
The black-robed man forgot how to speak. He even forgot how to breathe.
All he could do was make one final, instinctive struggle to survive.
He didn’t even realize that a thin line had cut across his wrist before he could move the old, bloodstained evil bell, which was practically everything he had.
Slice. Plop.
Everything came a moment too late.
The severed wrist hit the ground. Only then did its owner notice it was gone.
And the black-robed man recognized the pain only when it arrived at last, then let out a scream filled with fear.
Tap. Thud.
His body crumpled helplessly as the Sleep Acupoint was pressed.
Unable even to finish his scream, he plunged into pitch-black darkness with no end in sight. The voices of two people drifted after him, faint as a dream.
“I told you I’d kill you if you called me that one more time.”
“I’m sorry, Little Grandpa.”
“...This is driving me crazy. Let’s go find that guy.”
“Yes! Little Grandpa!”
Truly, right to the very end, it was like a nightmare.

“S-so you mean...”
“That’s right.
Like I said, I’ve been doing it for two days.”
The answer was innocent enough, but the black-robed man felt a shock run down his spine.
For two days?
And I never noticed?
It made no sense.
After grueling training, he’d gained the ability to control some five hundred monsters perfectly.
He could detect the life energy of a living human with his eyes closed.
But...
He’s not lying.
He could feel it instinctively.
Everything the intruder had said was true, without a single lie.
As far as he could tell, the man didn’t have the Intelligence to lie convincingly.
And now that he’d been caught so plainly, he had no reason to hide anything.
That realization finally brought the black-robed man to his senses.
Until now, he might as well have been bewitched.
“You...
You’re an orthodox faction lackey.”
The intruder gasped and hurriedly waved his hands.
“N-no, I’m not!”
“Shut up, you madman.”
“Madman?
That’s a very vulgar and bad word.
My grandfather told me never to say it.”
“You little piece of—!”
The black-robed man felt his blood rush to his head.
However unexpected the situation, he’d let this lunatic play him, if only for a moment.
He shook the evil bell in his hand, putting all his anger into the motion.
Jingle!
He hadn’t imagined the extra force in its sound.
The death energy possessed by sorcerers who commanded monsters made the ringing clearer and more sinister.
That chilling note carried two messages.
First, it alerted the other sorcerers stationed nearby to what was happening.
And second—
Whoosh!
Thud!
It ordered the hundred or so monsters he’d brought as guards to deal with the madman.
“You have one chance left to receive my mercy.”
The monsters swept around them with speed that belied their enormous frames, surrounding the intruder and forming an iron wall in front of the black-robed man.
From behind it, he ground out his offer.
“Surrender quietly and tell me everything you know.
I’ll give you a relatively quick and painless death.”
He wasn’t relying on numbers alone.
Each monster guarding him had skill comparable to a master ranging from at least Supreme First Rate up to Peak.
Their strength and speed surpassed human limits, and, more than anything, their tenacious vitality was a nightmare.
And there were a hundred of them.
Even if the intruder before him was a lunatic with tremendous skill, the outcome wouldn’t change in the slightest.
The monsters here weren’t the only ones he’d have to face.
“Struggle all you like.
In a few moments, you won’t even be able to do that.”
Thinking of his fellow sorcerers, who should have received the signal and be rushing here already, the black-robed man curled one corner of his mouth.
“But why haven’t they answered?”
The intruder’s sudden question made the black-robed man reflexively ask:
“What?”
“Answered.
Uh, should I call it an answering ring?
Anyway, I watched you for two days.
You always send a bell signal back, even for the smallest thing.”
The black-robed man suddenly realized something.
He hurriedly looked around.
No.
Looking would do him no good.
He focused every bit of his attention on listening for his fellow sorcerers’ reply—for the sinister ringing of bells like his own.
But all he heard was the wind blowing in from far away and the breathing of the monsters around him.
No answer came.
Nothing at all.
His heart lurched.
Something had gone wrong.
Terribly wrong.
As dread swept through him, his eyes turned toward the intruder.
Despite being surrounded by monsters, the fellow had his ears pricked and his hands cupped around them like a trumpet, listening too.
“Oh.
I definitely can’t hear anything.
Nothing at all.”
“You...
You...”
What could he say?
How was he supposed to make sense of this?
The black-robed man could barely get the words out.
Beyond the discolored monster hide, the intruder’s eyes curved clearly into crescents.
“What a relief.
I knew I could count on Little Grandpa.”
“Little...
Grandpa?”
“Yes.
He teaches me all sorts of things.
He gets really angry whenever I call him Little Grandpa, but sometimes I think he secretly likes it, too.”
The intruder caught himself rambling and snapped his mouth shut with a gasp.
“Oh, don’t tell Little Grandpa I said that.
He’ll get angry again.”
The black-robed man didn’t answer.
He no longer had the presence of mind to.
He stared at the intruder, who had finally stopped talking, and barely managed to force out the question that had just come to him.
“Who...
No, who are you people?”
His vision swam.
What he’d just heard had made him realize a truth he desperately didn’t want to believe.
The other thirty or so sorcerers who had come here with him were already dead.
They’d been killed the same way the intruder had slipped in beside him—or in a manner even more secretive and deadly.
If any were still alive, they wouldn’t be for long.
Not if the man whose sobriquet had just flashed through the black-robed man’s mind was here.
“Th-that Little Grandpa of yours...
Don’t tell me he’s...”
“What did you just say?”
The flat voice suddenly pierced his ears, and a shock like lightning striking the crown of his head swept over him.
He was here.
Little Grandpa—no, that man.
Right behind him.
Yet the black-robed man hadn’t sensed his breathing.
No breath had brushed the back of his neck when the man spoke.
He’d detected neither the slightest presence nor a trace of life energy.
The breathless voice sounded again in the black-robed man’s ear.
His body had gone rigid as a statue.
“I asked you.
What were you babbling about?”
The black-robed man forgot how to speak.
He even forgot how to breathe.
All he could do was make one final, instinctive struggle to survive.
He didn’t even realize that a thin line had cut across his wrist before he could move the old, bloodstained evil bell, which was practically everything he had.
Slice.
Plop.
Everything came a moment too late.
The severed wrist hit the ground.
Only then did its owner notice it was gone.
And the black-robed man recognized the pain only when it arrived at last, then let out a scream filled with fear.
Tap.
Thud.
His body crumpled helplessly as the Sleep Acupoint was pressed.
Unable even to finish his scream, he plunged into pitch-black darkness with no end in sight.
The voices of two people drifted after him, faint as a dream.
“I told you I’d kill you if you called me that one more time.”
“I’m sorry, Little Grandpa.”
“...This is driving me crazy.
Let’s go find that guy.”
“Yes!
Little Grandpa!”
Truly, right to the very end, it was like a nightmare.

chapters.title: Chapter 1073
paragraphs: Slice!
The moment I brought my spear down and cut through its first victim, my heart sank.
Was it because the enemy was stronger than I’d expected?
Or because some part of me was already turning over the word defeat?
No. Neither was true.
I’d believed we would win from the start. I’d never doubted it.
I was simply facing my own limits again.
The limits of a mere human—limits I could never completely escape, no matter how many times I broke through them.
How many people will die this time?
Of course I knew I wasn’t an all-powerful god who could save everyone. No one else could be one, either.
Not the heroes of distant myth. Not even Cheon Taemin, hailed as humanity’s savior.
To gain something, you had to pay a fitting price. Whether that price was time or lives.
But knowing that didn’t mean I could get used to it.
No. I must never get used to it.
If I did, I’d start taking it all for granted.
And another person’s sacrifice and death must never become something I took for granted.
Crraaaack!
Just once.
The spearhead swept through, wreathed in Force. Flesh tore with a sickening sound, and a thick mist of blood spread through the air.
If the enemy had been human, the sight would have struck them with shock and fear.
But even as dozens of monsters were minced into chunks and scattered, they didn’t so much as flinch. They surged in from every direction, a relentless tide.
Their tightly packed front line didn’t match the savage force of their charge.
Their Intelligence isn’t high enough for this. Someone’s definitely directing them.
Before the battle had begun in earnest, the eerie sound of bells had carried on the wind from every direction. I hadn’t imagined it.
Mutants, or monsters.
I didn’t know exactly what to call those hideous creatures, but one thing was clear: somewhere, someone was controlling them like puppets.
There was just one problem...
They’re well hidden.
Maybe they’d taken the presence of Supreme Peak masters like me into account. There had to be several of them, yet I couldn’t find a single one.
Neither could the person with the sharpest eyes among our allies.
Whoosh—BOOM!
Four streaks of light flew in succession toward the east, west, north, and south, swallowing the space before them as they exploded.
Amid the shock waves and thunderous blasts that shook the air on every side, a familiar, calm voice reached my ears.
“I can’t see or sense them from here. They’re at least a hundred jang away.”
Bow Saint had spoken as if she’d read my mind.
At the same moment, Jeok Cheongang appeared, drenched in the monsters’ blood.
“And there are a hell of a lot of them.”
Fwoosh—BOOM!
Before he’d even finished speaking, he thrust out a fist.
Flames raced forward, burning even the air, and swallowed the monsters in a blast of heat.
“Grrr...”
“Aaagh!”
Screams rang out one over another.
Yet even after that mighty strike brought down dozens more enemies, Jeok Cheongang’s expression didn’t brighten in the slightest.
“At this rate, it’ll never end. Unless we wipe out every last one of them, we won’t open a path.”
The battle was going our way. That much was clear.
The problem was what would happen by the time we’d killed all the monsters surrounding us.
A substantial number of our three thousand allies would be dead or wounded, and Dark Heaven would keep pursuing us afterward.
Damn it.
I swallowed the curse rising in my throat and looked around.
The battle against ten thousand monsters had begun only moments ago.
For now, thanks to the efforts of several Supreme Peak masters, myself included, we hadn’t suffered any notable casualties. But that was only a matter of time.
They were already exhausted. They’ll crumble soon.
Battle was a fight against yourself, too.
Our fighters might be handpicked elites, but unlike the enemy, they were human, made of flesh and blood.
Once you knew you stood between life and death, your body tired quickly and your thoughts began to blur.
The Supreme Peak masters were giving everything they had from the start to protect them, and we were burning through our strength faster than usual.
I was no exception.
Thwack! Thud!
My spearhead cut cleanly through the tendon in a monster’s calf. The hulking beast, a full two jang tall, dropped to one knee.
Its enormous frame looked nothing like a human’s.
The flesh covering these monsters was as tough as leather armor. Cutting through their bones, which were harder still, took even more strength.
Crack.
I poured a good deal of internal energy into a palm strike and crushed its skull. Gritting my teeth, I shouted, “Hold the formation!”
The order was repeated all around me, but the replies had already grown noticeably quieter and weaker.
Something has to change.
Fear.
The darkest emotion humans were given.
Of course they were afraid. They were surrounded by monsters they’d never seen or heard of before.
And right now, I had the power to break fear’s hold on them.
There was one move—our best chance to turn the situation around, even if it took a tremendous amount of strength.
One chance. Just one. I’ll find an opening and tear through their line in a single strike.
Even the strongest wall would fall once you forced a gap in it.
I slowly drew in a breath.
The world began to slow. The noise around me faded, and a new sense opened deep within me.
The Middle Dantian. It still felt unfamiliar.
Rumble...
The space around me suddenly trembled.
I reached out, sensing everything around me.
Or tried to.
Right then, someone appeared, letting out a roar loud enough to shatter my intensely focused senses.
“Gaaaaal!”
His voice brimmed with resolve.
With movements far too impish to match it, Great Sir stepped in front of me and swung an iron sword back and forth. I had no idea where he’d found it.
“You foolish, pitiful monsters! Gaettong, a divine general descended upon this land by Heaven’s will, has arrived! Kneel at once!”
A cold silence fell.
My allies stared blankly at Great Sir. So did the monsters charging at us from every direction.
What the hell is this guy?
Same look. Same thought.
But the man who’d worked the miracle of bringing humans and monsters together in a moment of shared bewilderment carried on in a stern voice, undeterred.
“Hey! What are you waiting for? Can’t you hear Chunja’s command?”
At the Great Sir’s pronouncement, having changed not only his name but his gender, Jeok Cheongang muttered like a man sighing, “We should’ve grabbed that guy and killed him first.”
A perfectly reasonable suggestion. I almost nodded, but that wasn’t what mattered right now.
The Great Sir showing up at the vanguard meant there was a gap in the left wing, led by Sama Pyo. And that meant our entire formation might soon collapse.
That lunatic...!
I’d known he wasn’t in his right mind. I just hadn’t expected him to pull this shit at such a critical moment.
But there was no time to vent my anger.
I held back the stream of curses rising from deep in my chest and was about to send Great Sir back to his post when—
BOOM!
The ground shook with a tremendous rumble. The nearest monster suddenly dropped to one knee.
“What... What is this?”
The sound that escaped someone’s lips gave voice to the question on all our minds, mine included.
Before we could find an answer, the other monsters surrounding us like an iron wall began to tremble.
“Grrk. Grrrk.”
“Kuwo?”
Their pupils dilated. They let out groans none of us could understand.
And then it began.
Thud. Rumble!
The ground shook as heavy bodies fell one after another, raising thick clouds of dust.
Hundreds fell, then hundreds more, then hundreds again.
It went on until every monster filling the vast reed bed had collapsed.
They fell like an enormous line of dominoes. Everyone, including me, stood speechless before the impossible sight.
Everyone except one person.
“Mm. Yes, that’s right. You’re finally behaving yourselves.”
Great Sir turned toward me, muttering smugly.
“Ahem. Did you see that? That’s what I can do.”
Of course I’d seen it.
I’d seen it perfectly clearly, right in front of me.
And at that moment, I could manage only one question.
“...What is this? Am I dreaming?”
“A dream, you say? Well put. A person’s life is like a dream in broad daylight.”
Great Sir nodded with a knowing smile.
Over his shoulder, Jeok Cheongang looked at me, half dazed.
“What... What in the world is going on?”
As if I knew. I was just as dumbfounded.
“I have no idea either,” I answered.
“You don’t know?”
“No.”
“Well, I’ve seen all sorts of strange things. Have I lived too long?”
“You have lived a long time.”
“Or could we be having the same dream?”
“Maybe. If you don’t mind, could I hit you once? I think it’d hurt too much if you hit me.”
“That sounds far too much like your usual bullshit for a dream. Come to think of it, it’s been a while since you got hit, hasn’t it?”
“That’s a very realistic reaction. Definitely not a dream, then.”
I swiftly shifted my stance to avoid the misfortune of getting hit by Jeok Cheongang, and a voice reached my ears from far away.
“Those two never change. They really don’t.”
I paused. It sounded like a boy who hadn’t even gone through puberty.
“Wow! I’ve never seen a Master and Disciple like that before!”
The next voice came on the wind, bright and impossible to forget. My lips parted before I knew it.
“...Cheongpung?”

chapters.title: Chapter 1074
paragraphs: There’s an old saying.
Those who meet must part; those who leave will surely return.
Every meeting ends in a farewell, and everyone who leaves will one day come back.
That old proverb came to mind as I stared wide-eyed at two figures approaching from far away, picking their way through the monsters strewn across the ground in the surrounding darkness.
“Over here! We’re over here!”
“How many times do I have to tell you not to shout like that...? Never mind. Do whatever the hell you want.”
“Yes! Thank you!”
“This is driving me insane.”
The young man bounced along as if he had springs in the soles of his feet, while the boy beside him sighed like an old man. To some people, they might have made a strange sight.
But I—or, rather, a tiny handful of people including me—already knew who they were.
Especially the young man bouncing along in front. You could meet him only once and never forget his energy.
“...Cheongpung?”
The name slipped from my lips before I knew it. The people who’d been frozen in a daze since the monsters’ bizarre collapse blinked.
“Cheongpung? Could it be...”
“T-the Huashan Divine Dragon?”
Their reaction was immediate.

There was only one Cheongpung I knew well enough to recognize at a glance who might turn up in a situation like this. You could turn the whole world upside down and shake it out without finding another.
Of course, someone raised a reasonable question.
“I can’t see that far. Captain, are you sure you’re not mistaken? Why would Cheongpung suddenly show up here...”
Hyuk Mujin had barely begun speaking in an uncharacteristically cautious tone when a clear voice rang out from beyond the darkness.
“Benefactooor!”
“...That’s him.”
“...It is.”
“...Just hearing him makes my head spin. It’s definitely him.”
At this point, that voice was practically a fingerprint.
Hyuk Mujin and I confirmed it, and then Jeok Cheongang put the matter to rest.
“Benefactor! I’m here!”
With that final shout, Cheongpung swept in like a gust of wind and waved at me, his face flushed.
“Wow, it’s been so long! Have you been doing well?”
How was I supposed to respond to that?
I stared at the first-time-experience menace before me, half bewildered and half glad to see him. After a moment, I finally managed to speak.
“No. Not at all.”
“Oh. You do look that way, actually.”
“Then why’d you ask?”
“I haven’t been doing well, you see. But I hoped things might be different for you. Hee-hee.”
Cheongpung said something gloomy as cheerfully as ever. Watching him, I realized how to respond.
Or rather, a quiet laugh escaped me before I could help it.
“Wait, why are you laughing?”
“You call that a question? He’s laughing because the way you act is ridiculous, you little punk.”
That wasn’t my answer.
Swish.
A boy appeared from the darkness, his presence as faint as a ghost’s—or rather, the greatest assassin of all time. He stared straight at me and added:
“Though the one laughing is just as much of a reckless brat.”
His tone was as blunt as ever.
But when I saw the faint smile at the corner of his mouth, I could only laugh aloud instead of answering.
We’d met again after several months.
Reunions with people you’ve missed are always a joy.
But none of us was stupid enough to sit around a campfire chatting in a situation like this.
“We’d best get out of here quickly. Follow me.”
Before the warmth of our reunion had even faded, the Slaughter Saint wiped the smile from his face and got moving as if nothing had happened.
“Throw away anything that might slow us down. Especially that idiot over there.”
Jeong Hogun, the idiot the Slaughter Saint had pointed out, replied.

“I don’t know what sort of elder you are, but you should at least show some courtesy. I am a Thousand Captain of the Embroidered Uniform Guard, serving under His Majesty the Emperor’s solemn command...”
Whoosh.
It happened in an instant.
The Slaughter Saint’s figure blurred. Wind swept past, and a gleaming blue dagger came to rest against Jeong Hogun’s neck.
“Go on. Keep talking. Waste even a few more moments and I’ll make you a late elder.”
Everyone, myself included, recognized the extraordinary loyalty Jeong Hogun and his Embroidered Uniform Guards bore the Emperor.
But reality was cold.
The Emperor was somewhere far away. The dagger was right against Jeong Hogun’s neck. He stared at it for a moment, then spoke with a grim face.

“As I said, I am a Thousand Captain of the Embroidered Uniform Guard, serving under His Majesty the Emperor’s solemn command...but you appear to have a close relationship with the Marquis of Shangshan, so I’ll let this pass.”
The Slaughter Saint replied dryly to that thoroughly undignified excuse for an Embroidered Uniform Guard.
“We’re not that close.”
“You seem to know each other at least somewhat, so I’ll let it pass.”
“Of course we know each other. I said we’re not close.”
“Just let it go. Understand?”
“I’ll take that as a yes.”

The Slaughter Saint had let him keep that last scrap of dignity in the name of martial-world etiquette. By the time he put away the dagger, most of our three thousand allies were staring at him in shock.
A boy who couldn’t be twenty, even by the most generous estimate, had subdued a Thousand Captain of the Embroidered Uniform Guard who had reached the far end of the Peak realm.
In a single move, so fast no one could see it.
Everyone was astonished, but Perfected Being Hyeoncheon seemed more shaken than anyone.

What you can see depends on where you stand.

Perfected Being Hyeoncheon was a seasoned Supreme Peak master, skilled enough to make out something of the Slaughter Saint’s true realm. Shock and confusion left him unable to say more, and Bow Saint spoke in his place.
“It’s been a long time. I never thought I’d see you again like this.”
The Slaughter Saint had seen through her identity, just as she had his. He answered with a bitter smile.
“I feel the same. After that day, I thought we’d never meet again.”
“Mountains and rivers have changed, and the world has changed with them. I had to act to set everything right.”
The people around them looked more confused with every word they exchanged. Bow Saint quietly added:

For an instant, the air seemed to crackle.
The Slaughter Saint.

Once condemned by the whole martial world, he had gone on to strike fear into countless great fiends after the Great War between the Orthodox and Demonic factions began. He was the greatest assassin of all time.
Those two words were enough to explain the situation to everyone.

“...I’ve gathered that much.”
The Slaughter Saint sighed as he watched Great Sir, who had somehow blended in among the Embroidered Uniform Guards and was enthusiastically stripping off his clothes.
“I’ll have to hear the details, but it seems clear enough that we’ve got one more madman.”
The original madman, of course, was watching the newcomer’s display of physical beauty from right beside him, full of admiration.

Jeong Hogun stopped Great Sir just as he was about to remove his underwear. Great Sir spotted Cheongpung, and his eyes lit up.
“Thank you for the compliment. And who might you be?”
“Hello! I’m Cheongpung!”
“You’re a spirited young man. I like that. I’m Soonja.”
“Nice to meet you, Auntie!”
No.
Are these guys seriously insane?

“War trophy.”

Or maybe it would be more accurate to say that they did, and they didn’t.
