After nearly two full days, he said, “They should be less of a nuisance from here on.”
Not one of our three thousand allies, myself included, failed to understand what he meant. He’d shaken off Dark Heaven’s relentless pursuit.
And we all knew how he’d dealt with the pursuers so quickly—and that it was he and Cheongpung, not Great Sir, who had taken down the nearly ten thousand monsters.
“Mmph, mmph.”
The war trophy—no, the black-robed man bound from head to toe in rope—wriggled. Taishan, who was running with him tucked under one arm like a piece of luggage, raised a fist as big as a cauldron lid.
“Don’t move. I’ll hit you.”
“Mmph. Mmmph!”
“Don’t make noise. I’ll eat you.”
It was a strange threat, but it worked perfectly.
The black-robed man went still and silent as a mouse. Our allies had been on a brutal forced march for days without rest, but before long we finally left that miserable wilderness behind.
Waiting for us was an enormous lake unlike any I’d ever seen. Around it, a group of beggars huddled together beside their campfires.
Among them was a very familiar face.
“Oh! They’re here! Over here!”
A face so shabby it made you reach for your wallet even from a distance.
Gung Gibang—the next beggar king, destined to lead a hundred thousand beggars.

Those who meet must part; those who leave will surely return.
Every meeting ends in a farewell, and everyone who leaves will one day come back.
That old proverb came to mind as I stared wide-eyed at two figures approaching from far away, picking their way through the monsters strewn across the ground in the surrounding darkness.
“Over here!
We’re over here!”
“How many times do I have to tell you not to shout like that...?
Never mind.
Do whatever the hell you want.”
“Yes!
Thank you!”
“This is driving me insane.”
The young man bounced along as if he had springs in the soles of his feet, while the boy beside him sighed like an old man.
To some people, they might have made a strange sight.
But I—or, rather, a tiny handful of people including me—already knew who they were.
Especially the young man bouncing along in front.
You could meet him only once and never forget his energy.
“...Cheongpung?”
The name slipped from my lips before I knew it.
The people who’d been frozen in a daze since the monsters’ bizarre collapse blinked.
“Cheongpung?
Could it be...”
“T-the Huashan Divine Dragon?”
Their reaction was immediate.
There was only one Cheongpung I knew well enough to recognize at a glance who might turn up in a situation like this.
You could turn the whole world upside down and shake it out without finding another.
Of course, someone raised a reasonable question.
“I can’t see that far.
Captain, are you sure you’re not mistaken?
Why would Cheongpung suddenly show up here...”
Hyuk Mujin had barely begun speaking in an uncharacteristically cautious tone when a clear voice rang out from beyond the darkness.
“Benefactooor!”
“...That’s him.”
“...It is.”
“...Just hearing him makes my head spin.
It’s definitely him.”
At this point, that voice was practically a fingerprint.
Hyuk Mujin and I confirmed it, and then Jeok Cheongang put the matter to rest.
“Benefactor!
I’m here!”
With that final shout, Cheongpung swept in like a gust of wind and waved at me, his face flushed.
“Wow, it’s been so long!
Have you been doing well?”
How was I supposed to respond to that?
I stared at the first-time-experience menace before me, half bewildered and half glad to see him.
After a moment, I finally managed to speak.
“No.
Not at all.”
“Oh.
You do look that way, actually.”
“Then why’d you ask?”
“I haven’t been doing well, you see.
But I hoped things might be different for you.
Hee-hee.”
Cheongpung said something gloomy as cheerfully as ever.
Watching him, I realized how to respond.
Or rather, a quiet laugh escaped me before I could help it.
“Wait, why are you laughing?”
“You call that a question?
He’s laughing because the way you act is ridiculous, you little punk.”
That wasn’t my answer.
Swish.
A boy appeared from the darkness, his presence as faint as a ghost’s—or rather, the greatest assassin of all time.
He stared straight at me and added:
“Though the one laughing is just as much of a reckless brat.”
His tone was as blunt as ever.
But when I saw the faint smile at the corner of his mouth, I could only laugh aloud instead of answering.
We’d met again after several months.
Reunions with people you’ve missed are always a joy.
But none of us was stupid enough to sit around a campfire chatting in a situation like this.
“We’d best get out of here quickly.
Follow me.”

“Throw away anything that might slow us down.
Especially that idiot over there.”

“I don’t know what sort of elder you are, but you should at least show some courtesy.

Whoosh.

chapters.title: Chapter 1075
paragraphs: Sometimes people you’ve been meaning to see all come back into your life at once.
Like right now.
“I’m Gung Gibang, a junior of Murim. It’s an honor to meet you, Seniors!”
Gung Gibang had come running as if his feet were on fire. At his hearty greeting, I spoke on everyone’s behalf in a stern voice.
“The Beggars’ Sect’s Successor Beggar, is it? Good. Pleased to meet you.”
“I’m Jin Taekyung. We’re about the same age, so from now on, feel free to call me Elder.”
“...You haven’t changed. Not one bit.”
I shrugged at the guy, whose already ugly face looked like he’d just swallowed shit.
“Of course I haven’t. If a perfectly normal person suddenly changes, it means he’s about to die.”
“I don’t think you were ever perfectly normal.”
“I was a lot better than you.”
“In what way, exactly?”
“Plenty of ways. Let’s start with our looks. We’re on completely different levels.”
“Damn it. I can’t deny that one.”
Gung Gibang let out a deep sigh, then chuckled.
“Still, I’m glad you haven’t changed.”
I laughed along with him.
It felt good to hear him say that. And I felt the same way about him.
Gung Gibang and the Beggars’ Sect disciples led us over to the campfires.

A winter-cold blizzard was howling all around us, but the warmth of the fires springing up here and there was enough to make us forget the cold. They’d also laid out dry rations to replenish our exhausted allies’ hunger and strength.
Plenty of them.
“Were you waiting for us?”
“Of course. We expected reinforcements to come from Gansu.”
Gung Gibang handed me some jerky and added, “We even figured those reinforcements might make the insane choice of crossing the Qilian Mountains.”
“Was it a rash decision? The missive from the Kunlun Sect made it sound like there wasn’t an hour to spare.”
“No. It was exactly the right call. We only got a chance to catch our breath a few days ago ourselves.”
A scab still marked Gung Gibang’s forehead, proof enough that he wasn’t lying.
A clear mark of battle.
His expression and voice were bright, but he’d recently been through a fight for his life, too.
“Oh, this? It’s nothing. Don’t worry about it. I survived, and that’s what matters.”
Gung Gibang gave me a bitter smile, doing his best to sound solemn. I looked him up and down.
“Yeah. It really is nothing.”
“What?”
“Could you let me hit you just once?”
“Hmm. If you ask nicely, maybe.”
“And what about revenge afterward?”
“Oh, come on. What do you take me for? Of course there’ll be revenge. I’ll beat you within an inch of your life.”
“...I had you pegged perfectly.”
Gung Gibang shook his head and went on. “Anyway, considering we stayed at the very rear until the end, we got off cheap. Though that was only thanks to help arriving at just the right time.”
Gung Gibang glanced toward the Slaughter Saint, who’d been chewing his jerky in silence.
“You were just lucky,” the Slaughter Saint said. “We happened to be nearby.”
“I was truly shocked at first. I never imagined you’d be in Qinghai with Cheongpung...”
“The more people who know about you, the harder it is to accomplish your goal. And I’m no Great Hero.”
In other words, he’d kept his existence hidden even from his own allies.
“Then had you been here the whole time since we left for the Nanman Beast Palace?” I asked.
“I wouldn’t say the whole time. We only arrived in Qinghai about a month ago.”
I thought back over the past few months.
The last time I’d seen the Slaughter Saint was just after the Two Dragons Pavilion was founded, with Cheongpung and me at its center, around the time we left for Nanman.
So even setting aside that month in Qinghai, he’d spent the past several months on some kind of mission with Cheongpung...
Why hadn’t I heard a single thing about it?
It was strange.
Since we’d parted, I’d been caught up in one major incident after another, starting with the Nanman Beast Palace. Each time, the whole world’s attention had turned our way.
Rumors traveled tens of thousands of ri without needing legs.
And yet I hadn’t heard anything about where the Slaughter Saint and Cheongpung had been or what they’d done.
The Slaughter Saint clearly didn’t want to tell me, either. Before I could ask, he spat out the jerky he’d been chewing.
“Tough. I’ll be resting nearby for a bit. Don’t look for me.”
He hadn’t said anything directly, but his actions made his meaning clearer than words.
“Always keeping secrets,” Jeok Cheongang muttered, clicking his tongue as he watched the Slaughter Saint walk away. “No wonder people say he’s got a foul temper.”
Then he saw my expression and frowned.
“What’s with that rotten look?”
“...What did I do?”
“Explain yourself.”
“N-nothing. You probably know better than I do.”
“What’s that supposed to mean?”
Cheongpung, sitting near the campfire with a drowsy expression, spoke up on my behalf.
“Obviously, it means Grandpa Jeok’s temper is just as foul, doesn’t it, Benefactor?”
“Huh? Am I wrong?”
Of course he was right.
But some uncomfortable truths couldn’t be said out loud. Especially when doing so might get you beaten to death.
Cheongpung, you little shit...

I stared at him with a dead-eyed look. He’d been gone a while, but apparently he’d learned a new assassination technique from the Slaughter Saint. I did my best to ignore Jeok Cheongang’s scorching gaze beside me and changed the subject.
“So, Cheongpung, where have you been and what have you been doing for the past few months?”
“Hmm. Little Grandpa told me not to say.”
“You can tell me.”
“He knew you’d say that. He told me not to say anything even if it was you, Benefactor.”
“I’m telling you, it’s fine. If you’re worried, just whisper it to me with Sound Transmission...”
“Wow, that’s amazing. He even told me to keep quiet if you tried to talk me into telling you by Sound Transmission.”
“He said he’d kill me if I said anything. I think I’ve heard ‘Silencing the Witnesses’ about five thousand times by now.”
“...Then I won’t ask.”

Of course, the Slaughter Saint wouldn’t try to silence the witnesses just because Cheongpung told me everything that had happened so far. But at this point, it would be polite not to press him further.
Well.
To be honest, I was also a little scared he really might try to silence the witnesses.
“What about what happened in Qinghai? Is that a secret, too?”
“No. He didn’t say anything about that, so I think it’s fine.”
Cheongpung answered innocently and gave us a rough account of the past month.
He started with why they’d slipped into Qinghai without telling anyone, and what they’d come to do.
“You were looking for spies who might already be inside?”
“Yes. Little Grandpa said a traitor at your back is scarier than an enemy right in front of you.”
He was right.
I’d learned that the hard way more than once. I couldn’t take those words lightly.
“So, did you find any spies?” Jeok Cheongang asked.
“No. At least, not as far as we could tell.”
If Cheongpung had been on his own, I might’ve checked his work a hundred times and still had my doubts. But if the Slaughter Saint was part of that we, I could trust it.
He wouldn’t have been called the greatest assassin of all time if he weren’t that thorough.
Still...
“It’s too soon to relax,” Jeok Cheongang said. “You never know what might happen in Murim.”
Spoken like a veteran of the martial world. Cheongpung nodded.
“That’s right. Little Grandpa thought so, too. So he was going to infiltrate the Kunlun Sect and investigate further.”
There was a big difference between was going to and did.
And I already knew what had stopped him.
“Dark Heaven attacked just then. Right?”
“Yes. It happened in an instant.”
They had an overwhelming advantage in numbers and strength.
Some of Qinghai’s martial artists, including those of the Kunlun Sect, immediately withdrew from the sect’s headquarters and retreated east. But the Slaughter Saint and Cheongpung stayed.
“We hid among them and waited for the right moment.”
Anyone else who’d tried that would have been discovered and killed long ago.
But the Slaughter Saint was an exception.
And so was the other person who’d spent the past several months learning from him.
“I held my breath and hid my presence, just like Little Grandpa taught me. No one noticed. Like this.”
As soon as he finished speaking, Cheongpung stopped breathing with a sharp hup. Instead of answering, I let out a hollow laugh.
Not because of how ridiculous he looked, but because his presence had faded to a ghostly blur, even though he was right in front of me.
Can he really do that? After only a few months?
I’d known the answer for a long time.
Yes—if it was Cheongpung.
With that insane talent of his, as if he didn’t need a System at all, he could learn even a concealment technique that difficult in no time.
With talent like that and the Slaughter Saint teaching him, of course they could avoid being noticed.
A first-rate teacher and a heaven-sent genius.
Together, they’d managed to infiltrate the enemy.
Of course, even they had their limits.
“I did my best, but unfortunately, I couldn’t get as far as Taiqing Hall.”
“Taiqing Hall...?”
“It’s on the highest peak of Kunlun Mountain. It’s where the Kunlun Sect decides everything, big and small. But there was a strange energy surrounding the area.”
Cheongpung shuddered, as if remembering how it had felt.
“I could feel something... something invisible and sticky. It gave me chills.”
“Sticky? And it gave you chills?”

“Yes. Enough to make me shudder. Little Grandpa must have felt it too, because he decided we should blend in with the monsters coming down the mountain just then and turn back. A few days later, we met you, Benefactor.”
Even after he finished, Cheongpung’s expression didn’t improve. I watched him with a deep, steady gaze and quietly turned over the two words that had come to mind the moment I heard his story.
Magical power.
And at that very moment—
Splash!
A gentle ripple spread across the broad blue river beyond the thick veil of fog.

The last time I’d seen the Slaughter Saint was just after the Two Dragons Pavilion was founded, with Cheongpung and me at its center, around the time we left for Nanman.
So even setting aside that month in Qinghai, he’d spent the past several months on some kind of mission with Cheongpung...
Why hadn’t I heard a single thing about it?
It was strange.
Since we’d parted, I’d been caught up in one major incident after another, starting with the Nanman Beast Palace.
Each time, the whole world’s attention had turned our way.
Rumors traveled tens of thousands of ri without needing legs.
And yet I hadn’t heard anything about where the Slaughter Saint and Cheongpung had been or what they’d done.
The Slaughter Saint clearly didn’t want to tell me, either.
Before I could ask, he spat out the jerky he’d been chewing.
“Tough.
I’ll be resting nearby for a bit.
Don’t look for me.”
He hadn’t said anything directly, but his actions made his meaning clearer than words.
“Always keeping secrets,” Jeok Cheongang muttered, clicking his tongue as he watched the Slaughter Saint walk away.
“No wonder people say he’s got a foul temper.”
Then he saw my expression and frowned.
“What’s with that rotten look?”
“...What did I do?”
“Explain yourself.”
“N-nothing.
You probably know better than I do.”
“What’s that supposed to mean?”
Cheongpung, sitting near the campfire with a drowsy expression, spoke up on my behalf.
“Obviously, it means Grandpa Jeok’s temper is just as foul, doesn’t it, Benefactor?”
“Huh?
Am I wrong?”
Of course he was right.
But some uncomfortable truths couldn’t be said out loud.
Especially when doing so might get you beaten to death.
Cheongpung, you little shit...
I stared at him with a dead-eyed look.
He’d been gone a while, but apparently he’d learned a new assassination technique from the Slaughter Saint.
I did my best to ignore Jeok Cheongang’s scorching gaze beside me and changed the subject.
“So, Cheongpung, where have you been and what have you been doing for the past few months?”
“Hmm.
Little Grandpa told me not to say.”
“You can tell me.”
“He knew you’d say that.
He told me not to say anything even if it was you, Benefactor.”
“I’m telling you, it’s fine.
If you’re worried, just whisper it to me with Sound Transmission...”
“Wow, that’s amazing.
He even told me to keep quiet if you tried to talk me into telling you by Sound Transmission.”
“He said he’d kill me if I said anything.
I think I’ve heard ‘Silencing the Witnesses’ about five thousand times by now.”
“...Then I won’t ask.”
Of course, the Slaughter Saint wouldn’t try to silence the witnesses just because Cheongpung told me everything that had happened so far.
But at this point, it would be polite not to press him further.
Well.
To be honest, I was also a little scared he really might try to silence the witnesses.
“What about what happened in Qinghai?
Is that a secret, too?”
“No.
He didn’t say anything about that, so I think it’s fine.”
Cheongpung answered innocently and gave us a rough account of the past month.
He started with why they’d slipped into Qinghai without telling anyone, and what they’d come to do.
“You were looking for spies who might already be inside?”
“Yes.
Little Grandpa said a traitor at your back is scarier than an enemy right in front of you.”
He was right.
I’d learned that the hard way more than once.
I couldn’t take those words lightly.
“So, did you find any spies?” Jeok Cheongang asked.
“No.
At least, not as far as we could tell.”
If Cheongpung had been on his own, I might’ve checked his work a hundred times and still had my doubts.
But if the Slaughter Saint was part of that we, I could trust it.
He wouldn’t have been called the greatest assassin of all time if he weren’t that thorough.
Still...
“It’s too soon to relax,” Jeok Cheongang said.
“You never know what might happen in Murim.”
Spoken like a veteran of the martial world.
Cheongpung nodded.
“That’s right.
Little Grandpa thought so, too.
So he was going to infiltrate the Kunlun Sect and investigate further.”
There was a big difference between was going to and did.
And I already knew what had stopped him.
“Dark Heaven attacked just then.
Right?”
“Yes.
It happened in an instant.”
They had an overwhelming advantage in numbers and strength.
Some of Qinghai’s martial artists, including those of the Kunlun Sect, immediately withdrew from the sect’s headquarters and retreated east.
But the Slaughter Saint and Cheongpung stayed.
“We hid among them and waited for the right moment.”
Anyone else who’d tried that would have been discovered and killed long ago.
But the Slaughter Saint was an exception.
And so was the other person who’d spent the past several months learning from him.
“I held my breath and hid my presence, just like Little Grandpa taught me.
No one noticed.
Like this.”
As soon as he finished speaking, Cheongpung stopped breathing with a sharp hup.
Instead of answering, I let out a hollow laugh.
Not because of how ridiculous he looked, but because his presence had faded to a ghostly blur, even though he was right in front of me.
Can he really do that?
After only a few months?
I’d known the answer for a long time.
Yes—if it was Cheongpung.
With that insane talent of his, as if he didn’t need a System at all, he could learn even a concealment technique that difficult in no time.
With talent like that and the Slaughter Saint teaching him, of course they could avoid being noticed.
A first-rate teacher and a heaven-sent genius.
Together, they’d managed to infiltrate the enemy.
Of course, even they had their limits.
“I did my best, but unfortunately, I couldn’t get as far as Taiqing Hall.”
“Taiqing Hall...?”
“It’s on the highest peak of Kunlun Mountain.
It’s where the Kunlun Sect decides everything, big and small.
But there was a strange energy surrounding the area.”
Cheongpung shuddered, as if remembering how it had felt.
“I could feel something... something invisible and sticky.
It gave me chills.”
“Sticky?
And it gave you chills?”
“Yes.
Enough to make me shudder.
Little Grandpa must have felt it too, because he decided we should blend in with the monsters coming down the mountain just then and turn back.
A few days later, we met you, Benefactor.”
Even after he finished, Cheongpung’s expression didn’t improve.
I watched him with a deep, steady gaze and quietly turned over the two words that had come to mind the moment I heard his story.
Magical power.
And at that very moment—
Splash!
A gentle ripple spread across the broad blue river beyond the thick veil of fog.

chapters.title: Chapter 1076
paragraphs: The river there was blue, and as wide as the sea.
Perhaps that was why.
Over a span of time stretching back beyond anyone’s memory, an unnamed freshwater lake had grown ever larger. Then, one day, people began calling it Qinghai Lake.
At this very moment, a shadow was crossing the blue waters of Qinghai Lake.
Splash.
A dozen or so oars pushed through the water in smooth, perfect unison.
Gentle ripples spread in their wake. The thick mist parted, revealing the shape it had concealed.
Sleek, streamlined curves.
A hull that was not especially large, but built of sturdy wood and reinforced with steel.
A sail billowing in the wind—and, seated cross-legged in perfect calm atop a mast so narrow no one would dare set foot on it, an old man.
“What a tailwind. Couldn’t ask for better.”
At the old man’s voice overhead, the middle-aged man standing at the bow, gazing beyond the mist, answered.
“The days ahead will be the same.”
“Even though we’ve already lost our sect’s headquarters?”
“We didn’t lose it. We gave it up to save precious lives.”
The middle-aged man continued steadily.

“Someone I respect once told me that what matters isn’t the house, but the people. A house where no one lives becomes an abandoned ruin. But where there are people, they can build a palace even on an empty plain.”
“I don’t know who told you that, but he must be an old man who talks a fine game and has nothing to show for it.”
“M-Master. How could you say that? I didn’t mean—”
“Ha ha. I know. I’m teasing.”
The old man, who had just called himself all talk and no substance, smiled at his flustered Disciple and went on.
“So the days ahead will carry us along like a tailwind... I could ask for nothing more, if only that were possible. But the headwind we’ve faced has been so fierce. What are we to do?”
The middle-aged man shook his head at his Master’s teasing, then answered firmly.
“No matter how fierce the wind is, it can’t overturn a mountain instead of a ship.”
“You’re right. But what if that fierce wind carries an ember?”
“The wind isn’t what we should fear. It’s a single ember hidden somewhere deep in the mountains, where no one knows to look. Before long, it might turn everything to ash.”
The middle-aged man pondered the meaning of his Master’s words. Then his expression tightened.
Master. Do you mean...?
A line of Sound Transmission slipped between his trembling lips.
But before he could hear the answer, the old man slowly rose and murmured:
“Even so, there should be a chance to fight fire with fire.”
At that moment—
Whoosh.
Beyond the mist as it scattered in all directions, hundreds of campfires lined the banks of Qinghai Lake, reflected in the old man’s gray-white eyes.
The sparks drifting on the wind were sparks of hope against the coming disaster.
The moment a sleek ship appeared through the mist, I knew who they were.
Or, more precisely, I recognized the old man gazing down at the shore from atop its towering mast.
Whoosh.
The sides of his robe spread and fluttered like wings.
He soared like a bird, crossed dozens of jang through the air, and began to descend. Cries of astonishment rose all around us.
“Th-that’s...”
“Stepping on Empty Air...!”
Stepping on Empty Air was a supreme lightness skill that required several jiazi of internal energy and deep enlightenment.
These people had fought a desperate battle against monsters they’d never seen or heard of until two days ago. But that hadn’t made them any less awed by the highest martial arts.
I, however, saw it a little differently.
“Now that’s a remarkable display of Stepping on Empty Air. Don’t you think so, too?”
At Jeok Cheongang’s probing question, I clicked my tongue.
“Do I look like an idiot to you?”
“What kind of rude answer is that?”
“You already know what I mean.”
“...Hm. So you’re not completely blind, after all.”
I couldn’t tell whether he was displeased that I hadn’t played along or pleased by the progress I’d made. Jeok Cheongang murmured and gazed into the air.
“Still, when it comes to lightness skills, he’s pretty good.”
I let out a quiet laugh.
Coming from Jeok Cheongang, that was extraordinary praise. But it still fell short of the lightness skill the old man was displaying as he slowly descended.
If you call Gliding Across the Void “pretty good,” every martial artist who’s learned a lightness skill should bite their tongue and die.
There’s always another sky above the sky.
Those whose knowledge of martial arts was shallow, or who had no place in Murim, considered Stepping on Empty Air the pinnacle. But there was a realm beyond it.

Not stepping on the air or kicking off it, but moving through it as naturally as if gliding. That was Gliding Across the Void. Only a handful of Supreme Peak masters, myself included, could recognize the difference. I could see it in the old man’s feet.
And in the past hundred years, only two people have reached the realm of Gliding Across the Void.
Jeok Cheongang had told me about them while I was training on Mount Jiuhua.
One had eventually come to be called a god. The other had returned to where he belonged.
To a land far to the west, to the vast slopes of a mountain that touched the sky.
Swish.
At last, his toes touched the ground without a sound, and his robes settled around him.
The kindly-looking old man clasped his hands in greeting to everyone.
“I am Cheongheoja of the Kunlun Sect. My greetings to all my fellow Daoists.”
An invisible wave of emotion swept through the crowd.
The old man who had appeared so suddenly with such astonishing skill was none other than the Sect Leader of the Kunlun Sect.
“W-We greet the Sect Leader!”
Urgent cries rose all around, accompanied by clasped-fist bows.
But, as always, there were exceptions.
“Fellow Daoist, my ass. You’ve gotten older and now you think you can treat this old man as an equal?”
That curt greeting from Murim’s veteran drill sergeant and the bane of every prestigious sect was only the beginning.
“It’s been a long time, Cheongheoja. You’ve got a lot more gray hair now. The last time I saw you, you still looked fairly young.”

Over the shoulder of the bow-wielding lady, who was at least from a respectable family and had bothered to use polite speech, a human butcher appeared—the man who’d become the greatest of all time through his skill at cutting people down.
“I thought you looked familiar. So you ended up becoming Sect Leader?”
The commotion over the Kunlun Sect Leader’s arrival died at once.
The Slaughter Saint, the Bow Saint, and the Fire King Jeok Cheongang.
What an insane lineup. Just looking at them was enough to take your breath away.

They might look middle-aged, mature, and boyish, respectively, but with the amount of time they’d spent in Murim, they could perform the miracle of feeding five thousand with five loaves and two fish.
And Cheongheoja’s ordeal wasn’t over.
“Mm. This humble Daoist is late in greeting you. How have you been all this—”
Perfected Being Hyeoncheon, the Sect Leader of the Kongtong Sect, had hesitated at the arrival of those martial-world veterans. He had only just managed to speak when—
“Hello, Grandpa Cheongheoja! I’m Cheongpung! We both have the surname Cheong, so I hope we get along from now on!”
“I am Soonja. We don’t share a surname, but the last syllable of our names is the same. Let’s get along well enough.”
“Taishan hungry. Did you catch any meat on your way here?”
A different kind of insane lineup.
Pure, unfiltered madness.
The arrival of that hopeless trio, every bit as disastrous as the Three Saints, made my vision dim. Yet, to my surprise, Cheongheoja chuckled.
“Some respected Seniors, and some juniors I’m meeting for the first time. It’s a pleasure to meet you all again.”
At that moment, I had a thought.
Maybe the greatest sect under heaven was the Kunlun Sect.
“...Wow. He actually put up with that.”
The exclamation slipped from my lips before I could stop it, and Cheongheoja turned his gaze toward me.
“This is the first time I’ve seen you up close. It’s good to meet you, Fellow Daoist Jin.”
As he’d said, I’d seen him before, though only from a distance.

And our connection went a little deeper than simply having crossed paths. During the Star-Array Grand Banquet, Hak Woo—the Kunlun Cloud Dragon—had spent some time with Gung Gibang and the others. He was Cheongheoja’s Disciple.
“I greet the Sect Leader.”
I belatedly clasped my hands in a formal bow. Cheongheoja nodded with a warm smile.
“It’s been a long time. I’ve heard a great deal about you since then. That boy Hak Woo was especially fond of you.”
“Um, by any chance...”
As if he’d seen through the question I couldn’t quite bring myself to finish, Cheongheoja answered gently.
“He’s doing well. You needn’t worry.”
“That’s a relief.”
I couldn’t say I’d known Hak Woo for long, but the guy I knew was a good one.
As a martial artist, and as a person.
So I was genuinely glad to hear what Cheongheoja said next.
“You’ll see him soon. Once we’ve left this place.”
“I see.”
I already knew Qinghai Lake wasn’t our home base. Gung Gibang and the Beggars’ Sect disciples had simply come ahead to meet us; the threat from Dark Heaven hadn’t disappeared completely.
But Cheongheoja’s words did raise one question...
“Even so, the boat seems a little, well... pretty small.”
I looked dubiously at the ship, which had nearly reached the shore.
It looked like it could hold a hundred people at most—nowhere near enough to carry our three thousand allies.
“Does it look that way to you, too?”
“Sorry, but yes.”
“Ha ha.”
Cheongheoja laughed aloud at my honest answer, then spoke again.
“I suppose it might. From what you can see now.”
“Pardon?”
“Ah, there they are at last.”
I followed Cheongheoja’s gaze. So did everyone else.
Splash.
Only then did we see dozens of ships emerge through the thick mist.

chapters.title: Chapter 1077
paragraphs: Around noon, a group of black-clad men appeared atop a low hill.
Swish.
Pat, pat, pat!
At a casual wave from the man in front, several dozen of them scattered across the area to investigate what had happened here and deal with the aftermath.
“So someone got here before us.”
The man murmured to himself as he looked down the hill at the vast reed beds stretching for more than ten li in every direction—and the countless birds filling the gaps between them with black.
“They must have been hungry. It can’t have been an easy journey.”

Qinghai Lake, a few days’ travel from here, was a haven for migratory birds. Reaching it meant beating their wings without rest for a thousand li, but enormous numbers came each year for its clean water and abundant food.
Of course, that was all in the past now.
Whoooosh.
A wind carrying a biting chill suddenly swept through the reeds. The migratory birds, busy filling their empty stomachs, shivered.

The cold was far too severe to be explained by the high elevation alone. At noon, when the sun should have been at its highest, black clouds covered the sky. Untimely frost had frozen the reed beds solid.
And these inexplicable changes, as though the seasons had forgotten their place, had been going on for more than a day or two.

Temperatures had fallen, and bitter cold raged day and night. Without enough sunlight, the plants had lost their former lushness. Elsewhere, severe drought had struck. It seemed the work of heaven’s whims or some supernatural power—especially when all of it had happened in little more than a year.
But Ma Sanbao saw things differently.
Crunch, crunch.
Frost broke beneath his feet as he slowly descended the hill. His thoughts deepened with each footprint he left behind.
This is no mere supernatural trick. His power borders on that of a heavenly god.
Heaven itself. An all-knowing, all-powerful god.

Thinking of his master, the Lord of Heaven, Ma Sanbao felt fear and reverence rise from the depths of his heart. Here was a being who could threaten the whole world, change the climate, and even bring the dead back to life.
Could someone like that truly be called human?
And why had he shared a portion of that unbelievable power with Ma Sanbao, who had abandoned even his own master—a man who had served the Lord of Heaven—and fled?
No. I’m different from my Master. I can be of far greater use to him in every way.
Ma Sanbao repeated the words to himself. The Eastern Heaven Demon Lord, whom he had served as Master all his life, had met a weak end. Ma Sanbao would not.
He would contribute greatly to the Lord of Heaven’s grand design, and rule over a part of this world as his new servant.
Caw.
Snapping out of his thoughts, Ma Sanbao noticed countless pairs of eyes glinting at him and gave a quiet laugh.
“Looks like I’ve interrupted your meal. Don’t mind me. Go on and finish.”
His kind words made no difference. The birds covering the reed beds greeted their unexpected visitor with sharp cries, their bloodshot eyes flashing.
The killing intent in those eyes was far too intense to belong to ordinary birds.
“Well, the changes have already begun.”
Clicking his tongue, Ma Sanbao studied them with interest.

Their beaks were smeared with blood. Their feathers and claws had grown thick and sharp, like those of predators. Beneath them lay the dishes that made up this lavish feast, giving off a stench of death as horrifying as the sight of them.
“Really, that instinct of yours is the problem.”
It wasn’t hard to work out what had happened.

The changing climate had frozen the plants to death, and the beasts and insects had long since disappeared. Unable to find food, countless migratory birds must have left Qinghai Lake and wandered the surrounding area. Some had finally found a meal in these nearby reed beds: the blood and flesh of monsters lying there like puppets with their strings cut.
“I needed to replenish my forces anyway. This worked out nicely.”
Ma Sanbao smiled at the birds as they began to mutate.
Lately, some lunatic called the Great Sir had been knocking his birds out of the sky wherever he found them, making it difficult to keep watch. This many new birds was an unexpected windfall.
Cawww!
First, though, he would have to imprint the birds, now savage from eating cursed blood and flesh.
“All right. From now on, I’m your master.”
Jingle.
The moment Ma Sanbao shook the ritual bell in his hand—
Whoooosh!
The countless birds hurtling toward him on beating wings changed course at once and shot high into the sky, obeying the bell’s dull, eerie chime.
And the birds weren’t the only ones to respond.
Shrrk. Rumble.
Bent knees straightened. Rigid backs unbent. Finally, tightly shut eyes opened halfway.
“More of them survived than I expected.”
As Ma Sanbao murmured, watching the monsters rise to their full height throughout the broad reed beds, the black-clad men who had gone off earlier returned to report.
“We’ve checked everything.”
“What did you find?”
One of the men respectfully held out something he was carrying.
Part of its face had been pecked away by birds. Otherwise, it looked just as it had in life, its perfectly natural expression frozen in place.
It was someone’s head. Until a few days ago, the man had been Ma Sanbao’s subordinate and their comrade.
“Most of them were in this condition.”
“This...”
Ma Sanbao’s eyes widened as he examined the head.
He was a sorcerer, but his martial skill had also reached Supreme Peak. Even so, the sword mark left on the head was so faint that it sent a chill down his spine.
“...A killing sword. One honed to its utmost.”
“What does that mean?”

“There’s a man called No Shadow. The Great Nation’s imperial household raised him as its finest assassin. He guarded the Son of Heaven from the shadows, and even the East Depot I once served couldn’t determine his true identity.”
But even No Shadow couldn’t leave a sword mark like this.
Ma Sanbao knew that well. Through relentless investigation and pursuit, he had once obtained the body of someone No Shadow had killed.
Now another man came to mind: a lame old man Jin Taekyung had killed during the bloodbath at the Grand Banquet a few months earlier.
Gye Yabu.
The last heir of Salcheonmun, the greatest assassin sect in the world, long believed to have vanished.
Why had he come to mind now?
Ma Sanbao soon found the answer.
“The Slaughter Saint...”
Yes. His presence explained everything.

Why not a single human corpse remained in these vast reed beds, where a fierce battle must have taken place. And why so many monsters had avoided a second death, even though the sorcerers had been eliminated.
“He finished it quickly. He knew exactly where we were vulnerable.”
Muttering to himself, Ma Sanbao flung his subordinate’s head far away.
The power bestowed on him by the Lord of Heaven allowed him to raise the dead, but not without limit.
“We’re leaving. By now, they must have left Qinghai Lake. We’ll hurry back and carry out the next order.”
The damage was done. At least they had recovered a considerable number of their forces and gained new subordinates. Ma Sanbao put his regret aside and turned to leave.
Or rather, he was about to.
“However...”
One of the black-clad men spoke up hesitantly.
“One man. Just one man is missing.”
“What?”
“We found a mutilated wrist, but no body anywhere.”
“Then...”
“It seems they captured him alive.”
Ma Sanbao’s face twisted before he could stop himself.
After all his warnings to be careful, the man hadn’t even died. He’d been captured.

But his anger and agitation lasted only a moment. They had lost some valuable subordinates, and one had been taken alive, but those men were only minor branches of a much greater whole. Ma Sanbao hadn’t entrusted them with much information.
What bothered him a little was what his subordinate said next.
“The ritual bells they were carrying are gone, too. Every last one.”
“...What are they, thieves? They made sure to take everything.”
Ma Sanbao frowned, thought for a moment, then shook his head.
“No need to worry. Even with the bells, they can’t do anything.”
A country bumpkin couldn’t become a Supreme Peak master overnight just by getting hold of a divine weapon. Likewise, using the bells properly required extensive training.
“Besides, even if the man they captured betrays us, he can command only a few hundred.”
“That’s impossible. We know him. He’s loyal to the Heavenly Court, yes, but more than that, he’s simply not the sort of man who could betray anyone...”
Seeing his subordinates defend their captured comrade, Ma Sanbao let out an involuntary laugh.
“He will.”
“Pardon?”
“He will betray us. No—they’ll make sure he does.”
Ma Sanbao added quietly, “If that son of a bitch I know is involved, they will.”
The face of that son of a bitch flashed before his eyes, and he reflexively reached inside his robe.

He remembered the note Jin Taekyung had handed him a few months earlier, pretending it was an important secret letter to deceive him. More precisely, he remembered the mysterious symbols written on it—symbols that even Ma Sanbao, for all his learning, couldn’t decipher.
—You fucking dumbass lol
Still unable to make sense of them, Ma Sanbao ground his teeth.
Just wait. I’ll pay you back soon.
His gaze, fixed on the east, seemed to be directed at someone crossing Qinghai Lake.

Swish.

Untimely frost had frozen the reed beds solid.

chapters.title: Chapter 1078
paragraphs: Qinghai Lake was like a small sea, just as its name suggested.
It was more than ten jang deep and stretched for thousands of li.

Without the ships, our allies—who’d even abandoned their horses on the way to Qinghai—would have had to walk for days and nights. But the dozens of ships that arrived after Cheongheoja, the Sect Leader of the Kunlun Sect, could easily carry all three thousand of us.
Shhhhh!
A bow carved with the shape of a cloud sliced through the water.
I was silently watching the lake, where the bitter cold had left thin ice in places, when a voice reached my ears.
“Isn’t it strange? Winter is still a long way off, yet we’re already seeing this.”

I turned to find a sturdy-looking middle-aged Daoist. His face and voice were still unfamiliar, but we’d exchanged a brief greeting when I boarded the ship yesterday. I had no trouble remembering his Daoist name.
“Oh, Perfected One Hakso.”
The Daoist’s smile turned awkward.
“It’s Hak Su. Not Hakso.”
The silence grew awkward fast. After a moment, I forced myself to speak.
“Uh, did you happen to change your Daoist name recently?”
“No. Not once since I joined Kunlun.”
“Then how long ago did you join?”
“Certainly not yesterday. It’s been over forty years.”
“I see.”
“Yes.”
No trouble remembering, my ass.
With nothing left to say, I looked up at the sky. “Uh, well. Nice weather.”
Rumble, crash!
Thunder and lightning suddenly broke out overhead. Hakso—no, Hak Su—glanced at the sky and answered uncertainly.
“You must like stormy weather.”
“...Of course. I don’t just like it—I’m crazy about it.”
I’m going to lose my mind.
It was far too late to take any of it back. I stared at the dark sky, knowing I’d screwed up, and Hak Su let out a quiet laugh.
“I understand. It happens now and then. Not so often that it particularly stands out.”
At that generous response, befitting a Daoist of the Kunlun Sect, I swallowed back tears and bowed my head.
“...I’m sorry.”
“There’s no need to apologize. We’ve known each other for only half a day. It’s an easy mistake to make. Besides, Fellow Daoist Jin, you have a great responsibility on your shoulders.”
Hak Su laughed heartily, but I’d still been rude. All the more so because the man standing before me was Cheongheoja’s Senior Disciple and might one day succeed him as Sect Leader of Kunlun.
“I’ve often heard about you, so I know what sort of person you are. Just as the third one said, you’re a very amusing man.”
“By the third one, you mean...”
“You’ve guessed correctly. Hak Woo, the Kunlun Cloud Dragon. He’s my youngest Junior Brother. Though given our ages, he’s closer to being my Disciple.”

Hak Su looked well past forty and nearly fifty, old enough that no one would have found it strange if Hak Woo, who wasn’t yet thirty, had been his Disciple. In fact, they were fellow Disciples of the same Master, Cheongheoja.
“In any case, I’ve wanted to meet you for a long time. It’s deeply unfortunate that we’ve met under these circumstances...but you came all this way to save our sect. Nothing could make me happier.”
Caught off guard by Hak Su’s praise, I scratched my head. I’d heard thanks like this before, but I had no desire to act the hero, as though I were somebody important.
Besides, the real battle hasn’t even begun.

Of course, the allies about to gather in one place were stronger than any force I’d ever seen. Two of the Three Saints had joined us, and the Fire King Jeok Cheongang—a master who could hold his own against them—was with us too.

If several other Supreme Peak masters, myself included, and our handpicked three thousand elites joined the main force, we might even have the upper hand against Dark Heaven’s massive army invading Qinghai.
But...
No one knows how things will unfold from here.

I couldn’t get an exact count, but as far as I could tell, Dark Heaven’s forces numbered close to a hundred thousand. Every last one was a monster, little different from the undead, with physical abilities far beyond those of a human.
That alone was a serious complication. But something else had been weighing on me with fear for some time now.
The Lord of Heaven.
An absolute being lurking beyond an abyss whose depths I couldn’t fathom, swallowing the world—heaven and earth alike.
I couldn’t even imagine what would happen if that bastard appeared before us soon.
There’s a good chance the Lord of Heaven will enter this battle. Dark Heaven can’t afford to back down.
Four Demon Lords and a Demon Empress, who’d been like his own limbs, had already fallen to my hand, and we’d inflicted heavy losses on his forces along the way.
If the Lord of Heaven lost an army of a hundred thousand in Qinghai as well, the blow would be enormous, even for him.
And yet, one thing still bothered me.
Then why make such an absurd choice in Gansu?
I bit my lip and recalled the Grand Sorceress’s words.
Get stronger. Even stronger than you are now.
She’d let me live instead of killing me when my life hung by a thread.
No.
What I remembered was the intent of whoever had given her that order.
The Lord of Heaven doesn’t want me—Jin Taekyung, the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon—to die.
The truth I’d realized on that snowfield, covered in blood and corpses, dug through my mind like a sharp awl, leaving questions I couldn’t answer and suspicions I could scarcely believe.
Maybe. Maybe the Lord of Heaven’s real purpose is...
A headache struck without warning. I barely swallowed the groan rising in my throat.
“...Fellow Daoist? Fellow Daoist Jin, are you all right?”
A voice broke through my thoughts. Hak Su was watching me with concern.
“Are you feeling unwell? Your face...”
As he trailed off, I reflexively looked down at the water. A rigid face stared back from the clear surface, then broke apart as the bow carried us forward.
Just like my thoughts.
“I’m fine. Just a little seasick.”
A feeble excuse from a Supreme Peak master. Hak Su studied me for a moment before speaking carefully.
“I can’t claim to know everything that troubles you, but if you ever wish to talk, you’re welcome to come to me.”
He laughed heartily, then added, “Of course, I wasn’t being entirely serious, so don’t worry about it. But I can at least tell you some good news that might lighten your heart a little.”
“What good news?”
“By now, word of the situation in Qinghai must have reached the Central Plains. Before long, the Sword Saint—no, the Alliance Leader—will lead the righteous warriors of the world here to join us.”
Hak Su sounded full of hope. For a moment, I’d wondered if he really had good news. Now my spirits sank.
Could that really happen?
First secure your own life, then strike your enemy.
It was an old saying from Go: make sure you survived before you attacked. And by that measure, the world was still an unstable stockpile of bombs.
Besides...
As long as they have the Moving Formation, it’s almost impossible to commit all our forces to Qinghai alone.
But I swallowed the words on the tip of my tongue. I couldn’t bring myself to crush the hope of the earnest, kind-looking Daoist before me—not while I was still confused myself.
“Hmm.”
“Is something wrong?”
Hak Su looked puzzled by my vague response. I held back a bitter smile and shook my head.
He’d learn the harsh truth soon enough, even if it wasn’t today.
“No. It’s better news than I expected, that’s all. Caught me off guard. Anyway, how much farther to our destination?”
“About half a day, I think.”
“Half a day. Two or three shichen at most, then.”
Crossing Qinghai Lake directly by ship had saved us a considerable amount of time. I nodded, thinking about what lay ahead, then muttered as I remembered something I’d almost forgotten.
“Oh, right.”
“Is there something you’re curious about?”
“No. It’s about time we hauled him out.”
“Pardon?”
Leaving Hak Su to puzzle over that, I shouted to the house elf who had to be somewhere nearby.
“Head down!”
A moment later, the rude house elf’s indignant voice rang out.
“This is driving me crazy! Why now?!”
“Just felt like calling you. Wanted to check where you were.”
The house elf—Hyuk Mujin—came running. At my casual answer, he looked like he’d swallowed shit.
“What am I, some stray dog?”
“Absolutely not. What sin did a good dog commit in a past life to deserve being compared to you?”
“...One of these days, I’m going to get sick of this shit and quit.”
“Good. Please do.”
I laughed quietly at his grumbling and started walking.
“Anyway, how’s the job I gave you going?”
“I was right in the middle of it. He’s more tight-lipped than I expected.”
“And?”
“So I made him heavier. Chained a water jug to his ankle. He loved it.”
“Good work. You’ve got a knack for this.”
“What can I say? I learned it all from you, Captain.”
As I walked along, chatting with Hyuk Mujin, Hak Su followed behind us, caught up in the situation. He blinked.
“Forgive me, but what in the world are you talking about?”
He stared at the empty deck. I shrugged.
“You’ll see.”
“But see what—”
“Mujin.”
“Yes, sir.”
Rrrrattle.
Hyuk Mujin stepped forward briskly and pulled on a chain extending over the side of the deck. A man in black, his whole body blue, rose out of the water.
“Gah! I-I’ll talk! I’ll talk!”
“On your life?”
“Of course—cough—of course!”
He’d spent a full day and night as one with the blue waters of Qinghai Lake. It was hardly surprising that he might be ready to cooperate now.
Still, I studied the panting man closely.
“If there’s even the slightest lie in what you tell us, your parents will live long, sick lives.”
“Devoted son, aren’t you? Right, Mujin?”
“Yes, sir!”
“N-No! Anything but that...!”
Rrrrattle. Splash!
Hyuk Mujin answered with gusto and released the chain. The blue water swallowed the man’s desperate scream.
The ancient tradition of dipping someone in the Yangtze lived on at Qinghai Lake.

If the Lord of Heaven lost an army of a hundred thousand in Qinghai as well, the blow would be enormous, even for him.
And yet, one thing still bothered me.
Then why make such an absurd choice in Gansu?
I bit my lip and recalled the Grand Sorceress’s words.
Get stronger.
Even stronger than you are now.
She’d let me live instead of killing me when my life hung by a thread.
No.
What I remembered was the intent of whoever had given her that order.
The Lord of Heaven doesn’t want me—Jin Taekyung, the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon—to die.
The truth I’d realized on that snowfield, covered in blood and corpses, dug through my mind like a sharp awl, leaving questions I couldn’t answer and suspicions I could scarcely believe.
Maybe.
Maybe the Lord of Heaven’s real purpose is...
A headache struck without warning.
I barely swallowed the groan rising in my throat.
“...Fellow Daoist?
Fellow Daoist Jin, are you all right?”
A voice broke through my thoughts.
Hak Su was watching me with concern.
“Are you feeling unwell?
Your face...”
As he trailed off, I reflexively looked down at the water.
A rigid face stared back from the clear surface, then broke apart as the bow carried us forward.
Just like my thoughts.
“I’m fine.
Just a little seasick.”
A feeble excuse from a Supreme Peak master.
Hak Su studied me for a moment before speaking carefully.
“I can’t claim to know everything that troubles you, but if you ever wish to talk, you’re welcome to come to me.”
He laughed heartily, then added, “Of course, I wasn’t being entirely serious, so don’t worry about it.
But I can at least tell you some good news that might lighten your heart a little.”
“What good news?”
“By now, word of the situation in Qinghai must have reached the Central Plains.
Before long, the Sword Saint—no, the Alliance Leader—will lead the righteous warriors of the world here to join us.”
Hak Su sounded full of hope.
For a moment, I’d wondered if he really had good news.
Now my spirits sank.
Could that really happen?
First secure your own life, then strike your enemy.
It was an old saying from Go: make sure you survived before you attacked.
And by that measure, the world was still an unstable stockpile of bombs.
Besides...
As long as they have the Moving Formation, it’s almost impossible to commit all our forces to Qinghai alone.
But I swallowed the words on the tip of my tongue.
I couldn’t bring myself to crush the hope of the earnest, kind-looking Daoist before me—not while I was still confused myself.
“Hmm.”
“Is something wrong?”
Hak Su looked puzzled by my vague response.
I held back a bitter smile and shook my head.
He’d learn the harsh truth soon enough, even if it wasn’t today.
“No.
It’s better news than I expected, that’s all.
Caught me off guard.
Anyway, how much farther to our destination?”
“About half a day, I think.”
“Half a day.
Two or three shichen at most, then.”
Crossing Qinghai Lake directly by ship had saved us a considerable amount of time.
I nodded, thinking about what lay ahead, then muttered as I remembered something I’d almost forgotten.
“Oh, right.”
“Is there something you’re curious about?”
“No.
It’s about time we hauled him out.”
“Pardon?”
Leaving Hak Su to puzzle over that, I shouted to the house elf who had to be somewhere nearby.
“Head down!”
A moment later, the rude house elf’s indignant voice rang out.
“This is driving me crazy!
Why now?!”
“Just felt like calling you.
Wanted to check where you were.”
The house elf—Hyuk Mujin—came running.
At my casual answer, he looked like he’d swallowed shit.
“What am I, some stray dog?”
“Absolutely not.
What sin did a good dog commit in a past life to deserve being compared to you?”
“...One of these days, I’m going to get sick of this shit and quit.”
“Good.
Please do.”
I laughed quietly at his grumbling and started walking.
“Anyway, how’s the job I gave you going?”
“I was right in the middle of it.
He’s more tight-lipped than I expected.”
“And?”
“So I made him heavier.
Chained a water jug to his ankle.
He loved it.”
“Good work.
You’ve got a knack for this.”
“What can I say?
I learned it all from you, Captain.”
As I walked along, chatting with Hyuk Mujin, Hak Su followed behind us, caught up in the situation.
He blinked.
“Forgive me, but what in the world are you talking about?”
He stared at the empty deck.
I shrugged.
“You’ll see.”
“But see what—”
“Mujin.”
“Yes, sir.”
Rrrrattle.
Hyuk Mujin stepped forward briskly and pulled on a chain extending over the side of the deck.
A man in black, his whole body blue, rose out of the water.
“Gah!
I-I’ll talk!
I’ll talk!”
“On your life?”
“Of course—cough—of course!”
He’d spent a full day and night as one with the blue waters of Qinghai Lake.
It was hardly surprising that he might be ready to cooperate now.
Still, I studied the panting man closely.
“If there’s even the slightest lie in what you tell us, your parents will live long, sick lives.”
“Devoted son, aren’t you?
Right, Mujin?”
“Yes, sir!”
“N-No!
Anything but that...!”
Rrrrattle.
Splash!
Hyuk Mujin answered with gusto and released the chain.
The blue water swallowed the man’s desperate scream.
The ancient tradition of dipping someone in the Yangtze lived on at Qinghai Lake.

chapters.title: Chapter 1079
paragraphs: If someone asked me whether a person could survive being dunked in a river hundreds of times over a full day and night, plus another half day, I’d answer without hesitation.
Of course they could.
They might even come out of it far more honest than they’d been before.
Naturally, there might be a few minor complications along the way.
“Ugh... ugh...”
“Captain, this guy’s eyes are completely glazed over.”
“If they’ve gone slack, we’ll just have to tighten them up.”
“How?”
“Slap him across the face. Nice and hard.”
“Ah.”
Hyuk Mujin nodded as though he’d gained a great insight and promptly raised his palm.
Smack!
“He’s not waking up.”
“Are you stupid?”
“Why?”
“You have to hit him harder. Until he wakes up.”
“Oh. Are you a genius?”
“Not a genius. Just exceptionally gifted.”
“Of course.”
Mujin gasped in admiration and raised both hands this time.
Smack! Smack! Smack!
“Uh, his eyes rolled back.”
“He’s exaggerating.”
“No, I’m serious. His body’s completely ice-cold, too.”
“Huh. So it is.”
“I told you.”
“This bastard’s cold because his heart is cold.”
“Now isn’t the time for nonsense. What if he dies?”
“He won’t. I’m here, and my heart’s warm.”
“What?”
The moment Mujin looked at me as if to say, What kind of bullshit is this idiot talking about now? I reached out without hesitation.
Boom!
My palm struck the black-robed man’s chest, delivering a burst of Scorching Yang Qi. His body, pale and growing rigid, shuddered. Then warmth flooded back into him—far more than he’d had before.
“...Wow. He actually survived.”
“Told you. I have a warm heart.”
“Isn’t it your internal energy that’s warm, not your heart?”
“Want to warm up like him? You look a little cold.”
“I must politely decline...”
Crack!
“Gah!”
“What?”
“He bit his tongue! There’s so much blood!”
“Oh, for fuck’s sake.”
“I told you not to release his Mute Acupoint! Even with his internal energy sealed, he could die like this!”
“If I’d sealed his Mute Acupoint, he might’ve drowned without getting a word out. Anyway, quit making a fuss and go fetch him.”
“Fetch who?”
“Who do you think?”
“Oh.”
A moment later, a man who’d mastered two utterly different trades—assassination and medicine—revived our emergency patient in the blink of an eye.
“I’ve stitched him up perfectly. He’ll have no trouble speaking once he recovers.”
“Thank you.”
“But is this the man I’m thinking of?”
“Yes. The one you brought in last time.”
“He’s so swollen I nearly didn’t recognize him. His wrist wound hasn’t healed yet, either, so don’t overdo it. If it gets infected and the flesh dies, that’ll be serious.”
“Oh, it’s not my body, so that’s fine.”
“True enough. But keep treating him so roughly and he’s liable to die. At a time like this, you’d be better off stabbing deep, three vertebrae below the cervical spine, then slowly...”
“Oh, that’s a handy tip. But wouldn’t that kill him?”
“He wouldn’t die. He’d wish he had.”

The expert, second to none in the world when it came to taking apart and treating the human body, passed on his useful tip and left. The black-robed man, who had watched the whole thing unfold right before his eyes, began to thrash.
“Mmph! Mmmph...”
“Hey, why are you acting up again? Hold still.”
“Mmmph!”
“This isn’t working. Mujin.”
“Yes, sir.”
“Hold him down for a bit. I’m trying to practice, but it’s hard when he keeps shaking. I used a Pressure-Point Strike, and he’s still struggling this much. How badly is he thrashing around?”
“This insolent bastard. The Captain’s trying to practice. Heave-ho. Is that good?”
“Yeah. Perfect. All right, I’m going to stab him.”
“Wait. Are you sure that’s the right spot?”
“Isn’t it? I thought he said to start two vertebrae below the cervical spine.”
“Huh? Wasn’t it two above?”
“No way. That’s a lethal acupoint.”
“Now I’m confused. Why don’t you go ask him again, Captain?”
“Why should I go? You go.”
“I could die if I go. He hates having to repeat himself.”
“You think it’d be any different if I went?”
“Fair point. How about stabbing both spots?”
“That’s not a bad idea. Shall we?”
“Yes, sir. Go ahead.”
“Mmmph! Mmmmmmph!”
Rrrrrumble!
The deck shook as if an earthquake had hit—though that might be a slight exaggeration.
The black-robed man thrashed with all his might despite the Pressure-Point Strike. I let out a quiet laugh to myself, then released his Mute Acupoint.
“Gah! Cough, cough!”
“What is it? Got any last words?”
“Th-three vertebrae.”
“Hm?”
“The cervical spine! Three vertebrae below it! Stop it, you madmen!”
There were only two reasons to call someone a madman when he could kill you with a flick of his hand.
First, you’d made peace with dying.
Second, you were too terrified to think straight, let alone worry about offending him.
He was clearly the latter.
That’s done.
One look at the terror in his eyes, one listen to his voice, and I knew he’d been reborn a far more honest man. I stood up.
“Huh? You’re not going to stab him?”
“Why would I? Get him something to cover himself with, then stay right beside him and have a chat.”
“What about you, Captain?”
“I’m about to get busy with something else. Isn’t that right?”
At my sudden question, Hak Su swallowed hard. He’d watched the whole scene with the expression of a man who’d seen a ghost.
“I-I’m not sure what you mean.”
“Oh, right. You can’t see it yet. Over there.”
Just as I raised my hand and pointed beyond the bow—
Whoosh.
The thick mist parted, revealing the green land it had hidden.
A group had gathered at the pier to wait for us. Beyond them, faint gray city walls rose in the distance.
Xining, the capital of Qinghai and the last stronghold against Dark Heaven.
So that’s Xining.
At that moment—
Ding.
A clear chime rang out above the waters parting before our boat.
The crowd waiting to welcome us was enormous.
No. Massive wouldn’t have been an exaggeration.
“Waaaaaah!”
“Reinforcements! The Murim Alliance reinforcements are here!”
Was this what those Roman triumphs I’d seen in textbooks had been like?
The cheers swelled as we drew closer to the walls, then shook the whole city the moment we entered. Everywhere I looked, the streets were packed with dark masses of people.
They filled the broad avenues and narrow alleys, as well as the rooftops of countless buildings—including rows of pavilions—and stretched both arms toward us as they cheered.
Even Cheongpung, who usually loved attention, swallowed nervously and whispered, “If this goes on much longer, my ears might burst, Benefactor.”
“Yeah?”
“Yes. I’m not joking. I’ve never heard anything this loud.”
“Mirror therapy works, all right.”
“Hm? What’s mirror therapy?”
“It’s... never mind. Even if I told you, Cheongpung wouldn’t change.”
Normally, Cheongpung would have been armed with pure, unbridled curiosity and pressed me to explain what mirror therapy meant. This time, though, he simply continued in a quiet voice.
“There are so many people. Seriously, so many. I stayed in Xining for a while, but it wasn’t anything like this.”
Cheongpung had spent about a month in Qinghai before I arrived, so the change must have struck him all the harder.
Of course, I already had a good idea where this enormous crowd had come from.
Everyone scattered across Qinghai must have gathered in Xining.
It was only natural. The same thing had happened earlier in Shanxi, then in Gansu.

The Great Nation’s imperial court had already declared Dark Heaven rebels and foreign invaders. A warning like that was essential if the common people, many of whom still thought there was nothing to fear, were going to take the threat seriously.
Unlike the Great Faction War, which had barely affected the common folk, Dark Heaven’s actions had long since gone far beyond the bounds of the Murim.
If the Heavenly Demon of the past had set his sights on the Murim, the Lord of Heaven now wanted the whole world.
No—
Maybe even more than that.
I forced down the unease that grew sharper with every passing moment and curled my lips into a smile.
So that the countless people surrounding us, covering every direction, might feel a little more at ease when they saw me smile.
“It’s Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung!”
“The Marquis of Shangshan is here!”
“Waaaaah! Long live the Great Nation! Long live His Majesty the Emperor!”
For all their numbers, most of these people knew little about the Murim.
In their eyes, I wasn’t just a young martial artist. I was a divine general, carrying out the Son of Heaven’s solemn imperial command to punish foreign invaders and save them.
As the cheers swelled, Cheongpung’s eyes widened.
“Wow. Everyone seems to like you, Benefactor.”
I swallowed a bitter smile and answered quietly.
“Looks that way. For now, at least.”
“They’ll like you from now on, too. You’re such a good person!”
“A good person...”
My voice trailed off as I looked at the crowd filling the city.
Hundreds of thousands, at a glance. Maybe more.
At this very moment, all those people were smiling brightly and cheering for me. But I had no way of knowing how long those smiles would stay on their faces.
Or, if the worst really did happen, how many of them would survive.
“Cheongpung.”
“Yes?”
“Yes?”
“Let’s try. As far as we can go.”
Still watching the crowd, I added quietly, “Even if it costs us our lives.”
Yeah.
Just as we always had.

chapters.title: Chapter 1080
paragraphs: Even as night deepened, the lights of Xining stayed lit.
The countless people still in the streets shared their joy freely, and the city’s leaders provided liquor and meat for them.
They hoped the small sparks of hope in those people’s hearts would burn a little longer—and a little brighter.
But while laughter still slipped through the gaps around the windows, the mood inside the pavilion was heavy.
“Judging by those long faces, I can guess how things are going.”
Jeok Cheongang broke the silence with a click of his tongue.
“Sounds like you’ve got some shitty news. Spit it out now instead of making a damn fuss later.”
“Well...”
Only Jeok Cheongang could say something like that. But with Jeok Cheongang on the receiving end, no one dared be the first to answer.
The leaders trailed off and exchanged glances. That was when I spoke up from beside the window.
“If it’s hard to say right now, let’s start with the situation inside the city.”
The martial world might spell it Fire Gate Clan and pronounce it bunch of bastards, but of course a young Disciple was easier to approach than an old monster notorious for his foul temper.
At my gentle tone, one of the leaders finally relaxed enough to speak.
“Things aren’t looking good.”
“Hmm. Not good?”
“That’s right.”
I pressed my lips together, then asked the speaker, “Understood. And your name?”
“Cheok Mo, Sect Leader of Qinghai’s Gonghwa Sect. I don’t know if you’ve heard of us.”
Of course I hadn’t.
I knew of Gonghwachun, but I hadn’t memorized the dozens of martial sects in Qinghai Province. And his first answer had already made it clear I wasn’t likely to remember him, either.
“All right, then. Sect Leader Cheok of the Gonghwa Sect.”
“I’m listening.”
He nodded lazily. I met his gaze and continued evenly.
“Do you want to be here?”
“You’re free to leave if you’re going to keep stating the obvious.”
“And since when are we on such familiar terms? What do you think, sir?”
I turned to a middle-aged official dressed in silk robes. He swallowed before answering.
“H-How could I possibly contradict the Marquis of Shangshan?”
“Strange answer. I don’t recall asking whether you’d contradict me.”
“Y-You are absolutely right!”
“Sure. Anyway, I’ve been standing for a while, and my legs are getting tired. Is there an open seat?”
I could have stood there for days without a problem, and a slight turn of my head would have shown me plenty of empty chairs. But the official sprang from his seat.
“There’s one right here!”
“Oh, you don’t have to do that. Especially when you’re so much older than me.”
“I-I don’t know what I should...”
“What do you mean, you don’t know? Are you trying to get me cursed out? Make it look like some wet-behind-the-ears kid is throwing his rank around to bully an elder?”
“Th-Then I’ll sit.”
The official’s eyes darted back and forth as he cautiously lowered himself toward the chair. I muttered as if to myself.
“He’s actually going to sit. Can’t read the room at all.”
“...Pardon?”
“Hm? What?”
“What you just said...”
“Oh, did you hear that?”
“I was only talking to myself. Go ahead and sit.”
“Why do you keep making me repeat myself? Sit down.”
A truly clueless man might have eased himself into the chair. This official could only stare at me, his eyes trembling, unable to sit or stand.
Then again, he must have been good at reading the room to have landed such an important post as City Lord at a relatively young age.
That same instinct must’ve helped him siphon off plenty over the years.
Leaving the City Lord of Qinghai sweating through an imaginary squat, I glanced to my side. Jeong Hogun was smiling with a crooked twist to his lips.
I didn’t make a habit of bullying my elders, but what Jeong Hogun had told me on the way to Xining had washed away any guilt I might have felt.
A textbook corrupt official.

The Embroidered Uniform Guard—the imperial family’s foremost military force, with intelligence capabilities comparable to the East Depot—had obtained the information long ago. There was no room for doubt.
More important, though, was the state of affairs his negligence had brought about.
“I heard the city’s food stores are running low. What do you have to say about that, City Lord?”
“Th-That’s...”
“Just the number. No lies.”
“W-We had far too many commoners flood the city in a short time...”
“You’ve got a long tongue. Want me to shorten it?”
“On-One month! One month!”
He blurted out the answer, then added uncertainly, “...Probably.”
“That won’t do. Thousand Captain Jeong?”
Step.
Jeong Hogun strode forward at my call. The City Lord squeezed his eyes shut and cried out.
“F-Fifteen days! The food we have in storage will last fifteen days at most!”
“Fifteen days. Are you sure this time?”
“I stake my life on it!”
Men with plenty to lose didn’t gamble with their lives. That made his answer convincing—and infuriating.
A huge number of refugees had arrived in a short time, but Xining had only been like this for about seven days.
Qinghai was a border province. It was only natural that it would have more military provisions stored away than the Central Plains, in case of an invasion.
And yet there was only enough food for fifteen more days.
He really helped himself.
I sighed and looked at the City Lord. Sweat streamed down his terrified face from his impromptu leg workout.
“Why are you so scared? Anyone would think I was trying to kill you. Wouldn’t they?”
“Th-Then...”
“Don’t worry. I won’t kill you.”
“Thank you!”
His face brightened at once. I added gently, “At least not right now.”
“I’ll devote my whole heart to serving the Marquis of Shangshan from now on... Pardon?”
“Why ask me to repeat it? You heard me.”
Three or four Embroidered Uniform Guards strode up behind him and surrounded him.
“W-Wait! You can’t do this!”
“Who says I can’t?”

It was a terrible turn of events for the City Lord. But I had saved the imperial family, and the Son of Heaven had personally appointed me a marquis. I had more than enough authority and grounds to do this.
Besides, his fate had been all but decided before I set foot in Xining.
“Send him off at sunrise. And don’t forget to give him some company for the journey. He might get lonely.”
“As you command!”
Jeong Hogun’s answer was firmer than ever. At his gesture, the other Embroidered Uniform Guards waiting nearby swiftly carried out their orders.
“Songak of Qinghai’s Regional Military Commission. Is that you?”
“I-I haven’t done anything wrong!”
“That’s for us to decide. Not you.”
“These are the Marquis of Shangshan’s strict orders. Come quietly if you want to see tomorrow’s sunrise.”
It happened in an instant.
Generals in ornate armor and officials in robes as stiff as their necks were dragged out one after another, their faces pale.
Not one of them resisted. No—they didn’t even dare try.
The presence of Supreme Peak masters who could shake the world played a part. But if they opposed the imperial Embroidered Uniform Guard, their entire families could be branded traitors.
Beheaded as corrupt officials in league with the City Lord, or branded traitors and wiped out along with their families. Faced with that choice, they could do only one thing.
Accept reality.
And despair without end.
Unlike the men dragged out wailing as though everything was over, the people would rejoice and draw closer together once this tumor was removed.
And along with that—
“Looks like we’re finally ready to have a proper discussion.”
The dozen or so seats emptied in an instant. Yet the void they left was filled by the presence of the man who had emptied them.
Me.
Jin Taekyung, the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon.
“What does everyone think?”
Suffocating silence weighed on the pavilion.
Those close to me smiled without a sound. Those who didn’t know me exchanged dark looks.
Backs that had once been relaxed were now rigidly straight. Fingers tapped the table slowly, anxiously.

Perhaps some of them had dismissed me in private, or tried to diminish what I’d done. Rumors always grew in the telling. And in troubled times like these, people sometimes made heroes because they needed them.
But they were wrong.
There had always been people like that, everywhere. The result had always been the same.
And there had always been people who watched in silence, giving nothing away. Like the young Daoist who looked straight at me now while a few others avoided my gaze.
“Rumors are made from what people see and hear. As usual, I didn’t put much stock in them.”
His Daoist robes were neat, without a single wrinkle, and I couldn’t begin to read the depths of his eyes.
“But now that I’ve met you, fellow Daoist, I see once again that I was right.”
His voice was as calm and composed as his appearance.
“Rumors can’t be trusted. Sometimes the truth falls short of them. Other times... it far surpasses them.”
Rustle.
The young Daoist rose, clasped his hands in greeting, and spoke.
“I am Hak Eui, a First-Generation Disciple of the Kunlun Sect. It is an honor to meet you, Great Hero Jin Taekyung.”

“Well...”
Only Jeok Cheongang could say something like that.

The leaders trailed off and exchanged glances.
