chapters.title: Chapter 1087
paragraphs: While Zhuge Feng gazed west with an earnest wish in his eyes, a low laugh rang out from the highest peak in the western lands.
“Good. This is how it should be. Exactly how it should be.”
At the Blood Lord’s smiling nod, the messenger who had just finished his report felt a quiet sense of relief.
He had brought news good enough to satisfy him.
Unlike his comrades, who had become cold corpses one after another, he wouldn’t be killed by the violent man before him.
But it was too soon to feel safe.
This hour wasn’t over yet.
“So they’re all just watching and waiting to see what happens?”
At the Blood Lord’s question, the messenger lowered himself further, prostrating himself before he answered.
“That is correct. The Nine Sects and One Gang and the Five Great Families are watching the situation and strengthening their defenses, but they have made no further moves.”
“They used to praise one another as chivalrous heroes. Now that the moment has come, they’re scared stiff.”
The Blood Lord’s smile deepened. Then a clear voice rang out from somewhere.
“Better a coward than an idiot like you. Don’t you think?”
The Blood Lord frowned despite himself when he saw who had spoken, but soon answered in a leisurely tone.
“Couldn’t agree more. Stupidity leads straight to incompetence. That must be why he entrusted this plan to me.”
“And taking the sorcerers under my command and starting this without my permission?”
“I’ve been entrusted with everything in Qinghai. Why would I need to consult a defeated general?”
The Grand Sorceress smiled coldly at the reminder of her failure in Gansu.
“Your eloquence has certainly improved. Last time, was it your head that got cut off instead of your arm? I suppose I should praise you for getting a little smarter.”
For an instant, the smile on the Blood Lord’s lips faded.

Ever since Sword Saint Mae Jonghak’s strike had taken one of his arms during the incident the Central Plains Murim called the Shaolin Bloodshed, it had become a sore point he could not bear to have touched.
That damned woman.
Of course, he had accomplished his mission well enough.
He had stolen the Green Jade Buddha Staff, the most important prize, and killed numerous Shaolin Temple martial monks, including the Abbot, Hong Dao, dealing the temple a devastating blow.
But despite the success, the wound to his pride from how it had happened showed no sign of healing.
Merely remembering that violet Sword Force sent a chill through him. The place it had severed still throbbed, even now that a new arm had taken its place.
And he still carried his anger toward one reckless young pup who had stood against him to the very end without the slightest fear.
“Shut your mouth, bitch. You weren’t even there, so you’ve got no right to talk about it.”
The Blood Lord’s voice sank low. The Grand Sorceress gave him a faint smile.
“Right. That’s what I regret most.”
What?
“If I’d been there, you never could’ve come out with that nonsense about losing after fighting the Sword Saint for hundreds of exchanges.”
“Be honest. After a life-and-death duel with the Fire King—that violent old man—you fought the Sword Saint for hundreds of exchanges? You’ve got some nerve, lying to him like that.”
“You’re imagining things. I’ve always told him the truth.”
The Blood Lord replied as calmly as he could, but he knew better than anyone that the Grand Sorceress was right.
It was true.
He had lied to the Lord of Heaven about his final fight with Mae Jonghak.
The first time he had ever lied—and the last.
Why?
It was simple.
He had been furious, and afraid.
If he had known Mae Jonghak’s identity from the start, prepared for his arrival, and conserved his strength, he wouldn’t have lost his arm before lasting even three exchanges.
And if he had reported everything without leaving out a single detail, the master he trusted and worshiped like a god might have cast him aside.
But he believed in me. That’s enough.
The Blood Lord quietly settled his thoughts.
It didn’t matter what the Grand Sorceress said to his face.
Whether the Lord of Heaven truly believed him or had simply pretended not to know, he had made no issue of it—and he never would.
“Enough. Keep this up and I’ll want to blow your head off.”
At the Blood Lord’s warning, his composure now restored, the Grand Sorceress shrugged.
“I doubt you could, but let’s leave it there. We have important work ahead. I don’t want to waste my strength.”
The Blood Lord nodded without a word.
The two of them had snarled at each other without pause, as if they’d been enemies since a past life. But carrying out the mission their master had given them mattered more than anything else.
“As you’ve probably guessed, the Central Plains won’t be able to interfere in Qinghai’s affairs for now.”
The Green Forest Alliance and the Yangtze River Channel League were still pushing west even as they spoke.

Of course, if the Murim Alliance gathered the Central Plains’ strength and brought it all to bear, it could crush them in an instant. But with the Moving Formations shackling it, taking that first, heavy step would be difficult.
No—not just difficult. Nearly impossible.
Sending enough troops to save Qinghai would leave cracks in the Central Plains’ solid wall of defense.
“So if they want to save Qinghai, they leave the Central Plains exposed. And if they want to defend it, they have to abandon Qinghai.”
The Blood Lord’s smile returned as he continued.
“Looks like all that effort we put into those Central Plains bandits has paid off. A perfect checkmate, wouldn’t you say?”
Unlike him, the Grand Sorceress’s lips did not move beneath her veil.
“Of course I know. That’s why I regret it even more.”
“Why regret it? It’s only a matter of time before Xining, where they’ve gathered, is surrounded from both sides.”
“Is that all?”
“Take complete control of Qinghai, then, if possible, secure Jin Taekyung according to further orders. Wasn’t that what he instructed?”
The Grand Sorceress let out a hollow laugh at the Blood Lord’s question.
“I take back what I said earlier. You’re still just as stupid.”
What?
“Don’t you understand? If the Murim Alliance had moved this time, we could have taken the Central Plains Murim—or even everything he wants.”
The Grand Sorceress stared straight at the Blood Lord through her fine veil and added quietly,
“The whole world.”
“You should have consulted me before making your decision. To waste those precious Magic Formations, each usable only twice, on something like this...”
A low hum rose.
Qi surged with her cold voice.
At that moment, the Grand Sorceress was truly furious.
Furious that the Blood Lord had moved so many troops without so much as a word of discussion with her.
In doing so, he had wasted the dozens of Magic Formations Dark Heaven had spent so long planting throughout the world—and missed a golden opportunity to take it.
Yet even as she seethed, the smile on the Blood Lord’s lips did not disappear.
If anything, it grew even broader.
What?
The Grand Sorceress realized something was wrong a moment too late. The Blood Lord spoke with a sneer.
“I think you need to take back what you just said. Did you really think I was that stupid?”
“What are you talking about?”
“The Yangtze and the Green Forest. We recruited those mangy bandits as bait from the start. I never intended to put real effort into bait.”
The Grand Sorceress’s eyes widened as she grasped what he meant.
“Then perhaps...”
“That’s right. It was for show. Though I wondered if the Central Plains might take the bait. Unless those fools are complete idiots, they’ve been on guard against Magic Formations for some time.”
That was why he needed to test them.
Had the dozens of Magic Formations Dark Heaven’s sorcerers secretly set up throughout the world been discovered?
And if not, did they still work?
“And now we know for certain.”
The test had succeeded.

A total of ten thousand Dark Heaven faithful had crossed into the Central Plains through the Magic Formations and joined the Green Forest Alliance and the Yangtze River Channel League. The Blood Lord had only just received the news.
From the messenger still unable to raise his head before them.
“Perfect. Unfortunately, a couple of the Magic Formations used when we attacked Shaolin may have lost their power, but most still have one use left.”
The Grand Sorceress, who had fallen silent as she listened, murmured,
“That’s enough. With that much...”
They wouldn’t need to bring all of Dark Heaven’s forces into play.
They could drop tens of thousands of troops into the heart of the Central Plains at once and bring down its major sects. A single great war would be enough to conquer the world.
But that alone could not quell all her anger.
The Grand Sorceress fixed the Blood Lord with a piercing gaze.
“I understand your reasons and your justification. But it’s not enough.”
“Why not?”
“We still have one last chance to activate the Magic Formations. But now they’ll be even more wary of us.”
“No. It’s the other way around.”
What?
“When bandits start rampaging all around them, wouldn’t it be stranger if we did nothing to help or intervene?”
“It was something we had to do anyway, if only to keep watch over those two bandit gangs in case they change their minds again.”
If they could betray once, they could do it twice or three times.
The ten thousand Dark Heaven faithful sent ahead were also a deterrent against another betrayal.
Another shackle to keep the Green Forest Alliance and the Yangtze River Channel League from entertaining other ideas.
To make sure they wouldn’t even dare.
“No matter how this goes, we have nothing to lose.”
The Blood Lord rose to his feet and continued,
“If the Central Plains’ chivalrous heroes can’t bear their guilt and rise from their seats, the Magic Formations will prove their worth.”
Step. Step.
His voice scattered as his footsteps rang out slowly.
“And if they stay where they are, we’ll pass through Qinghai and head into the Central Plains.”
Rumble.
At the Blood Lord’s outstretched hand, the massive iron doors swung open.
Below them stood a vast army, blackening the mountain range.
“Raise the army. We march on Xining.”

The place it had severed still throbbed, even now that a new arm had taken its place.
And he still carried his anger toward one reckless young pup who had stood against him to the very end without the slightest fear.
“Shut your mouth, bitch.
You weren’t even there, so you’ve got no right to talk about it.”
The Blood Lord’s voice sank low.
The Grand Sorceress gave him a faint smile.
“Right.
That’s what I regret most.”
What?
“If I’d been there, you never could’ve come out with that nonsense about losing after fighting the Sword Saint for hundreds of exchanges.”
“Be honest.
After a life-and-death duel with the Fire King—that violent old man—you fought the Sword Saint for hundreds of exchanges?
You’ve got some nerve, lying to him like that.”
“You’re imagining things.
I’ve always told him the truth.”
The Blood Lord replied as calmly as he could, but he knew better than anyone that the Grand Sorceress was right.
It was true.
He had lied to the Lord of Heaven about his final fight with Mae Jonghak.
The first time he had ever lied—and the last.
Why?
It was simple.
He had been furious, and afraid.
If he had known Mae Jonghak’s identity from the start, prepared for his arrival, and conserved his strength, he wouldn’t have lost his arm before lasting even three exchanges.
And if he had reported everything without leaving out a single detail, the master he trusted and worshiped like a god might have cast him aside.
But he believed in me.
That’s enough.
The Blood Lord quietly settled his thoughts.
It didn’t matter what the Grand Sorceress said to his face.
Whether the Lord of Heaven truly believed him or had simply pretended not to know, he had made no issue of it—and he never would.
“Enough.
Keep this up and I’ll want to blow your head off.”
At the Blood Lord’s warning, his composure now restored, the Grand Sorceress shrugged.
“I doubt you could, but let’s leave it there.
We have important work ahead.
I don’t want to waste my strength.”
The Blood Lord nodded without a word.
The two of them had snarled at each other without pause, as if they’d been enemies since a past life.
But carrying out the mission their master had given them mattered more than anything else.
“As you’ve probably guessed, the Central Plains won’t be able to interfere in Qinghai’s affairs for now.”
The Green Forest Alliance and the Yangtze River Channel League were still pushing west even as they spoke.
Of course, if the Murim Alliance gathered the Central Plains’ strength and brought it all to bear, it could crush them in an instant.
But with the Moving Formations shackling it, taking that first, heavy step would be difficult.
No—not just difficult.
Nearly impossible.
Sending enough troops to save Qinghai would leave cracks in the Central Plains’ solid wall of defense.
“So if they want to save Qinghai, they leave the Central Plains exposed.
And if they want to defend it, they have to abandon Qinghai.”
The Blood Lord’s smile returned as he continued.
“Looks like all that effort we put into those Central Plains bandits has paid off.
A perfect checkmate, wouldn’t you say?”
Unlike him, the Grand Sorceress’s lips did not move beneath her veil.
“Of course I know.
That’s why I regret it even more.”
“Why regret it?
It’s only a matter of time before Xining, where they’ve gathered, is surrounded from both sides.”
“Is that all?”
“Take complete control of Qinghai, then, if possible, secure Jin Taekyung according to further orders.
Wasn’t that what he instructed?”
The Grand Sorceress let out a hollow laugh at the Blood Lord’s question.
“I take back what I said earlier.
You’re still just as stupid.”
What?
“Don’t you understand?
If the Murim Alliance had moved this time, we could have taken the Central Plains Murim—or even everything he wants.”
The Grand Sorceress stared straight at the Blood Lord through her fine veil and added quietly,
“The whole world.”
“You should have consulted me before making your decision.
To waste those precious Magic Formations, each usable only twice, on something like this...”
A low hum rose.
Qi surged with her cold voice.
At that moment, the Grand Sorceress was truly furious.
Furious that the Blood Lord had moved so many troops without so much as a word of discussion with her.
In doing so, he had wasted the dozens of Magic Formations Dark Heaven had spent so long planting throughout the world—and missed a golden opportunity to take it.
Yet even as she seethed, the smile on the Blood Lord’s lips did not disappear.
If anything, it grew even broader.
What?
The Grand Sorceress realized something was wrong a moment too late.
The Blood Lord spoke with a sneer.
“I think you need to take back what you just said.
Did you really think I was that stupid?”
“What are you talking about?”
“The Yangtze and the Green Forest.
We recruited those mangy bandits as bait from the start.
I never intended to put real effort into bait.”
The Grand Sorceress’s eyes widened as she grasped what he meant.
“Then perhaps...”
“That’s right.
It was for show.
Though I wondered if the Central Plains might take the bait.
Unless those fools are complete idiots, they’ve been on guard against Magic Formations for some time.”
That was why he needed to test them.
Had the dozens of Magic Formations Dark Heaven’s sorcerers secretly set up throughout the world been discovered?
And if not, did they still work?
“And now we know for certain.”
The test had succeeded.
A total of ten thousand Dark Heaven faithful had crossed into the Central Plains through the Magic Formations and joined the Green Forest Alliance and the Yangtze River Channel League.
The Blood Lord had only just received the news.
From the messenger still unable to raise his head before them.
“Perfect.
Unfortunately, a couple of the Magic Formations used when we attacked Shaolin may have lost their power, but most still have one use left.”
The Grand Sorceress, who had fallen silent as she listened, murmured,
“That’s enough.
With that much...”
They wouldn’t need to bring all of Dark Heaven’s forces into play.
They could drop tens of thousands of troops into the heart of the Central Plains at once and bring down its major sects.
A single great war would be enough to conquer the world.
But that alone could not quell all her anger.
The Grand Sorceress fixed the Blood Lord with a piercing gaze.
“I understand your reasons and your justification.
But it’s not enough.”
“Why not?”
“We still have one last chance to activate the Magic Formations.
But now they’ll be even more wary of us.”
“No.
It’s the other way around.”
What?
“When bandits start rampaging all around them, wouldn’t it be stranger if we did nothing to help or intervene?”
“It was something we had to do anyway, if only to keep watch over those two bandit gangs in case they change their minds again.”
If they could betray once, they could do it twice or three times.
The ten thousand Dark Heaven faithful sent ahead were also a deterrent against another betrayal.
Another shackle to keep the Green Forest Alliance and the Yangtze River Channel League from entertaining other ideas.
To make sure they wouldn’t even dare.
“No matter how this goes, we have nothing to lose.”
The Blood Lord rose to his feet and continued,
“If the Central Plains’ chivalrous heroes can’t bear their guilt and rise from their seats, the Magic Formations will prove their worth.”
Step.
Step.
His voice scattered as his footsteps rang out slowly.
“And if they stay where they are, we’ll pass through Qinghai and head into the Central Plains.”
Rumble.
At the Blood Lord’s outstretched hand, the massive iron doors swung open.
Below them stood a vast army, blackening the mountain range.
“Raise the army.
We march on Xining.”

chapters.title: Chapter 1088
paragraphs: I’d made it through more crises than I could count.
Even if I counted only the life-or-death situations I’d faced inside Gates, I had enough experience to rival any old hand in Murim.
So I knew one thing very well: the worse the situation, the more clearheaded I had to be.
And now, four days after arriving in Xining, clearheaded judgment and a few more pieces of information had finally led me to a conclusion.
“Mujin.”
“Yes, sir. Just give the order.”
Hyuk Mujin looked at me with blazing eyes and thumped his chest.
“Your reliable right-hand man is right here, Captain.”
I addressed the guy who was more like a shabby little toe.
“I think we’re fucked.”
“Pardon?”
“I said I think we’re fucked. For real.”
“...Are you serious?”
The fire in his eyes went out as if someone had doused it with cold water, but I could only answer calmly.
“Yeah. Completely.”
“But you weren’t saying that a few days ago.”
“I wasn’t. Not at first.”
But the situation had changed beyond recognition.
The Yangtze River Channel League and the Green Forest Alliance.
As if getting blindsided by those two bands of thieves wasn’t enough, Potala Palace in Tibet had joined forces with Dark Heaven.
Potala Palace’s rise at precisely this moment also meant we could no longer count on support from Sichuan.
And the Central Plains—
“Now that even the Great Nation’s military vessels guarding the Yangtze’s tributaries have been wiped out, the waterways through the Central Plains are practically in their hands for the time being.”
I wanted to deny it, but I couldn’t anymore.
A messenger eagle had arrived the night before, confirming the reports that Seafaring King Pa Ryun’s Yangtze River Channel League pirates had scored an overwhelming victory against the Great Nation.
“Even if they suffered a crushing defeat this time, don’t they still have plenty of military vessels left? The Great Nation has more strength than that, and the Yangtze is huge.”
Mujin had a point.
The Great Nation wasn’t called great for nothing.

The battle with the Yangtze River Channel League had dealt it a terrible blow, but if that alone were enough to make it lose control of the entire Yangtze, it never could have claimed to rule the world in the first place.
The important thing, though, was—
“Time. Time is the problem, isn’t it?”
A familiar voice cut in.
Bow Saint emerged from behind Jeok Cheongang, who had appeared at some point.
“Even that little time they’ve gained will be more damaging to us than anything.”
Exactly.
Whether their reign lasted only three days or their glory faded as quickly as a flower, there was no way to stop the Yangtze River Channel League right now.
By the time the Great Nation invoked its authority to requisition every ship it could and gathered its naval forces from across the land, it would already be too late.
By then, Qinghai—no, Xining itself—would be completely surrounded, front and back.
“So how many of those damn bandits have gathered?”
I answered Jeok Cheongang.
“Our estimate so far is around thirty thousand.”
“Hah. They’re coming in packs like dogs. Then again, numbers are about the only thing those dark-path bastards have to brag about.”
“If it were just numbers, that would be much better. Take out their leaders, and the rest would collapse on its own.”
As was true everywhere, dark-path figures and unorthodox factions were especially dependent on the people at their center.
They gathered and scattered around individuals who became their leaders through overwhelming strength and the ability to command others.
Seafaring King Pa Ryun.
And Green Forest Battle King Tae Gunak.
If we took out those two Supreme Peak masters who embodied the dark path, the combined forces of the Yangtze River Channel League and the Green Forest Alliance might not be such a difficult opponent.
Of course, that was only if no new uninvited guests showed up.
“Right, Dark Heaven. You said they’d joined them.”
“Yes. Ten thousand of them. A full third of their forces.”
Jeok Cheongang smacked his lips at my answer.
“They’ve put a tight leash on those two. Made sure they won’t dare bare their teeth at their master.”
“That’s what makes it worse. Even if Pa Ryun and Tae Gunak are taken out now, their forces will still come after us.”
“Of course. Those cowards have seen for themselves that the dark arts they’d only heard about are real. They’ll tuck their tails between their legs even tighter.”
Ten thousand enemies had appeared.
Right in the heart of the Central Plains.
The existence of Moving Formations had always worried the Central Plains Murim. Having that fear become reality was another matter entirely.
It seemed even great sects like the Zhuge Clan and Wudang couldn’t ignore it.
Though they all but ruled Hubei’s Murim, even they had chosen to avoid a direct confrontation.
I’d heard the Zhuge Clan had gone so far as to flee to Mount Wudang, leaving behind the family home where they’d put down roots for hundreds of years.
They’re weaker than the other great sects, so I understand. But was that really the best choice?
I found myself thinking of Zhuge Feng, Family Head of the Zhuge Clan and the Crouching Dragon Guest.
We hadn’t known each other all that long, but from what I’d seen of him while I was in Hubei, he was a good man.
Like a rock in a raging current, he was free-spirited yet steadfast, with the ability to back up that resolve.
And more than anything, he deserved to be called a Great Hero.
So why?
I wanted to ask.
Not in the privacy of my own thoughts, but to their faces.
The Nine Sects and One Gang. The Five Great Families. The many Sect Leaders and Family Heads of the orthodox factions.
The Murim Alliance—the single banner they had all raised together.
I wanted to look those people, who had never hesitated to call themselves righteous, straight in the eye and ask:
Was this the righteous path they were so proud of?
Was their so-called great cause the reason they couldn’t stop the traitors heading west?
Crack.
The bones in my fist popped. I hadn’t realized how tightly I’d clenched it.
Jeok Cheongang, who had been watching me with a somber gaze, spoke.
“Anyone can become a coward when faced with a crisis.”
“I know.”
I added quietly, remembering a past that still lingered like a scar.
“I’ve been one myself.”
“It sounds like you’re saying you’ll never do it again.”
“I promised myself.”
“You must feel it in your bones, but even judging by what we know so far, their strength is beyond anything we imagined. If Xining is surrounded, we’ll be in for a very difficult fight.”
As if agreeing, Bow Saint nodded quietly. Both had reached heights martial artists could scarcely dream of, and yet even they had to consider the possibility of defeat. That was how dire things were.
“I told you before: anyone can become a coward in a crisis.”
Jeok Cheongang fixed his deep gaze on me. His voice was low and steady.
“In a situation like this, not a soul under heaven could blame you for withdrawing to fight another day.”
Withdraw to fight another day.
Mujin’s eyes widened as he understood what Jeok Cheongang meant. Bow Saint stayed silent.
And I—
“Probably. No, definitely.”
I met Jeok Cheongang’s gaze and continued.
“Even if I withdrew to fight another day—no, if I ran away—they’d have no right to criticize me.”
“Even if they did, it wouldn’t matter. If anyone dared to criticize you, I’d personally rip out his tongue. If anyone pointed a finger at you, I’d turn it to ash.”
“I know that too.”
“Then?”
“I’m staying. Here.”
At my calm reply, Jeok Cheongang’s brow furrowed.
“Why?”
“Because if we leave, Qinghai is finished. The countless civilians staying in Xining won’t even have time to escape.”
“If we fight to the death here, it may not just be Qinghai that falls into their hands. It could be the whole world.”
He wasn’t being arrogant. He wasn’t exaggerating.
The Three Saints and Ten Kings were symbols of the Murim world, and its strongest forces.
It was embarrassing to admit, but I, too, had become something of a symbol.
And a gap in our forces could lead straight to defeat.
As I fell silent, Jeok Cheongang went on with something like a sigh.
“The world has already looked away. The Nine Sects and One Gang, the Five Great Families, the Murim Alliance—they’ve all turned their backs. And you still mean to make such a foolish choice?”
That was when I finally parted my tightly closed lips.
“Even so, we have to.”
“What?”
“No. Because everyone has turned away and abandoned us, we have to do it even more.”
Jade is beautiful even as it shatters.
The light it gives off as it breaks into dozens of pieces is more brilliant than ever.
That is jade shattering.
That is why it is called jade shattering.
It is so brilliant, you forget the word destruction.
Because it breaks rather than be defiled.
“Have you ever seen jade covered in filth and dust?”
Jeok Cheongang stared at me, eyes wide. I continued, slowly but clearly.
“I haven’t. But I know that jade already covered in filth loses its value, at least for a while.”
Even then, the jade’s true nature doesn’t disappear.
It might look like nothing but filth, but the light is still hidden within it.
Yet no one who sees its beautiful surface covered in grime will want to touch it.
Not unless a sudden downpour washes the jade clean.
Not unless someone who remembers what it looks like finds it and carefully wipes it off.
So—
“Better to break than to be defiled.”
I felt the air tremble and let out the breath I’d been holding.
Yes. This was right.
Even if it ended in death, I couldn’t let that original brilliance fade.
I had to make everyone remember. I had to make them realize what mattered most—the thing they’d briefly forgotten amid excuses about the great cause and fears of what they might lose.
The jade called justice.
And I would do everything in my power to protect it.
I wouldn’t break. I wouldn’t be defiled.
There was still far too much to do before I faced that brilliant final moment.
The greatest, strongest wall casting its shadow over the world was still standing.
The Lord of Heaven.
Just then, as the meaning of those two words rang through my heart and drew nearer than ever, Jeok Cheongang—head bowed, lost in thought amid the heavy silence—suddenly spoke.
“You asked whether I’d ever seen jade covered in filth and dust?”
He muttered as if speaking to himself, then raised his head.
Though his body had grown young again, a familiar face was reflected in eyes that held the weight of his years.
“Yes. I saw it. I remember it very clearly.”
He looked at me.
His gaze, drawn back to that day in the not-so-distant past, began to shine.
“That was when I realized how brilliant a light the mangy, weak little whelp in front of me was carrying.”
“I told you, didn’t I? If anyone dared to criticize you or point a finger at you, I’d personally punish them. But do you know something?”
The furrows between his brows deepened.
With a clear smile on his face, he slowly reached out and rested a hand on my shoulder.
“If you’d made the same choice as them, I never would have forgiven you.”
Bow Saint spoke with a faint smile.
“Unfortunately, that won’t be happening. Your Disciple is far too good for that.”
A laugh escaped me before I knew it.
Yeah. That was probably true.
The Jeok Cheongang I knew had been that sort of person from the start.
First, he’d go find everyone who insulted his one and only Disciple and beat them to a pulp. Then he’d use whatever strength he had left to give his idiot Disciple a thorough beating.
“Looks like you’ll have to use that strength somewhere else.”
Jeok Cheongang laughed out loud at that.
“That’s the plan. I’ll squeeze out every last drop of strength I’ve got.”
And before half a day had passed, his words became reality.

With a clear smile on his face, he slowly reached out and rested a hand on my shoulder.
“If you’d made the same choice as them, I never would have forgiven you.”
Bow Saint spoke with a faint smile.
“Unfortunately, that won’t be happening.
Your Disciple is far too good for that.”
A laugh escaped me before I knew it.
Yeah.
That was probably true.
The Jeok Cheongang I knew had been that sort of person from the start.
First, he’d go find everyone who insulted his one and only Disciple and beat them to a pulp.
Then he’d use whatever strength he had left to give his idiot Disciple a thorough beating.
“Looks like you’ll have to use that strength somewhere else.”
Jeok Cheongang laughed out loud at that.
“That’s the plan.
I’ll squeeze out every last drop of strength I’ve got.”
And before half a day had passed, his words became reality.

chapters.title: Chapter 1089
paragraphs: As the hour of the Rooster began, an old beggar watched the sun inch toward the western mountains and muttered to himself.
“How strange. It’s not time for the sun to set yet.”
The other beggars huddled around a nearby campfire reacted to his words.
“Then what about weather like this at this time of year? Does that make sense?”
“Right. It’s not like this just started yesterday or the day before.”
“Branch Master, don’t stand out there in the cold wind. Come warm yourself by the fire. Have a bowl of hot soup, too.”
They had a point. The world hadn’t gone haywire just yesterday.
The old beggar—Man Chong, Branch Master of the Beggars’ Sect’s Xining branch in Qinghai—sighed and walked toward the fire.
Gung Gibang, the Successor Beggar, had returned to Xining several days ago. Man Chong, however, had stayed behind with around thirty Beggars’ Sect disciples under his command to gather information.
“Got anything to eat?”
“Of course. We may not have a damn thing to our names, but we always find a way to fill our bellies.”
“You saved some for the ones out on patrol?”
“Come now. Do you take us for beggars with no decency? Don’t worry. There’s enough for them to come back and eat till they burst.”
One of the beggars grinned, yellow teeth showing, and offered him a steaming bowl. Man Chong found himself smacking his lips.
“That smells incredible.”
“Just eat it. You’ll see it tastes as good as it smells.”
He was right.
Man Chong emptied the bowl in no time, then patted his full belly with a satisfied smile.
It looked like a hodgepodge if ever there was one, but perhaps because it was made with fish freshly caught in Qinghai Lake, it tasted like the work of a first-rate chef.
Well, I’m old. I deserve a little luxury like this.
Drowsy with contentment, Man Chong picked his teeth with a fish bone and looked around.
As he watched the waters of Qinghai Lake slowly take on the colors of the sunset, he felt his worries wash away, if only for a moment.
Reality, of course, was still bleak.
What good are a pretty view and a full belly? I can’t sleep easy until those bastards are gone.
Dark Heaven. At the thought of those terrifying Fiends, a shadow fell over Man Chong’s face.
The situation had hardly improved since Jin Taekyung and the reinforcements passed through here to join the others in Xining about four days ago.
No—it was getting worse by the day, as if to crush that brief glimmer of hope.
At this rate, we’ll be surrounded from both sides for sure... Damn it. We’re caught in a hell of a mess.

The mere thought of Dark Heaven’s massive army occupying Kunlun Mountain sent a chill down his spine. And from the rear, bandits who’d dealt the Central Plains Murim a vicious blow were said to be swarming in like ants.
There was only one thing they had going for them: Dark Heaven’s main force had yet to make a serious move.
But that’s only a matter of time. They’re coming, and soon.
The fullness in his belly vanished. Anxiety and fear took its place.
“...Damn it.”
His mood souring in an instant, Man Chong snatched up a pebble within reach and hurled it.
Whoosh!
His clothes were shabby, but he was a seasoned Branch Master and a master of the Beggars’ Sect.
The pebble shot from his fingertips toward the endless expanse of Qinghai Lake.
Splash!
The water split violently. Only then did the tightness in his chest ease a little. Man Chong snorted and turned away.
Or tried to.
He stopped when the ripples from the pebble settled and the water slowly grew still again.
What is it?
It didn’t take him long to place the sudden sense of déjà vu.
The color. The color of the water...
It was dark.
No—as black as if someone had poured ink into it.
Only moments ago, the waters of Qinghai Lake had glowed with the sunset. Now there was nothing beautiful about them, and even the quiet conversation behind him sounded strangely ominous.
“Man, why’s it getting dark so fast today? Usually the sunset alone lasts half an hour.”
“What can we do about it? It is what it is. Have some more food before the patrol comes back.”
“Don’t mind if I do. Branch Master, would you like another bowl?”
Man Chong didn’t answer. More precisely, he couldn’t.
At that moment, his instincts were sounding a red alarm in his head.
Something’s... wrong.
Of course, it could be nothing, as the other Beggars’ Sect disciples seemed to think.
Frost had fallen before harvest season, and giant monsters that barely looked human were running wild. What was left to be surprised by?
But he had a feeling he couldn’t explain. More than sixty years of experience—and an old veteran’s instinct, etched into his bones.
“The patrol. When are they due back?”
“Huh? Why do you ask all of a sudden?”
“Answer me. Now!”
The old Branch Master was usually so easygoing that his sudden bark left the disciples stammering.
“Th-they should be back soon.”
“W-well, they’re about half a gak later than usual, but they must be close by now. There’s no need to worry, Branch Master... Huh?”
One of the disciples trailed off, eyes widening as he looked over Man Chong’s shoulder. Everyone turned.
On a low hill about two hundred zhang away, a group of men and horses had just appeared, tiny as specks. They were slowly descending through the gathering darkness.
“Speak of the devil. There they are.”
“Look at those lazy bastards. They’re already late, and now they’re taking their sweet time?”
“Branch Master, stay put. I’ll give them a proper scolding this time.”
As everyone tossed out remarks while watching Man Chong’s expression, he stared at the patrol with sunken eyes and muttered,
“Twelve.”
“What?”
“Twelve. Unless my eyes are playing tricks on me.”
“What does that—”
The disciple’s question died on his lips.
The patrol that had left to survey the area about two shichen ago had numbered ten.
“Th-that means...”
“Could be one of two things. Either they found survivors who made it through by sheer luck...”
Man Chong drew the iron staff, worn smooth from years of handling, from his waist and added quietly,
“Or some sons of bitches who deserve to be chewed up alive are pretending to be the patrol.”
“Get to the boat now. We’ll raise anchor, put some distance between us, then see what happens.”
“Y-yes, Branch Master!”
At last grasping the danger, the disciples moved as one.
By the time they’d boarded the boat moored by the shore and rowed far enough away, the mysterious group—friend or foe, they couldn’t tell—had reached the campfire they’d left behind.
“Seok Sam! Seok Sam, are you there?”
Man Chong’s sudden shout was answered from beyond the darkness, which had grown noticeably deeper.
“I’m here! What is it?”
In that instant, Man Chong’s face went rigid.
So did every other Beggars’ Sect disciple’s. Not one of those staying at Qinghai Lake could have spoken down to Man Chong, their Branch Master and the oldest among them.
Worse, the voice from the darkness sounded exactly like Seok Sam’s.
“B-Branch Master...”
Leaving the Beggars’ Sect disciples behind, their faces pale as if they’d seen a ghost, Man Chong gritted his teeth and shouted again.
“Who are you bastards?”
For a moment, silence fell.
It lasted only a moment, but felt longer than ever—like an eternity.
Then an unfamiliar voice suddenly rang out, shattering the silence that seemed ready to suffocate them.
“Well, I guess beggar bastards are quick on the uptake.”
With a buoyant voice that even carried a hint of laughter, the figure that had only been a silhouette emerged into view, heading for the still-burning campfire.
Tap-tap.
Amid the sparks rising into the air, a man and horse crossed the gravel without the slightest sound. Man Chong’s eyes widened.
“W-what is that...?”
For a moment, he couldn’t speak.
The horse was a skeleton, its white bones exposed. But it was the man seated so casually on its back who filled him with a fear unlike anything he’d ever known.
The man grinned, baring unnaturally white teeth and fangs as sharp as a wild beast’s.
His blood-red eyes gleamed even at this distance. Just meeting his gaze felt as though it bound Man Chong’s body and mind.
“Y-you...”
The man shrugged at the trembling Man Chong.
“You know who I am, more or less.”
His nonchalance only made him more terrifying. Man Chong forced out a question.
“The patrol... What happened to them?”
“Aw. How touching. All that begging together must have made you close.”
“You bastard! Answer me!”
“How am I supposed to talk with a beggar yelling at me? Fine, fine. Don’t get so worked up.”
The man waved a hand as though calming him down, then smacked his lips.
“To sum it up, they’ve gone to a better place. Didn’t taste like much, though.”
“W-what did you say?”
Man Chong froze, his mind settling on a suspicion too horrible to put into words. The man frowned.
“Hey, don’t get the wrong idea. Maybe it’s because they were mangy beggar bastards, but their bodies weren’t much to write home about either. I only drank a little blood, just to have some fun.”
“What? Was that not good enough for you? I thought I got the voice pretty close.”
Grit.
The pungent scent of blood filled Man Chong’s mouth. Even so, he clenched his teeth with all his strength.
It wasn’t only rage at losing a subordinate who had been like a brother to him. He had to do this—had to hold on somehow—to bear the fear tightening its grip on him with every passing moment.
Dark arts.
Never had those words felt so chilling.
Nor had he ever felt as if his head could be severed at any moment by someone standing a hundred zhang away.
“So you’re the one. The leader we’ve heard about.”
“Well, let’s say I am. At least here, that person has entrusted everything to me.”
The man—the Blood Lord—smiled at Man Chong.
Then he slowly swept his gaze over the twenty Beggars’ Sect disciples, frozen like statues around him, and spoke.
“So, who’ll it be?”
“What?”
“I’m planning to let at least one of you live. One of you gets to survive, and I get someone to deliver a message. Good for both sides, isn’t it?”
“Look at your faces. What, did you think you could just run away?”
The Blood Lord grinned at their rigid faces a hundred zhang away, then turned to look behind him.
“Time to get moving, isn’t it? It’s something we have to do anyway.”
At his words, one of the figures waiting in the darkness stepped forward.
Swish.
Long robes brushed the gravel. As if the Blood Lord weren’t worth answering, the Grand Sorceress passed him, reached the lakeshore, and extended her hand.
“Cold north wind...”
Wooooom.
The air trembled. A vast chill swept across Qinghai Lake.
And then, they saw it.
“Freeze.”
Crack-crack-crack!
With a crack of ice, Qinghai Lake froze white.
Man Chong and all twenty Beggars’ Sect disciples stared, wide-eyed.
A miracle that should not—and could not—exist.
Faced with that impossible sight, they could do nothing.
Not even when the foul stench of monsters began to drift toward them from beyond the thick darkness in the distance.
Not when the Blood Lord crossed the frozen lake as casually as if out for a stroll, climbed onto the bow of their boat, and looked down at them.
“Whoever survives, go tell them. I—the Blood Lord—am coming.”
At that moment, Man Chong forced out his voice with everything he had.
“You’ll never win—”
Crunch!
Scarlet blood sprayed across the white ice.
“So, have you decided who gets to survive?”
In the cold, deep night, the Blood Lord’s blood-red eyes gleamed.

chapters.title: Chapter 1090
paragraphs: Qinghai was unquestionably a border region.
It was among the largest provinces in the world and had some of the most beautiful scenery, but its supplies and households were nowhere near as plentiful as those of the Central Plains.

So whenever people compared Qinghai to the Central Plains—which had stood at the center of the world for thousands of years and developed its culture in every direction—the people of Qinghai liked to joke:
“Qinghai and the Central Plains have only three things in common. They see the same sun, they’re connected by the same water—the Yellow River—and they both have beggars.”
Beggars were common everywhere, after all.
They lived along busy main roads, in dark, filthy alleys, and in shantytowns beside streams. It made no difference whether they were in the Central Plains or out on the border.
There were so many that people joked the Beggars’ Sect could found a nation of its own if it took in every beggar under heaven.
But near daybreak, a scouting party searching through the faint morning mist came across a white-haired beggar unlike any they had ever seen.
No—there was something so strange about him that it made the fine hairs on their bodies stand up.
Step. Step.
He staggered as though he might collapse at any moment. His eyes were empty, as if his soul had left his body.
And then...
“Tell them. Without fail. Whoever survives.”
His voice trembled with terror as it slipped between his blue lips.
Perhaps that was why the scouts stood frozen for a moment before they noticed the two knots tied at the beggar’s waist.
“...The Beggars’ Sect.”
There was no mistaking it. The beggar before them was a Beggars’ Sect martial artist.
A two-knot disciple, just one rank below a Branch Master.
And as far as they knew, there was only one reason a Beggars’ Sect disciple would appear here, a hundred li west of Xining, where the scouts had set out from.
“Old man, what on earth happened at Qinghai Lake—”
One scout hurriedly dismounted and started toward him, then caught his breath and stared.
Only then did he see it.
Through the pale mist, the disciple’s hair had looked white with age. In truth, it was frozen stiff, like the hair of someone trapped in a glacier.
And the face turned white beneath it belonged not to an old man, but to a young one.
“W-what is this...?”
Was this what it felt like to have a bolt of lightning strike through the crown of your head?
All twenty scouts fell silent, a chill running down their spines.
They had no idea that the disciple’s next words would be the last spark of his life, spoken with every ounce of strength he had left.
“Tell them. I’m coming. I’ll go to Xining and kill and burn everything there.”
For an instant, the scouts trembled, their eyes wide with shock.
Because of the terrifying killing intent in those words?
No. That wasn’t it.
The Beggars’ Sect disciple was smiling. And crying at the same time.
As though imitating whoever had ordered him to deliver the message.
As though grieving for the comrades who were already dead.
Then, in the suffocating silence that pressed down on them all, his body tilted. His difficult journey had come to an end, and his voice had grown faint.
“Just wait. I, the Blood Lord, have returned—”
Thud.
His body crumpled like a rotten log.
The scouts stared blankly at the Beggars’ Sect disciple’s corpse. Then, all at once, they raised their heads and looked west.
Why?
Was it the fear already taking root in their hearts, or an instinctive sense of what they were about to face?
Beyond the thick mist, they could almost hear the shrieks of hideous monsters and smell their stench.
“...See to his body.”
The commander had to force the words out, and even then his voice couldn’t hide his fear.
“We’re going back to Xining. Right now.”
The office of the Qinghai City Lord—now a headless corpse—was as impossibly spacious and luxurious as ever.
As though it existed to prove why he’d had to die.
Its expensive ebony table was large enough to seat dozens of people at once. He had even used Shu brocade, prized as a first-rate luxury in Sichuan, to keep out the sunlight.
But the City Lord could never have known that the gaudy luxuries he’d treasured until his death would now be put to use for a shabby beggar.
“Enjoying this kind of luxury when you’re only a two-knot disciple. You forgot what it means to be a beggar.”
Gung Gibang muttered, doing his best to sound calm.
The corpse lay on the ebony table, wrapped in Shu brocade. Gung Gibang’s eyes glistened as he looked at it.
“I didn’t know him long, but he was a good kid. Still young, and already talented enough to be granted the second knot.”
I said nothing.
Neither did any of the other leaders gathered in the office.
“He asked if he could visit the Central Plains someday, once things got better. I snapped at him for saying something so childish... Damn it.”
Gung Gibang swore in a hollow voice and gave a bitter smile.
“What can you do? He and the others were just unlucky.”
Nearly thirty Beggars’ Sect disciples had been left on the other side of Qinghai Lake. Only one young, nameless disciple had made it back to Xining.
And even he had died along the way.
He’d been in such a terrible state that the scouts who found him could barely speak.
But his final words, which might as well have been a will, contained information more valuable than this entire goddamn lavish office.
“The Blood Lord. If it’s the Blood Lord...”
I nodded at the murmur from Cheongheoja, the Kunlun Sect Leader.
“It’s the same one you’re thinking of, Sect Leader. The one behind the Shaolin Bloodshed.”
An invisible ripple passed through the room.
Those who already knew of the Blood Lord let out low murmurs without a word. Those who hadn’t known the details stared in shock.
The Fire King, Jeok Cheongang, belonged to neither group.
“A name I’ve longed to hear again.”
His voice was quiet, his expression barely changed.
But I knew better than anyone how furious Jeok Cheongang was.
And how hard he was fighting to hold that fury back.
“Now I can hold my head up in front of that damned monk.”

Hong Dao had been the Abbot of Shaolin Temple, known as the Mount Tai and Northern Dipper of the Murim, and respected enough to earn the title of Dharma King. Yet Jeok Cheongang had always called him “that damned monk.”
He’d been one of the very few friends Jeok Cheongang had ever had. Maybe the only one.
There was no way Jeok Cheongang had forgotten, even for a moment, his grudge against the man who had killed Hong Dao.
But right now, there was something more pressing than his grudge.
“So they mean to throw everything they have into this after all.”
A young Daoist spoke in a voice so calm it almost sounded cold. Hak Eui, Cheongheoja’s second Disciple, continued.
“They went to the trouble of releasing a Beggars’ Sect disciple they’d already captured. That must mean they’re certain they’ll win.”
“S-second brother.”
Hak Su, his Senior Brother, had been watching the room uneasily and tried to stop him. Hak Eui paid him no mind.
He’d gained a measure of influence since the last meeting about the Qinghai City Lord.
“But it’s unfortunate we didn’t receive the most important information. If we’d known even the enemy’s numbers, we could have made a much better plan—”
“What?”

Hak Eui answered his anger evenly.

No—the whole of Xining.

sentences.text: Qinghai was unquestionably a border region.
It was among the largest provinces in the world and had some of the most beautiful scenery, but its supplies and households were nowhere near as plentiful as those of the Central Plains.

So whenever people compared Qinghai to the Central Plains—which had stood at the center of the world for thousands of years and developed its culture in every direction—the people of Qinghai liked to joke:
“Qinghai and the Central Plains have only three things in common.
They see the same sun, they’re connected by the same water—the Yellow River—and they both have beggars.”
Beggars were common everywhere, after all.
They lived along busy main roads, in dark, filthy alleys, and in shantytowns beside streams.
It made no difference whether they were in the Central Plains or out on the border.
There were so many that people joked the Beggars’ Sect could found a nation of its own if it took in every beggar under heaven.
But near daybreak, a scouting party searching through the faint morning mist came across a white-haired beggar unlike any they had ever seen.
No—there was something so strange about him that it made the fine hairs on their bodies stand up.
Step.
Step.
He staggered as though he might collapse at any moment.
His eyes were empty, as if his soul had left his body.
And then...
“Tell them.
Without fail.
Whoever survives.”
His voice trembled with terror as it slipped between his blue lips.
Perhaps that was why the scouts stood frozen for a moment before they noticed the two knots tied at the beggar’s waist.
“...The Beggars’ Sect.”
There was no mistaking it.
The beggar before them was a Beggars’ Sect martial artist.
A two-knot disciple, just one rank below a Branch Master.
And as far as they knew, there was only one reason a Beggars’ Sect disciple would appear here, a hundred li west of Xining, where the scouts had set out from.
“Old man, what on earth happened at Qinghai Lake—”
One scout hurriedly dismounted and started toward him, then caught his breath and stared.
Only then did he see it.
Through the pale mist, the disciple’s hair had looked white with age.
In truth, it was frozen stiff, like the hair of someone trapped in a glacier.
And the face turned white beneath it belonged not to an old man, but to a young one.
“W-what is this...?”
Was this what it felt like to have a bolt of lightning strike through the crown of your head?
All twenty scouts fell silent, a chill running down their spines.
They had no idea that the disciple’s next words would be the last spark of his life, spoken with every ounce of strength he had left.
“Tell them.
I’m coming.
I’ll go to Xining and kill and burn everything there.”
For an instant, the scouts trembled, their eyes wide with shock.
Because of the terrifying killing intent in those words?
No.
That wasn’t it.
The Beggars’ Sect disciple was smiling.
And crying at the same time.
As though imitating whoever had ordered him to deliver the message.
As though grieving for the comrades who were already dead.
Then, in the suffocating silence that pressed down on them all, his body tilted.
His difficult journey had come to an end, and his voice had grown faint.
“Just wait.
I, the Blood Lord, have returned—”
Thud.
His body crumpled like a rotten log.
The scouts stared blankly at the Beggars’ Sect disciple’s corpse.
Then, all at once, they raised their heads and looked west.
Why?
Was it the fear already taking root in their hearts, or an instinctive sense of what they were about to face?
Beyond the thick mist, they could almost hear the shrieks of hideous monsters and smell their stench.
“...See to his body.”
The commander had to force the words out, and even then his voice couldn’t hide his fear.
“We’re going back to Xining.
Right now.”
The office of the Qinghai City Lord—now a headless corpse—was as impossibly spacious and luxurious as ever.
As though it existed to prove why he’d had to die.
Its expensive ebony table was large enough to seat dozens of people at once.
He had even used Shu brocade, prized as a first-rate luxury in Sichuan, to keep out the sunlight.
But the City Lord could never have known that the gaudy luxuries he’d treasured until his death would now be put to use for a shabby beggar.
“Enjoying this kind of luxury when you’re only a two-knot disciple.
You forgot what it means to be a beggar.”
Gung Gibang muttered, doing his best to sound calm.
The corpse lay on the ebony table, wrapped in Shu brocade.
Gung Gibang’s eyes glistened as he looked at it.
“I didn’t know him long, but he was a good kid.
Still young, and already talented enough to be granted the second knot.”
I said nothing.
Neither did any of the other leaders gathered in the office.
“He asked if he could visit the Central Plains someday, once things got better.
I snapped at him for saying something so childish...
Damn it.”
Gung Gibang swore in a hollow voice and gave a bitter smile.
“What can you do?
He and the others were just unlucky.”
Nearly thirty Beggars’ Sect disciples had been left on the other side of Qinghai Lake.
Only one young, nameless disciple had made it back to Xining.
And even he had died along the way.
He’d been in such a terrible state that the scouts who found him could barely speak.
But his final words, which might as well have been a will, contained information more valuable than this entire goddamn lavish office.

chapters.title: Chapter 1091
paragraphs: Xining, the capital of Qinghai, stood on a vast plateau.

Tributaries of the Yellow River flowed to its east and west, stretching all the way to the Central Plains. Mountains large and small surrounded the city, making for a view beautiful enough to draw gasps from anyone who saw it.
But at that moment, not one of the countless people crowding Xining’s high walls could think the view before them was beautiful.
It wasn’t that they failed to appreciate it. They couldn’t.
A mountain that should have stood tall and still, as it always had, was moving. The sight alone was enough to send a chill down their spines.
Rrrk. Rrrrk.
A tremendous rumble unlike anything they had ever felt.
The whole city shook with it. So did its people, body and soul.
And at the end of all those gazes, filled with undisguised horror, was a pitch-black mountain drawing closer from the distance.
No—an army moving like a single mountain.
Dark Heaven.
At last, they had come.
Fiends from beyond the desert, come to blacken the blue sky and green earth alike.
I couldn’t have been the only one who felt as though the world had suddenly grown dark.
It was dark everywhere.
Clouds hid the sun, and a chill that swallowed its light filled the space it left behind.
And.
At the center of it all, they stood.
Dark Heaven’s vast army of monsters and humans.
“...Benefactor.”
Cheongpung had come up onto the wall at some point. His voice was lower than usual, with a faint tremor in it, but I didn’t answer.
More precisely, I couldn’t.
I was overwhelmed, too, by the sight of the enemy advancing beyond the wall, filling everything in view.
I couldn’t let anyone see that. Not ever.
But even if I could fool the whole world, there was one person I couldn’t fool.
—Are you afraid?
At Jeok Cheongang’s Sound Transmission in my ear, I quietly bit my lip.
Yes. I am.
At this moment, I was terrified enough to shudder.
Their strength was far greater than I’d imagined. And the moment I saw them for what they truly were, the word defeat had come to me by instinct. That frightened me.
Squeeze.
Warmth spread through the fist I’d clenched without realizing it. I curled my fingers tighter to keep the beads of blood from slipping between them, and answered.
—Yes. I’m afraid.
—What are you so afraid of?
—Myself, most of all. I made up my mind. I prepared for this. And I still shrank back. I’m afraid of what might happen because of that.
I wouldn’t claim I wasn’t afraid of dying.
That would deny every desperate struggle I’d made to survive. It would be laughable hypocrisy.
But I feared something far more: the hundreds of thousands of lives behind this wall being lost because I’d made the wrong choice.
Because of me, and no one else.
Jeok Cheongang saw right through me.
—Yes. That’s the difference between you and this old man.
Before I could ask what he meant, his next Sound Transmission reached me.
—Not once in my life have I pursued some grand cause. I simply went where my feet took me, where the wind blew. The deaths of strangers I’d never met didn’t trouble me much.
People saw Jeok Cheongang as the foremost of the Ten Kings, one of the great figures of the orthodox faction. But the truth was different.
He was a free man.
Like the Sect Leaders of the Fire Gate Clan before him, he belonged to none of the orthodox, unorthodox, or demonic factions. He had walked only his own path.
—Perhaps that’s why the title of Great Hero, which stuck to me before I knew it, always felt like clothes that didn’t fit.
—But you deserve to be called one.
—No. That’s wrong.
Jeok Cheongang answered firmly and fixed me with a deep, searching gaze.
—Only someone who fears the pain of others and knows how to shed tears deserves to be called a Great Hero. Someone like you.
—But remember one thing. If you don’t want to shed tears later, you must first overcome the fear in front of you.
Then Jeok Cheongang added quietly,
—Only then do you become a hero.
A hero. A hero, huh.
I mouthed those two words in my mind. They had always felt so far away. Then I gave a bitter smile.
—I never wanted to be one.
—That doesn’t matter. Wanting to be a hero isn’t what makes you one. You earn the title when the world calls you one.
—Like how they call you a Great Hero, Old Master?
—What?

—You just said it yourself. You never went out of your way to pursue a grand cause. You went where your feet took you, where the wind blew—and before you knew it, people were calling you a Great Hero.
Jeok Cheongang stared at me, eyes wide. Then he licked his lips.
—You got me with that one.
—Let’s call it even.
—You haven’t lost your knack for running that mouth. Now you’re finally starting to feel like the little hellion I knew.
Jeok Cheongang let out a quiet laugh and gestured with his chin beyond the wall.
—Well? Still afraid?
—Yes.
I answered without hesitation, then added calmly,
—But I won’t look away from that fear.
Everyone carries fear somewhere in their heart.
But only those who admit it and face it head-on can find the strength to stand against it.
Just as I was doing now.
Rumble. Rrrumble!
The rumbling grew stronger by the moment, and the ground shook as if an earthquake had struck.
I felt the powerful vibrations travel up the tall, sturdy wall and through my whole body.
At the same time, I saw him.
At the head of the enemy forces, so numerous I couldn’t begin to count them, one man was grinning as he looked straight at us.
The Blood Lord.
He looked quite different from the last time I’d seen him, but the moment I saw that crooked smile, I knew by instinct.
The thick killing intent and madness about him seemed as though they’d rub off if I touched him. Even the Blood-Sword Demon Lord I’d defeated in Gansu couldn’t compare.
And in the instant we recognized each other, his lips moved.
“Looking up at you is a pain in the neck. Why don’t you come down for a bit and say hello?”
His words rang out through the deafening rumble and clouds of dust. Jeok Cheongang, who had already been staring hard at the Blood Lord, had a reddish gleam in his eyes.
“I was itching for a fight anyway. How kind of him to offer.”
The Bow Saint immediately sensed what was coming and tried to stop him.
“He’s baiting you. It couldn’t be more obvious.”
At her look for support, the Slaughter Saint, who had appeared out of nowhere and taken up a place on the wall, calmly nodded.
“Yeah, it’s crazy.”
Jeok Cheongang furrowed his brow. The Slaughter Saint added,
“Then again, no one here is in their right mind.”
As Jeok Cheongang’s brow smoothed, I delivered my solemn verdict.
“Let’s do it now.”
“Right. It’s not like we’ll die or anything.”
Whoosh!
There wasn’t even time for anyone to stop us.
Reciting the number-one last words of men everywhere, the three of us sprang off the wall together.
Behind us came the sharpest, loudest shout I’d ever heard from the Bow Saint.
“I told you not to go!”
Uh.
Sorry.
The moment he saw three figures hurtling across the distant sky toward him, the Blood Lord muttered without realizing it,
“They’re crazy. They’re actually coming?”
He’d only tossed out a casual remark. After a few words between them, he hadn’t expected them to charge straight at him without a moment’s hesitation.
“What are they, half-mad fighting dogs...?”
The Blood Lord trailed off, more than a little taken aback. By then, the three men had closed to a dozen or so zhang, moving like flashes of light. They spoke at once.
“You told us to come down, you son of a bitch.”
“You’re lower than a dog. You goddamned bastard. Burning you alive wouldn’t be enough, you miserable—”
“So you’re the Blood Lord I’ve heard about. I know this is a strange request for a first meeting, but would you mind calmly offering your neck and stepping aside?”

First came Jin Taekyung, whose curses had an oddly satisfying ring to them. Then Jeok Cheongang, hurling every obscenity he knew. And finally the Slaughter Saint, whom the Blood Lord was meeting for the first time.
For a moment, surprise had covered the Blood Lord’s anger. Now he felt it surge back to the surface.
“Are you done talking?”
At the Blood Lord’s low voice, Jin Taekyung hesitated briefly and glanced at the Slaughter Saint.
“Anything else you’d like to say?”
“Probably not. We’ve only just met, so I don’t have much to say.”
The Slaughter Saint had already been remarkably rude for someone meeting him for the first time, but Jin Taekyung merely nodded and answered the Blood Lord.
“This one says he’s done.”
Crack.
The Blood Lord clenched his teeth at that nonchalant response and opened his mouth.
Or tried to.
Before he could, another wave of obscenities swept over him.
“I’ll grind down every last bone in your body. I’ll toss your flesh to the Nanman Beast Palace for feed, then scatter your remains in the Shaolin Temple latrines, and—”
“Ah, this one isn’t done yet. Give him a moment. Honestly, aren’t you a little curious what comes next?”
At that moment, the Blood Lord’s last thread of reason snapped. His vision went white.
“Hah!”
KWA-A-A!
A powerful wave of qi swept out in every direction.
The immense internal energy packed into that single shout made Dark Heaven’s seemingly endless army and the people on the wall a hundred or so zhang away hold their breath.
But the three men closest to him, who felt the full force of it, were the exception.
Whoosh!
A single sharp gust cut through the billowing dust.
At its center, Jin Taekyung had already slashed down with his clear, almost transparent spearhead. He grinned.
Just as the Blood Lord had before they came down from the wall.
“Why are you getting so worked up? I’m just glad to see you after all this time.”
An explosion meant destruction. Destruction, in turn, was bound up with Erasure.
The Blood Lord had gathered his anger and unleashed it all at once. Now he stared at Jin Taekyung with eyes gone cold.
“You’re just the same as before. That damned mouth of yours.”
The smile vanished from Jin Taekyung’s lips.
“This time will be different. Everything else will be.”
