chapters.title: Chapter 1097
paragraphs: The moment he saw the Blood Lord’s savage smile, the Dalai Lama felt a chill race up his spine.
What in the world is this man?
He was different. Unmistakably different.
Something about the man before him stirred the primal fear every human being carried.
A darkness as deep as an abyss, enough to make even the ruler of vast Tibet shudder.
A predator.
He looked at the Dark Heaven followers who had surrounded him and the Twelve Secret Monks as if to enclose them.
“This humble monk... has been discourteous.”
For a moment, he had forgotten what sort of man the Blood Lord was. And who stood behind him.
But when the Blood Lord bared the fangs he’d kept hidden, the Dalai Lama remembered the reality he’d let slip from his mind.
Who was weak, and who was strong.
If a conflict broke out now that neither side could take back, which of them would be devoured?
That was why the king of the theocratic state that ruled Tibet had no choice but to bow his head slowly.
“I swear, I had no intention of insulting someone the Lord of Heaven favors. It’s only that I was troubled, and made a mistake...”
“A mistake.”
The Blood Lord cut him off and ran his red tongue over his lips, like a beast savoring the sight of its prey.
Then he smiled at the Dalai Lama.
“I understand. Anyone can make a mistake now and then. Once.”
The meaning in the Blood Lord’s quiet final words was unmistakable.
Once. Just once.
He would not tolerate a second mistake.
The Blood Lord had gone back to addressing him respectfully as though nothing had happened. His attitude said the opposite. The Dalai Lama gritted his teeth and accepted it.
“Thank you for saying so.”
“Come now, there’s no need to be so formal. We’re comrades working toward a great cause, aren’t we?”
“...You’re absolutely right.”
Of course, the Dalai Lama knew how hollow those words were.

The balance of power had been settled decades ago, when he took the hand the Lord of Heaven had offered him. This was the generosity only the strong could afford—a carrot tossed his way after a crack of the whip.
But by now, the Dalai Lama and the Potala Palace had only one choice left.
They had to acknowledge it and accept it all.
Only then could they avenge the grudge passed down from their predecessors and survive in the new world Dark Heaven would one day rule.
“The Potala Palace will do everything it can to repay, in some small measure, the grace the Lord of Heaven has bestowed upon us. However...”
“However?”
The Blood Lord’s eyebrow twitched. The Dalai Lama went on in a low, subdued voice.
“I trust you’ll honor your promise.”
The Blood Lord studied him as though he could see right through him, then clicked his tongue.
“So that’s what you meant... Don’t worry. The Fire Gate Clan’s lineage will end right here in Xining.”
“I don’t doubt you, donor, but couldn’t they escape Xining and flee to the Central Plains before the Green Forest Alliance and the Yangtze River Channel League seal off the rear completely?”
“Escape? Did you just say escape? The Fire King and Jin Taekyung, of all people?”
Before the Dalai Lama could answer, the Blood Lord laughed aloud and continued.
“Palace Lord, you hate the Fire Gate Clan more than anyone, yet you know nothing about them.”

“If we’re talking about a small handful of people—those two in particular—I’d say they have plenty of chances to get away. Even the Fire Gate Clan’s fools, who can’t tell up from down, might decide to live to fight another day when the odds are this bad.”
He was right.
They weren’t talking about the tens of thousands of troops huddled in Xining, or its hundreds of thousands of people. They were talking about a tiny handful.
And if those people were the Fire King Jeok Cheongang and the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung, they could break out through the rear right now and tear a hole in the encirclement.
But the Dalai Lama’s concern only made the Blood Lord laugh harder.
“Impossible. Absolutely impossible.”
“What makes you so sure?”
“Don’t you know? You just said it yourself.”
“What do you—”
The Dalai Lama’s question was cut short. The Blood Lord suddenly stopped laughing and spoke in a hoarse voice.
“Fucking idiots who can’t tell up from down. That’s the Fire Gate Clan.”
“Master and Disciple alike, not one of them gives a damn about his own life. And with tens of thousands of allies and hundreds of thousands of civilians still here... well, that settles it.”
If those two had wanted to live to fight another day, they wouldn’t be in Xining now.
No. None of what they’d done up to this point would have happened.

Once they lost their temper, they’d charge straight in whether their opponent was the Demonic Cult or the Jade Emperor himself. And even with their lives at stake, if there was something they had to protect, they protected it.
Someone like the Blood Lord might mock their deeds as idiocy rather than chivalry.
But that was the Fire Gate Clan.
“I’ll say it one last time: they will never leave Xining. I’ll stake my life on it.”
More certain than ever, the Blood Lord recalled the young pup who had dared to face him a year ago in a blood-soaked valley on Mount Song, and how desperately he had fought.
He recalled the fire in the eyes of the young beast he’d faced again today—one he could no longer call a pup.
At last, he knew for certain what sort of person the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung was.
And he made up his mind.
Even if he had to defy the Lord of Heaven’s command, he would kill Jin Taekyung and eliminate the threat.
Even if someone inside smuggles him out through the rear, it won’t matter.
Farmers worried about their crops being washed away watched the sky closely. Everyone else noticed the storm clouds only when raindrops landed on their heads.
The peace that had lasted more than fifty years was long. And the storm clouds that had crept slowly toward them were now overhead.
Even as Dark Heaven’s concealed blade, planted deep within their ranks long ago, pierced their flesh, they had yet to notice it.
The moment I get the signal from inside, I’ll strike and finish this in one go.
The Blood Lord smiled faintly and looked up.
One by one, raindrops fell from the dark sky, heralding a downpour unlike any before it.
An omen of the storm that would sweep away everything in Qinghai.
Tap. Plip.
As I felt the sudden raindrops wet the top of my head, I thought:
For a victory celebration, this is pretty damn soggy.
We’d fought a battle we hadn’t planned on, but for such a short fight, we’d accomplished plenty.
By my estimate, we’d taken down hundreds of enemies. That included the Black Ghost Jeok Cheongang had reduced to ash with a full-powered strike.
Of course, that was only a fraction of them.
I kept that thought to myself and stared past the wall at the army blackening the land beyond it.
Hundreds fewer enemies. Thousands more.

For a moment, the balance of power had edged the tiniest bit closer to even. With the Potala Palace’s arrival, it had tipped further against us than before. The weight of it pressed down on one corner of everyone’s heart, mine included.
“Maybe... we’ve already missed our chance.”
Watching the enemy build an ever tighter, more impregnable encirclement, Bow Saint continued in a heavy voice:
“Since we were already committed, we should’ve finished things before the Potala Palace arrived. We might’ve had a chance then.”
At that one sentence, which put into words what everyone already felt, someone who’d been standing with his arms crossed in silence spoke up.
“Even so, if we use the cover of night to eliminate their entire leadership, we’ll have a good chance.”
If Hyuk Mujin had said that, I’d have hung him upside down and thrown him over the wall. Thankfully, it hadn’t come to that.
The words had come from the assassin hailed as the greatest of all time.
The others looked at him hopefully, waiting for him to go on. I shook my head without hesitation.
“Absolutely not.”
The Slaughter Saint asked:
“Why do you object?”
“Can I be honest?”
“When have you ever been anything else? Go on.”
“It’s simple. You’d go in there just to die like a dog.”
The mood sank at once. The Slaughter Saint gave me a long, searching look.
“That goes beyond honesty. It’s almost a provocation.”
“I like joking around, and I’m good at provoking people. But I don’t do that to allies in the same boat. You already know that.”
“I learned something from facing them myself just now. If I go, there’s a chance.”
“How much of a chance?”
“One in ten.”
The Slaughter Saint answered as if the slim odds were no big deal, then looked at the rain, growing heavier by the moment.
“One in five, if the heavens lend a hand.”
“That’s all?”
“That’s as much as one in five. Considering what we’d gain if I succeeded, my life would be a bargain.”
He was right.
Even so, I could only smile bitterly.
“If we stood to gain anything at all, I wouldn’t have called it dying like a dog.”
“Now that they know I’m here, I expect them to prepare. They might even set every Black Ghost they have left to guard their leaders.”
“I know. I know you’ve considered the other possibilities, too.”
“Then why?”
“Because it’s simple.”
Naturally, I wasn’t the one who answered.
Jeok Cheongang had been silent all along. Now he spoke up and continued as everyone turned to look at him.
“Dark arts—no, Magic. When it comes to that damned stuff, even the greatest assassin of all time is as good as deaf and blind. Am I wrong?”
I nodded.
No—more precisely, before I could even nod, Jeok Cheongang grabbed my shoulder and made me move.
Before I could ask why, his low Sound Transmission slipped into my ear, and I had no choice but to fall silent.
—So, are you really not going to tell me until the very end?
Jeok Cheongang stared at me, his gaze sunk deep.
—What nonsense that bastard the Blood Lord was spouting at the last moment.

sentences.text: The moment he saw the Blood Lord’s savage smile, the Dalai Lama felt a chill race up his spine.
What in the world is this man?
He was different.
Unmistakably different.
Something about the man before him stirred the primal fear every human being carried.
A darkness as deep as an abyss, enough to make even the ruler of vast Tibet shudder.
A predator.
He looked at the Dark Heaven followers who had surrounded him and the Twelve Secret Monks as if to enclose them.
“This humble monk... has been discourteous.”
For a moment, he had forgotten what sort of man the Blood Lord was.
And who stood behind him.
But when the Blood Lord bared the fangs he’d kept hidden, the Dalai Lama remembered the reality he’d let slip from his mind.
Who was weak, and who was strong.
If a conflict broke out now that neither side could take back, which of them would be devoured?
That was why the king of the theocratic state that ruled Tibet had no choice but to bow his head slowly.
“I swear, I had no intention of insulting someone the Lord of Heaven favors.
It’s only that I was troubled, and made a mistake...”
“A mistake.”
The Blood Lord cut him off and ran his red tongue over his lips, like a beast savoring the sight of its prey.
Then he smiled at the Dalai Lama.
“I understand.
Anyone can make a mistake now and then.
Once.”
The meaning in the Blood Lord’s quiet final words was unmistakable.
Once.
Just once.
He would not tolerate a second mistake.
The Blood Lord had gone back to addressing him respectfully as though nothing had happened.
His attitude said the opposite.
The Dalai Lama gritted his teeth and accepted it.
“Thank you for saying so.”
“Come now, there’s no need to be so formal.
We’re comrades working toward a great cause, aren’t we?”
“...You’re absolutely right.”
Of course, the Dalai Lama knew how hollow those words were.
The balance of power had been settled decades ago, when he took the hand the Lord of Heaven had offered him.
This was the generosity only the strong could afford—a carrot tossed his way after a crack of the whip.
But by now, the Dalai Lama and the Potala Palace had only one choice left.
They had to acknowledge it and accept it all.
Only then could they avenge the grudge passed down from their predecessors and survive in the new world Dark Heaven would one day rule.
“The Potala Palace will do everything it can to repay, in some small measure, the grace the Lord of Heaven has bestowed upon us.
However...”
“However?”
The Blood Lord’s eyebrow twitched.
The Dalai Lama went on in a low, subdued voice.
“I trust you’ll honor your promise.”
The Blood Lord studied him as though he could see right through him, then clicked his tongue.
“So that’s what you meant...
Don’t worry.
The Fire Gate Clan’s lineage will end right here in Xining.”
“I don’t doubt you, donor, but couldn’t they escape Xining and flee to the Central Plains before the Green Forest Alliance and the Yangtze River Channel League seal off the rear completely?”
“Escape?
Did you just say escape?
The Fire King and Jin Taekyung, of all people?”
Before the Dalai Lama could answer, the Blood Lord laughed aloud and continued.
“Palace Lord, you hate the Fire Gate Clan more than anyone, yet you know nothing about them.”
“If we’re talking about a small handful of people—those two in particular—I’d say they have plenty of chances to get away.
Even the Fire Gate Clan’s fools, who can’t tell up from down, might decide to live to fight another day when the odds are this bad.”
He was right.
They weren’t talking about the tens of thousands of troops huddled in Xining, or its hundreds of thousands of people.
They were talking about a tiny handful.
And if those people were the Fire King Jeok Cheongang and the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung, they could break out through the rear right now and tear a hole in the encirclement.
But the Dalai Lama’s concern only made the Blood Lord laugh harder.
“Impossible.
Absolutely impossible.”
“What makes you so sure?”
“Don’t you know?
You just said it yourself.”
“What do you—”
The Dalai Lama’s question was cut short.
The Blood Lord suddenly stopped laughing and spoke in a hoarse voice.
“Fucking idiots who can’t tell up from down.
That’s the Fire Gate Clan.”
“Master and Disciple alike, not one of them gives a damn about his own life.
And with tens of thousands of allies and hundreds of thousands of civilians still here... well, that settles it.”
If those two had wanted to live to fight another day, they wouldn’t be in Xining now.
No.
None of what they’d done up to this point would have happened.
Once they lost their temper, they’d charge straight in whether their opponent was the Demonic Cult or the Jade Emperor himself.
And even with their lives at stake, if there was something they had to protect, they protected it.
Someone like the Blood Lord might mock their deeds as idiocy rather than chivalry.
But that was the Fire Gate Clan.
“I’ll say it one last time: they will never leave Xining.
I’ll stake my life on it.”
More certain than ever, the Blood Lord recalled the young pup who had dared to face him a year ago in a blood-soaked valley on Mount Song, and how desperately he had fought.
He recalled the fire in the eyes of the young beast he’d faced again today—one he could no longer call a pup.
At last, he knew for certain what sort of person the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung was.
And he made up his mind.
Even if he had to defy the Lord of Heaven’s command, he would kill Jin Taekyung and eliminate the threat.
Even if someone inside smuggles him out through the rear, it won’t matter.
Farmers worried about their crops being washed away watched the sky closely.
Everyone else noticed the storm clouds only when raindrops landed on their heads.
The peace that had lasted more than fifty years was long.

Even as Dark Heaven’s concealed blade, planted deep within their ranks long ago, pierced their flesh, they had yet to notice it.

chapters.title: Chapter 1098
paragraphs: The human body holds more information than anyone might imagine.
And Supreme Peak masters, whose five senses have reached their limits, can read what lies behind the slightest change in another person’s expression or movement.
Just like right now.
—So, you’re planning to keep quiet until the very end?
A low Sound Transmission. Eyes so deep I couldn’t guess what lay beneath them.
That alone was enough.
I hadn’t managed to hide my momentary agitation, and the flicker in my eyes was practically a confession.
—What nonsense did that bastard the Blood Lord spout at the last moment?
As Jeok Cheongang’s deep gaze seemed to see through everything, his Sound Transmission coming as if he were spitting out the words, I suddenly realized something.
Even if he hadn’t been one of the world’s foremost Supreme Peak masters, even if I hadn’t let my agitation show, nothing would have changed.
Branches growing from the same root remain connected, however far apart they spread. My old master would have seen straight into his disciple’s heart anyway.
So there was only one answer I could give.
—Maybe getting younger sharpened your hearing.
I’d be lying if I said I hadn’t seen this coming at all.
Jeok Cheongang had once overheard the Roaring Fury Swordsman’s Sound Transmission when the man came to the Jin Family of Taiyuan to threaten me. Then he’d beaten him to a pulp.
But comparing the Roaring Fury Swordsman to the Blood Lord was almost embarrassing.

I’d assumed that even Jeok Cheongang couldn’t make out the Sound Transmission of someone who’d grown stronger still since the Shaolin Bloodshed. When he showed no sign of knowing anything after we returned to the city, I’d secretly felt relieved.
Looking back, though, I’d only had half the answer at best.
“Answer me. Now.”
Jeok Cheongang spoke aloud.
Dozens of pairs of eyes turned toward me at once. I took a deep breath.
Then, at last, I told him the truth.
“You were right. The Blood Lord made me an offer.”
“What offer?”
“He said he’d give me one day. I’m to leave the city alone, sever the sinews and meridians in all four of my limbs myself, and surrender.”
An invisible ripple shivered through the air.
Murmurs rose from the people who were only now grasping what had happened. Jeok Cheongang’s face went stiff as stone.
“And in exchange for your life, he promised to spare everyone else?”
Just as I’d expected.
I nodded with a bitter smile.
“Yes.”
“Why... didn’t you tell me from the start?”
“Because I was thinking it over. If this hadn’t happened, I’d still be thinking it over.”
“Thinking it over? That ridiculous load of crap?”
“The Blood Lord himself swore on the Lord of Heaven’s name. If he keeps his word, everyone’s safety is more than worth one life. Isn’t it?”
The Slaughter Saint frowned when I met his eyes and threw his own words back at him.
“Yes, perhaps. But you’re overlooking the most important thing.”
“What’s that?”
“Trust. Whether you can trust the person you’re making a deal with.”
The Slaughter Saint answered without hesitation, then continued:
“They’ll never keep their promise. When I spoke of taking a gamble earlier, I was betting on my own skill. You’re trying to strike a deal with someone who can’t be trusted in the first place.”
I bit my lip.
Honestly, I didn’t know.
No. Maybe some part of me already did.
Jeok Cheongang and the Slaughter Saint were right. The killing intent the Blood Lord had shown me before making his final offer had been all too real. So had his vow to kill me.
But there was another reason I couldn’t dismiss this absurd deal.
“Right now, the Lord of Heaven wants only one thing. Me.”
Looking back, the Lord of Heaven had always wanted me.
For a very long time.

Otherwise, he wouldn’t have left me alone all this time as I grew stronger by the day—so quickly that the saying “treat someone with new eyes” couldn’t keep up—even though I kept standing in the way of his path to ruling the world.
Why did the Lord of Heaven want me?
I didn’t know.
But I thought I could make out one thing, however dimly.
“To him, I’m more important than anything else right now. Maybe...”
My voice trailed off. The hairs all over my body stood on end, and I let out the breath I’d been holding.
“Even more important than the world itself.”
The truth had become too clear to hide. It was chillingly cold and dark.
Like the air around us, frozen in an instant.
And like the other reason I couldn’t stop weighing his offer.
Whoooosh.
Rain hammered down all around us. I turned my head toward somewhere far to the east.
The sound filling my ears reminded me of water parting around a ship’s prow.
They’re coming.
I couldn’t see them.
But I could feel them.
The final wave that would break the balance of this already-lopsided battlefield—and sweep away every last person in Xining.
Sometimes, there are nights like that.
The birds and insects and even the fish are asleep, and only the moon shines brightly overhead.
The fishermen of the Yangtze liked nights like those.

Whether they cast their nets or not, whether they were fishermen or not, on those nights everyone went down to the river. They’d bathe and set out in boats, filling their cups with cheap strong liquor and drinking their fill.
Grateful for the vast river that had given them so much, they’d row across the moon’s reflection on the water, singing and enjoying a little time for themselves.
There had been a time like that.
There really had.
Splash!
Deep in the night, the pitch-black river split open.
Before the moon emerged from the clouds to see its own face reflected in the water, hundreds of prows covered the surface and surged ahead.
Fiercely. Endlessly.
It was like watching a city move. Like a wave that nothing could stop.
A mighty current that defied the order of heaven and dreamed of defying Heaven itself, one not even the Son of Heaven—the father and ruler of all under it—could stop.
And the countless flags streaming from the swollen sails had long since become objects of fear in their own right.
“What brings you here?”

Leaning against the prow, the old man had been looking silently up at the five characters painted on a flag in bold, imposing strokes: Yangtze River Channel League. Now he turned slowly and added, “Alone, and without sending word.”
At the Seafaring King Pa Ryun’s quiet voice, the subordinate who’d brought the unexpected visitor lowered his head, his face stiff.
“My apologies, Alliance Leader. It’s just—”
“Enough.”
Pa Ryun cut him off with a word, then addressed the visitor standing in the mast’s shadow.
“I said anyone who neglected their duties before we reached our destination would be severely punished. Have you already forgotten?”
The visitor shook his head.
“No.”
“Then did you think my disciple would be an exception?”
“No.”
“Then?”
Thud.
With a heavy step, Ship-Fire Boy Mu Song emerged from the shadows.
“I came to watch the moon with you, Master.”
Watch the moon.
Pa Ryun found himself looking up at the cloud-filled sky. His voice stayed gruff.
“Under the League’s rules, you’ll receive thirty strokes with the oar on deck at dawn.”
Mu Song faltered, then promptly asked, “Wasn’t it twenty?”
“You disobeyed an order and spouted nonsense on top of it. You knew what you were getting into. Thirty.”
“But—”
“Forty.”
Mu Song fell silent. Pa Ryun turned to the subordinate, who was still standing there.
“You neglected your duty as well. Ten strokes.”
“B-But, Alliance Leader—”
“Leave us. I’ll let this matter go.”
The Yangtze River Channel League’s punishment was no ordinary beating.
A Peak master charged with enforcing discipline administered it with an oar of hard birchwood, drenched in water.
He didn’t use internal energy, but ten strokes were enough to leave a man’s backside raw and break several bones. The victim could expect to spend a couple of months in bed.
Yet Seafaring King Pa Ryun’s strictness made no exceptions—not for his own disciple, nor for a subordinate who’d followed him for over thirty years.
In the end, the subordinate left without another word. By the time his presence had completely faded, Pa Ryun, still watching the river split around the ships, spoke abruptly.
“Perhaps I should make it fifty.”
“What?”
“It’s clear whose fault this is. You’re at least ten years younger and in better shape, so you can take his ten strokes for him.”
Mu Song stared at his master, then nodded with a bitter smile.
“I will. Fifty strokes should keep me from moving for three months. Maybe that would be for the best.”
“There’s a barb in your words.”
“Then you heard me right.”
Mu Song took a deep breath and dropped to his knees.
Thump.
“Please. Please reconsider your decision, just this once.”
Before the sound had faded, he pressed his forehead to the deck.
“No matter how I look at it... this isn’t right.”
But even as his Disciple suddenly prostrated himself, the Master kept his eyes on the Yangtze.
“Not right, you say.”
“I know it sounds absurd. I’ve been a bandit since I was a snot-nosed kid, too.”
Pillaging had been Mu Song’s trade.
Ever since he’d taken charge of Water Dragon Stronghold at thirty, he’d led a large family of followers, taking what belonged to others and sharing it with them.
But... he had never wanted this. Not once.
“The Yangtze is being stained with blood. And it’ll keep happening. That wide, blue river we all love.”
Mu Song’s voice had begun to tremble. Pa Ryun suddenly spoke.
“Is that why you led the way in taking so many imperial troops prisoner in the last battle?”
“You knew...?”
“Do you think anything happens on the Yangtze without this old man knowing?”
“It wasn’t only you. The Third Disciple and quite a few senior members pulled much the same trick. Or should I call it insubordination?”
“Master, it wasn’t insubordination. We only—”
“How dare you raise your voice before me?”
Pa Ryun turned and looked down at Mu Song, his gaze dark and steady.
“This old man ordered them killed, and you should have killed them. They were people it was all right to kill.”
“No. There was no need to kill them.”
Had they been strong, Mu Song might not have shown them mercy. He had himself and his followers to protect.
But the imperial troops he’d faced that day had been so weak that spilling their blood frightened him.
“That—that wasn’t a battle. It was a massacre.”
“Yes. That’s what this old man wanted.”
“But in the end, only your Senior Brother and the Elders carried out my orders to the letter.”
Hiss.
Mu Song shuddered.
He had to stop.
Knowing his master’s anger, he ought to stop right now.
But he clenched his teeth and held out against the overwhelming aura bearing down on him.
Someone came to mind.
A man with martial arts strong as hell and a foul temper, who’d put Mu Song through no end of trouble. But he’d also shown Mu Song that even a river bandit like him could pursue chivalry.
Jin Taekyung.
“D-Do you still not understand?”
Struggling to breathe beneath that mighty aura, Mu Song forced the words out.
“Eldest Senior Brother—and those damned Elders, too. They weren’t following you.”
“What?”
“They’re loyal to someone else. Maybe they have been for a long time, M-Mas...”
Thump.
That was as far as he got.
As far as he could endure the aura of Pa Ryun, one of the Ten Kings.
His Disciple had lost consciousness before he could finish speaking. Pa Ryun looked down at him with a deep gaze, then turned back to the river and muttered.
To the tributary of the Yellow River, to be precise, its waters already beginning to turn the color of yellow earth.
“Yes. Better to stay as you are. Even if you stepped in now, nothing would change. Things would only rush toward their end.”
Just then, the moon peeked out between the clouds again, spilling its light over the earth.
At the same time, figures began gathering among the grasses not far from the riverbank.
Thousands of shadows. No, tens of thousands.
A voice, its laugh as faint as moonlight, spoke.
“It does seem a fine night for watching the moon after all.”
Hundreds of ships bearing the Yangtze River Channel League’s flags began preparing to welcome their new allies.

They’d bathe and set out in boats, filling their cups with cheap strong liquor and drinking their fill.
Grateful for the vast river that had given them so much, they’d row across the moon’s reflection on the water, singing and enjoying a little time for themselves.
There had been a time like that.
There really had.
Splash!
Deep in the night, the pitch-black river split open.
Before the moon emerged from the clouds to see its own face reflected in the water, hundreds of prows covered the surface and surged ahead.
Fiercely.
Endlessly.
It was like watching a city move.
Like a wave that nothing could stop.
A mighty current that defied the order of heaven and dreamed of defying Heaven itself, one not even the Son of Heaven—the father and ruler of all under it—could stop.
And the countless flags streaming from the swollen sails had long since become objects of fear in their own right.
“What brings you here?”
Leaning against the prow, the old man had been looking silently up at the five characters painted on a flag in bold, imposing strokes: Yangtze River Channel League.
Now he turned slowly and added, “Alone, and without sending word.”
At the Seafaring King Pa Ryun’s quiet voice, the subordinate who’d brought the unexpected visitor lowered his head, his face stiff.
“My apologies, Alliance Leader.
It’s just—”
“Enough.”
Pa Ryun cut him off with a word, then addressed the visitor standing in the mast’s shadow.
“I said anyone who neglected their duties before we reached our destination would be severely punished.
Have you already forgotten?”
The visitor shook his head.
“No.”
“Then did you think my disciple would be an exception?”
“No.”
“Then?”
Thud.
With a heavy step, Ship-Fire Boy Mu Song emerged from the shadows.
“I came to watch the moon with you, Master.”
Watch the moon.
Pa Ryun found himself looking up at the cloud-filled sky.
His voice stayed gruff.
“Under the League’s rules, you’ll receive thirty strokes with the oar on deck at dawn.”
Mu Song faltered, then promptly asked, “Wasn’t it twenty?”
“You disobeyed an order and spouted nonsense on top of it.
You knew what you were getting into.
Thirty.”
“But—”
“Forty.”
Mu Song fell silent.
Pa Ryun turned to the subordinate, who was still standing there.
“You neglected your duty as well.
Ten strokes.”
“B-But, Alliance Leader—”
“Leave us.
I’ll let this matter go.”
The Yangtze River Channel League’s punishment was no ordinary beating.
A Peak master charged with enforcing discipline administered it with an oar of hard birchwood, drenched in water.
He didn’t use internal energy, but ten strokes were enough to leave a man’s backside raw and break several bones.
The victim could expect to spend a couple of months in bed.
Yet Seafaring King Pa Ryun’s strictness made no exceptions—not for his own disciple, nor for a subordinate who’d followed him for over thirty years.
In the end, the subordinate left without another word.
By the time his presence had completely faded, Pa Ryun, still watching the river split around the ships, spoke abruptly.
“Perhaps I should make it fifty.”
“What?”
“It’s clear whose fault this is.
You’re at least ten years younger and in better shape, so you can take his ten strokes for him.”
Mu Song stared at his master, then nodded with a bitter smile.
“I will.
Fifty strokes should keep me from moving for three months.
Maybe that would be for the best.”
“There’s a barb in your words.”
“Then you heard me right.”
Mu Song took a deep breath and dropped to his knees.
Thump.
“Please.
Please reconsider your decision, just this once.”
Before the sound had faded, he pressed his forehead to the deck.
“No matter how I look at it... this isn’t right.”
But even as his Disciple suddenly prostrated himself, the Master kept his eyes on the Yangtze.
“Not right, you say.”
“I know it sounds absurd.
I’ve been a bandit since I was a snot-nosed kid, too.”
Pillaging had been Mu Song’s trade.
Ever since he’d taken charge of Water Dragon Stronghold at thirty, he’d led a large family of followers, taking what belonged to others and sharing it with them.
But... he had never wanted this.
Not once.
“The Yangtze is being stained with blood.
And it’ll keep happening.
That wide, blue river we all love.”
Mu Song’s voice had begun to tremble.
Pa Ryun suddenly spoke.
“Is that why you led the way in taking so many imperial troops prisoner in the last battle?”
“You knew...?”
“Do you think anything happens on the Yangtze without this old man knowing?”
“It wasn’t only you.
The Third Disciple and quite a few senior members pulled much the same trick.
Or should I call it insubordination?”
“Master, it wasn’t insubordination.
We only—”
“How dare you raise your voice before me?”
Pa Ryun turned and looked down at Mu Song, his gaze dark and steady.
“This old man ordered them killed, and you should have killed them.
They were people it was all right to kill.”
“No.
There was no need to kill them.”
Had they been strong, Mu Song might not have shown them mercy.
He had himself and his followers to protect.
But the imperial troops he’d faced that day had been so weak that spilling their blood frightened him.
“That—that wasn’t a battle.
It was a massacre.”
“Yes.
That’s what this old man wanted.”
“But in the end, only your Senior Brother and the Elders carried out my orders to the letter.”
Hiss.
Mu Song shuddered.
He had to stop.
Knowing his master’s anger, he ought to stop right now.
But he clenched his teeth and held out against the overwhelming aura bearing down on him.
Someone came to mind.
A man with martial arts strong as hell and a foul temper, who’d put Mu Song through no end of trouble.
But he’d also shown Mu Song that even a river bandit like him could pursue chivalry.
Jin Taekyung.
“D-Do you still not understand?”
Struggling to breathe beneath that mighty aura, Mu Song forced the words out.
“Eldest Senior Brother—and those damned Elders, too.
They weren’t following you.”
“What?”
“They’re loyal to someone else.
Maybe they have been for a long time, M-Mas...”
Thump.
That was as far as he got.
As far as he could endure the aura of Pa Ryun, one of the Ten Kings.
His Disciple had lost consciousness before he could finish speaking.
Pa Ryun looked down at him with a deep gaze, then turned back to the river and muttered.
To the tributary of the Yellow River, to be precise, its waters already beginning to turn the color of yellow earth.
“Yes.
Better to stay as you are.
Even if you stepped in now, nothing would change.
Things would only rush toward their end.”
Just then, the moon peeked out between the clouds again, spilling its light over the earth.
At the same time, figures began gathering among the grasses not far from the riverbank.
Thousands of shadows.
No, tens of thousands.
A voice, its laugh as faint as moonlight, spoke.
“It does seem a fine night for watching the moon after all.”
Hundreds of ships bearing the Yangtze River Channel League’s flags began preparing to welcome their new allies.

chapters.title: Chapter 1099
paragraphs: That night was unusually long.
Maybe it was the torrential rain, which showed no sign of letting up. Or maybe it was the dark clouds that still hadn’t budged after several shichen.
The meeting dragged on beneath them, in an atmosphere so stifling that it didn’t end until the hour of the Rabbit.
“Only one final battle remains. I ask every Great Hero here to rest well and carry out the duties entrusted to you.”
I sounded far more formal than usual.
But not one of the leaders gathered there seemed uncomfortable with my new manner—or with a junior so far beneath them presiding over the meeting.
Anyone who might have stirred up trouble had already been replaced.
The eminent masters and generals of Qinghai Murim paid their respects with courtesy and resolve, then left to carry out their respective duties.
All except one old Daoist, who was still sipping from a cup of tea that had gone cold long ago.
“Nothing tastes worse than cold tea. What do you say? Shall this old man warm it up for you?”
Jeok Cheongang stopped on his way out to make the offer. The old Daoist shook his head.
“Cold tea has its own flavor, as does hot tea. Besides...”
His voice was as airy as drifting clouds. He turned to me with a smile.
“Why trouble Senior when I could ask this young Fellow Daoist here?”
Anyone else might have thought he was just playing with words. Cheongheoja—the old Daoist, and Sect Leader of the Kunlun Sect—could easily have warmed the tea himself with Samadhi True Fire.
But his answer was a roundabout refusal. He still had something to discuss with me alone.
Jeok Cheongang understood.
“Spouting airy nonsense. A Daoist through and through. Do as you please.”
He gave a quiet snort and left. Once we were alone, Cheongheoja picked up the teapot.
“Would you care for a cup, Fellow Daoist?”
I didn’t know what he wanted to say, but I had no reason to refuse.
“I’d be grateful.”
“No need for gratitude.”
Cheongheoja smiled faintly as he poured. I took a polite sip, and a taste I couldn’t quite describe, along with a bitter aroma, filled my mouth.
“Well? How is it?”
“Uh, cold.”
“And?”
“Bitter. Really bitter.”
“I often drink it cold. I should have warmed it to suit your taste.”
“Mm. It’s fine. Tea doesn’t really suit my taste even when it’s warm.”
“Is that so? I put a good deal of effort into growing those tea leaves.”
Why the hell would he wait until now to tell me that?
Cheongheoja burst into hearty laughter at the look on my face.
“I’m joking. I do tend my own tea garden, but in a situation that urgent, why would I have packed tea leaves?”
“Oh.”
I shook my head as I realized he’d caught me. Of course it made no sense to bring tea leaves when a hundred thousand enemies were bearing down on Mount Kunlun.
It wasn’t as if he were Geum Jandi, honorary Sect Leader.
“You got me. I didn’t know you were like this.”
“Likewise.”
“Pardon?”
Before I could ask what he meant, Cheongheoja smiled and went on.

“You have many sides to you, Fellow Daoist. When you uprooted the Qinghai City Lord and his faction in one stroke, you seemed like a Great General who could command the world. At other times, you seem an immature hero who leaves everything to his emotions. Yet in the end, you have the bearing of a grand master whom everyone can’t help but follow.”
Hmm.
What was I supposed to say to that?
Embarrassed by the sudden praise, I scratched my chin.
“You’re too kind.”
“No one would think so. At least, no one who has ever met that person.”
That person.
I knew who he meant from the reverence in those two words. Cheongheoja spoke slowly.
“The Martial God. The greatest grand master of any age. Though his whereabouts have long been a mystery... I sensed something of him in you, Fellow Daoist.”
A thought occurred to me.
Maybe Cheongheoja’s words touched on a truth that was growing clearer in my mind.
Someone who had crossed between the modern world and Murim before me.
A Player who had roamed this world—a world that truly existed somewhere among the endless dimensions—as if it were a game.
Maybe that was why a murmur escaped me before I could stop it.
“...Maybe.”
“Hmm?”
“No, nothing. I just meant I’d like to become like him.”

It was a flimsy excuse even to me, but Cheongheoja didn’t seem to dwell on what I’d said. My voice had been barely audible, and unlike the Martial God, whose very existence was a mystery, my origins were known.
“I see. I believe you could.”
He nodded without a hint of suspicion, took another sip of tea, and added, “Unlike a certain Daoist who devoted his whole life to the task and never even reached the man’s feet.”
Cheongheoja had lived a life of great renown, both as the Kunlun Sect Leader and as a Daoist. Yet his self-deprecating voice held a regret I couldn’t place.

“The Martial God was a truly great man. He always concealed his appearance with a disguise technique and never properly revealed his true identity. Even so, everyone under heaven trusted and followed him.”
Cheongheoja wasn’t belittling his own accomplishments or martial arts by comparing them to the Martial God’s. He was talking about character, tolerance, and leadership.
And the conversation was drawing closer to the real reason he’d wanted to speak with me.
“Of course, even he wasn’t perfect. Dark Heaven’s schemes had taken root out of sight long ago.”
“Do you think this wouldn’t be happening if he were still here?”
“Of course. I lack the gift for reading the heavens that Master Hong Dao had before he passed away, but I’m certain Dark Heaven would have thought differently if the Martial God were still with us.”
Cheongheoja answered firmly, then sighed.
“But I could never become like him. The age of turmoil that drenched the world in blood ended, and peace came. Yet I couldn’t properly lead even my own sect, let alone all under heaven.”
I frowned before I could help it.
Don’t tell me...
My instincts said this was no small matter. What he was about to tell me might be crucial to the coming battle.
Cheongheoja noticed the change in my expression and stroked his teacup with a bitter look.
“Until now... I didn’t mind if the tea was cold as ice. I thought that if I could swallow it—if I could accept it that way—it would be enough.”
Until now.
He had definitely said until now.
“I take it that’s changed.”
“It has. If the cold made this old man sick, that would be one thing. But I can’t let hundreds of thousands of people suffer stomachaches, can I?”
“Hundreds of thousands...?”
At those words, I knew for certain.
There was a traitor inside Xining.
Dark Heaven had hidden a sword deep within our ranks—close to us.
Along with that realization, Cheongheoja’s low voice pierced my ears.
Now I understood why he’d wanted to be alone with me. Why he looked so pained and sounded so bitter toward himself.
“It’s my fault. I failed to teach that child properly.”
As I stared at him wide-eyed, the old Daoist with an unworthy Disciple silently raised his teacup.
By then, he had heated it with Samadhi True Fire.
Fwoosh.
Warmth spread through the air. Steam rose from the tea as Cheongheoja drank it slowly. Then he spoke, his voice heavier than I had ever heard it.
“I have a favor to ask.”
At that moment—
Ding.
A System alert rang in my ears, and a translucent holographic window appeared before my eyes.
And then... a day passed.
The air in Xining was heavier and colder than ever.

Only a few days ago, the townspeople had smiled as they welcomed the newly arrived reinforcements. Now their faces were as dark as the sky overhead, as though they had some dim sense of the future before them.
Destruction and death.
The erasure of every living thing that would come at the end.
But who was it that said humans were creatures of hope? That they found their greatest strength when something was being taken from them, not when they sought to take from others?
And so they had not fallen into utter despair.
Here and now, with the last sliver of hope and yearning in their hearts, they looked toward the saviors who would light up the darkness settling all around them.
Splash. Splash.
Dozens of people marched in step, sending up splashes from rainwater that had risen to their calves.
The rain was still falling so hard it obscured their vision. Yet the countless townspeople filling the main road made way for them, scarcely daring to breathe.
Whoooosh.
Amid the clamor of the rain, the human tide slowly parted.
At the head of the procession, striding without hesitation through the countless people, was one man.
A young giant who had already carved his name into the minds of the people under heaven and the martial artists of Murim.
Jin Taekyung.
By now, everyone knew him.
Some might remember the young man as the Marquis of Shangshan; others might know him by his sobriquet, the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon.
But however they saw him, one fact would not change.
Today’s battle, and the name Jin Taekyung, would enter the long record of history.
Even if his story ended in a hollow, miserable death.
“Fuck, did a hole open up in the sky or something?”
The young giant muttered the coarse curse almost too quietly to hear. Anyone who overheard him would have been shocked. He lifted his head.
The sky was dark.
Dark as fucking hell.
“Just the kind of weather I don’t want to die in.”
With a rueful snort, Jin Taekyung watched the shapes drawing closer through the distant rain.
A horrifyingly vast enemy army.
And at that moment—
Wooooong.
The opening shot of a battle that would decide the fate of Qinghai—perhaps of all under heaven—cut through the air.
Shhheeeek!
Hundreds of ice spikes.

chapters.title: Chapter 1100
paragraphs: Someone once said that people feel the greatest wonder and fear when they come face-to-face with the unknown.
When they encounter something they’ve never experienced before and see it for what it is, every emotion is pushed to its extreme.
Jin Taekyung wholeheartedly agreed.
He also agreed with something a certain philosopher had said: Humans are creatures of learning.
Whooosh!
Hundreds of ice spikes shot through the curtain of rain amid a tremendous surge of energy.
Yet even as the powerful, wide-ranging spell took shape, Jin Taekyung didn’t flinch.
He’d expected it.
“Defend!”
The instant his shout, infused with deep reserves of internal energy, burst from between his lips—
Shhk! Fwssh!
Shields rose in a wave above the allies packed shoulder to shoulder along the high city wall. At the same time, brilliant beams of light shot up from all along it toward the hundreds of ice spikes.
Boom!
A thunderous crash. A flash of light.
The spikes shattered under the Sword Energy unleashed by the Peak masters, and fragments ricocheted toward the wall at high speed. But that was all.
Clang! Clang!
The massive rectangular shields, clad in steel on the outside, did their job.
If the spikes had retained their full force, things might have been different. But after that first blow had weakened them, the fragments couldn’t break through the solid wall of shields.
“Everyone’s safe!”
Excited reports came from all around.
But Jin Taekyung, who had anticipated the attack and prepared for it, didn’t let his guard down.
They’d gotten the battle off to a good start. Holding off magic—something almost indistinguishable from a supernatural miracle in this world—had lifted their morale, too. That was no small gain.
But Jin Taekyung knew better than anyone that this was only the beginning.
So did the Grand Sorceress and the Blood Lord, watching from beyond the wall.
“Loose!”
At the forceful shout, the signalers on the wall waved their flags to pass along the command. Arrows that had gleamed from between the shields finally left their taut bowstrings.
Whooosh!
Thousands of arrows poured down, blackening a swath of the sky.
They were meant to pierce the throats of the enemies advancing below—the merciless invaders.
But the defenders’ desperate hopes came to nothing the moment the red lips hidden behind a veil in the distance moved.
“O invisible veil.”
There is a power in human speech that no one can explain.
A mage’s spoken command gives that power form.
Fwoom.
An invisible wall forced its way between spaces and split the air.
It was a powerful protective spell, one that steel arrowheads could never pierce.
Crack!
Thousands of arrowheads snapped or bounced away in an instant.
The people on the wall gasped at the impossible sight. But the woman responsible remained as calm as ever.
“They’ve prepared thoroughly enough. Their countermeasures aren’t bad, either.”
At the Grand Sorceress’s murmur, the Blood Lord spoke quietly.
“Of course. They have to fight with everything they’ve got.”
“Don’t you think we gave them more time than we needed to?”
“That’s a pointless thing to say. You know better than anyone this is the surest way. And besides...”
The Blood Lord looked calmly at the Grand Sorceress.
“You used that time to prepare, too.”
She gave a short laugh and nodded.
Her slender white fingers were already forming a hand seal. The movement looked perfectly gentle, but it held another spell of terrible destructive power.
Rumble.
The air began to tremble. Strange patterns etched beneath the Grand Sorceress’s feet flared with light in a multitude of colors.
There were dozens of them: Magic Formations she had prepared over the past two days for this battle.
“So, what do you want?” she asked.
The Blood Lord briefly considered the question.
What do I want?
Jin Taekyung’s death, of course.
But he had to swallow the words welling up in his throat.
That stupid bitch would never defy that person’s will, and even he had no idea how she would react if she learned what he was thinking.
So he forced himself to answer calmly.
“The wall. Aim for the wall. Hit it hard enough to bring it down in one blow.”
The Dalai Lama, who had listened to their exchange in silence like a docile lamb, suddenly spoke.
“If the wall falls before the rear is completely sealed off, won’t the enemies give up resisting and flee?”
His suggestion sounded reasonable at first, but neither the Blood Lord nor the Grand Sorceress paid it the slightest mind.
Bringing the wall down wasn’t their only reason for targeting it first.
Fwoosh.
The Grand Sorceress slowly extended a hand. High overhead, the rain pouring endlessly from the sky stopped at her will, then began to gather.
By the time it had formed dozens of enormous spheres of water, she spoke again.
“Fly.”
At her quiet command, the spheres hurtled toward the wall. Each carried the weight and force of ten thousand geun, surging forward with a speed and momentum that seemed to brook no interference.
ROOOAR!
That was when the archers, who had been firing without pause at the approaching enemy, stared with their mouths open. The shield bearers guarding the front lowered their shields without realizing it.
At last, they stepped forward.
Whoosh!
Dazzling flashes cut through the air.
Some were as hot as lava. Others were stealthy enough to send a chill down the back of the neck. Still others were as swift as lightning.
By the time the martial artists and imperial troops on the wall sensed them, it was over.
Fwoosh! Boom!
The enormous spheres of water evaporated, were sliced apart, and burst.
Spheres that had looked capable of flattening a mountain, let alone the city wall. Terrifying calamities that had seemed as impossible for a human to stop as a natural disaster.
Those who’d instinctively sensed their imminent deaths opened their eyes wide in unison.
At the same time, they remembered something they had momentarily forgotten.
Those terrifying dark arts called magic weren’t the only thing beyond human power.
“They’re coming in hard from the start.”

Across the world, only ten great martial artists had earned the right to a king’s throne. Jeok Cheongang, the Fire King, held the highest seat among them, shoulder to shoulder with the stars in the heavens.
He spat out some phlegm and grinned.
“How’d they know this old man likes that sort of thing?”
His voice rumbled like a beast’s growl, and warmth rose in the people’s chests.
The tiny spark of hope, beginning to stir again, blazed brighter still when the giants who appeared next came into view.
“They’re trying to wear down our key fighters.”
He looked more like a boy than a young man. But everyone knew now that the boy, who still looked as if he hadn’t even lost all his baby fuzz, was the Slaughter Saint, once revered by all.
They knew, too, that another man whose legend could rival his stood among them.
“Obvious, but effective.”
The voice was clearer than raindrops. At odds with it, a rough finger drew back a bowstring.
Whoosh!
A beam of light shot forth.
And then, destruction.
Crack!
The beam shattered the invisible protective veil over the enemy forces in an instant, then exploded with a thunderous roar.
It tore through the ground and pierced the enemies beneath it.
BOOM!
The ground shook. The blast swallowed their screams.
Neither the hulking monsters moving like little hills nor the Dark Heaven followers advancing behind them under their cover could withstand that One Strike.
The name Bow Saint was no empty boast.
We can do this.
A glimmer of hope flashed through the minds of the people on the wall, and they trembled with emotion.
They saw the radiance of those who had not lost their light, even in a world this dark.
They saw the other Supreme Peak masters stepping forward to block the magic that kept crashing toward the wall, and Jin Taekyung, who remained completely unfazed even in this dire situation.
They were moved. They shuddered.
They stood shoulder to shoulder with living legends, and those legends were giving everything they had to save them.
Thud. Thud-thud. Thud-thud-thud!
A massive rumble rippled outward like a wave.
As if they had all agreed to it, they stamped their feet. They slammed down their shields, beat their spear shafts, and struck their swords and sabers together.
Even as a fierce rain of fire poured down. Even as lightning flashed and ice bearing a terrible chill came flying at them. Even as the rain that should have soaked their heads turned to arrows.
They did not yield.
No—they never doubted that, whatever end awaited them here today, they too would become part of the legend.
And as the little sparks in their hearts grew into a great torch—
Rumble!
The hulking monsters, who’d steadily advanced despite the relentless rain of arrows and other attacks, charged toward the wall with a roar like an earthquake.
—GRAAAAH!
Their roar made the defenders’ hair stand on end.
At the same instant, one of the monsters launched its body forward with strength and speed far beyond human limits and slammed into the wall with all its might.
RUMBLE!

When they encounter something they’ve never experienced before and see it for what it is, every emotion is pushed to its extreme.
Jin Taekyung wholeheartedly agreed.
He also agreed with something a certain philosopher had said: Humans are creatures of learning.
Whooosh!
Hundreds of ice spikes shot through the curtain of rain amid a tremendous surge of energy.
Yet even as the powerful, wide-ranging spell took shape, Jin Taekyung didn’t flinch.
He’d expected it.
“Defend!”
The instant his shout, infused with deep reserves of internal energy, burst from between his lips—
Shhk!
Fwssh!
Shields rose in a wave above the allies packed shoulder to shoulder along the high city wall.
At the same time, brilliant beams of light shot up from all along it toward the hundreds of ice spikes.
Boom!
A thunderous crash.
A flash of light.
The spikes shattered under the Sword Energy unleashed by the Peak masters, and fragments ricocheted toward the wall at high speed.
But that was all.
Clang!
Clang!
The massive rectangular shields, clad in steel on the outside, did their job.
If the spikes had retained their full force, things might have been different.
But after that first blow had weakened them, the fragments couldn’t break through the solid wall of shields.
“Everyone’s safe!”
Excited reports came from all around.

They’d gotten the battle off to a good start.
Holding off magic—something almost indistinguishable from a supernatural miracle in this world—had lifted their morale, too.
That was no small gain.

So did the Grand Sorceress and the Blood Lord, watching from beyond the wall.
“Loose!”

Arrows that had gleamed from between the shields finally left their taut bowstrings.
Whooosh!
Thousands of arrows poured down, blackening a swath of the sky.
They were meant to pierce the throats of the enemies advancing below—the merciless invaders.

“O invisible veil.”
There is a power in human speech that no one can explain.
A mage’s spoken command gives that power form.

An invisible wall forced its way between spaces and split the air.

Crack!

The people on the wall gasped at the impossible sight.

“They’ve prepared thoroughly enough.
Their countermeasures aren’t bad, either.”

“Of course.
They have to fight with everything they’ve got.”
“Don’t you think we gave them more time than we needed to?”
“That’s a pointless thing to say.
You know better than anyone this is the surest way.
